EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of heavy rain fell across the northern mountains of West Virginia during the pre-dawn hours of the 17th. Of particular interest were three downpours that moved across the upper basin of the Middle Fork of the Tygart Valley River between midnight and 7 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Generally 2 to 3.5 inches of rain fell across the upper portions of the Tygart Valley River basin. No flooding occurred, partly because local creeks and streams were running fairly low at the start of the rainfall. However, this is where the story gets interesting. The 17th was a Friday, and by mid afternoon, a dozen or more locals were swimming and hanging out on the large rocks and islands in the Middle Fork River as it meanders through Audra State Park. The water from the morning rainfall arrived into Audra State Park between 3 and 4 o'clock that afternoon. Water levels rose rapidly as the crest approached, catching those in the river by surprise. Witness accounts say the water rose 4-5 feet in under an hour, with swiftly flowing current cutting off access or even submerging some of the rock outcroppings. Three separate water rescues were performed by first responders, who rescued a total of 12 individuals.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large upper ridge over the southwestern U.S. strengthened over California during the weekend of July 11 and 12 providing the Kern County Deserts with a period of excessive heat and the San Joaquin Valley, West Side Hills and Sierra foothills with a period of significant heat. Afternoon temperatures were well into the triple digits in these areas during the weekend although no new records were set. Temperatures lowered some on July 13 in reponse to the ridge breaking down as a trough moved through the Pacific Northwest.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Daytime highs ranged between 104 and 108 degrees on July 11 and July 12.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. Numerous reports of hail and wind damage were received along with some minor flash flooding due to heavy rainfall.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were downed onto the road along Highway 13 between Port Wing and the Bayfield/Douglas County Line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan on the evening of April 7th to far-southwestern Ontario Province by very early morning of April 8th. The accompanying warm front initially extended east-southeastward from the low and across Lake Erie. This warm front moved northward to the northern lakeshore by very early morning of the 8th. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front moved southeastward to far-western Lake Erie. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward across Lake Erie during the late evening of the 7th. Elevated weak to primarily moderate most-unstable CAPE and strong vertical wind shear allowed the squall line to remain organized as it crossed the relatively-cool waters of Lake Erie. Despite a cool and stable marine boundary layer reducing the strength of downdrafts, gale force wind gusts occurred along or just behind the squall line's downshear gust front as it came ashore in northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: C-MAN Station MRHO1 at Marblehead measured a 38 kt marine thunderstorm wind gust.

This was one three separate storm that produced severe hail in Amarillo on this day. In addition, several small and weak landspout type tornadoes were reported with these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball size hail fell 6 miles northeast of Washburn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense low pressure system crossed into the Ohio Valley during the early morning hours on the 13th, with a strong line of thunderstorms aligned along a surface cold front. Multiple areas saw tree and structural damage with these storms. A tightened pressure gradient formed over the state, inflicting strong synoptic winds outside of the thunderstorms. Numerous trees were blown down, knocking power out to multiple areas. Near Mt. Hope in NW Fayette County, a 50 foot section of brick wall collapsed at the municipal stadium. Other buildings sustained roof damage around Mt. Hope. Nearby, the Beckley ASOS gusted to 53 mph. Many personal and DOT weather stations measured gusts around 50 mph across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down in the towns of Mount Nebo, Summersville, Nettie, Snow Hill, and Birch River. In the town of Prosperity, a trampoline was blown up onto a power pole and hung up along the power lines. The ASOS at the Beckley airport observed a maximum wind gust of 53 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mainly penny size hail but a few hailstones to quarter size. Hail fell for around 15 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: MD-289 was closed north of John Hanson Rd due to downed trees and wires. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary was draped in the area of southern New Jersey and Delmarva on July 30. Meanwhile, another cold front was approaching the region from the northwest. A warm and very humid air mass developed ahead of this second front, leading to the development of moderate to strong instability over much of the mid-Atlantic. The approach of the front also gradually increased wind shear values, though greater shear remained further north over New York and New England. Nonetheless, frontal forcing in the unstable air mass was sufficient to trigger scattered thunderstorms, some of which became strong to severe and produced a number of reports of damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were reported down near Zieglrersville. Time estimated from radar.

An upper level ridge of high pressure centered over the Southern Plains began to amplify and expand north-northeast into the Plains and Mississippi Valley through the middle portions of July, resulting in increased subsidence and hence, hotter temperatures as readings climbed into the mid to upper 90s across much of the Ark-La-Tex. A weak surface boundary became stationary on the 13th across portions of Northeast Texas, Southern Arkansas, and North Louisiana, which resulted in low level moisture pooling near and south of this boundary. Thus, very oppressive heat indices were observed across much of Northeast Texas on the 13th, with heat indices ranging from 110-112 degrees.

Thunderstorms developed over the deserts to the west of Phoenix during the afternoon hours on July 23rd and some of the stronger storms generated locally heavy rainfall. The heavy rain was sufficient to lead to an episode of flash flooding to the southwest of Phoenix, between Gila Bend and Buckeye, just to the west of Highway 85. The flash flooding resulted in the closure of old Highway 80 about 15 miles southwest of Buckeye. The highway was closed by Rainbow Wash and the flooding was captured on video by a trained spotter. There were no reports of accidents or injury due to the flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms with heavy rain developed to the southwest of Phoenix during the afternoon hours on July 23rd, resulting in an episode of flash flooding approximately 15 miles to the southwest of the town of Buckeye. Flash flooding resulted in the closure of old US 80 at Rainbow Wash at about 1515MST. The wash quickly rose over 3.5 feet. The timing of the flooding was based on stream gage data from the Maricopa County Flood Control network. Flash flooding was observed on video by a trained weather spotter; he could see the flood waters moving through the wash and approaching highway 80. There were no reports of accidents or injury due to the flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Energy rotating around an upper level low over the northeast resulted in the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple water rescues were conducted due to flash flooding on Frank E Rodgers Boulevard South south of Bergen Street in Harrison.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large healthy tree was split on the 2000 block of Foxwood Country Club Run on the north side of Normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As monsoonal moisture continued to stream into New Mexico, a backdoor cold front that moved through eastern NM helped set the stage for severe weather on July 15, 2020. With increasing low-level moisture, instability, and shear focused along this boundary, the storms that moved off the central mountain chain interacted with the boundary and intensified. Through the afternoon and evening hours, the storms grew upscale into a broken line that moved northeast through the eastern plains. Strong thunderstorm winds were reported ahead of these storms while large hail was reported near Capulin. A brief gustnado was also observed in rural Socorro County along a strong outflow boundary moving through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters near Capulin reported hail up to ping pong size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The center of upper level high pressure continued moving west into Arizona by the end of July while moisture was recharged across the state behind a strong back door cold front. North to south steering flow with abundant shear and instability led to the development of numerous showers and storms during the early to mid afternoon hours. Several of these storms were strong to severe as they progressed southward across the eastern plains and through the Rio Grande Valley. A storm near Las Vegas dumped hail up to the size of golf balls with very heavy rainfall and strong winds. Another storm moved south across Interstate 25 near San Jose and produced quarter size hail. Storms that developed over the Jemez Mountains moved south through Cochiti Pueblo with quarter size hail before blasting through the Albuquerque metro area with damaging winds and heavy rainfall. Ruidoso also experienced severe weather with quarter size hail and heavy rainfall. Minor flooding was reported in many areas as well. Swift runoff into the urban drainage system in Albuquerque washed two individuals down the Embudo Arroyo. One individual was rescued however the other died in the flood waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel size hail was observed at the Pecos River RV Campground as a severe thunderstorm continued to move south through San Miguel County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from June 2020 continued in July.

Airtankers and helicopters supported the hotshot crews on the fireline through the day. A pilot died on July 7 when his helicopter crashed while transporting supplies for fire fighting operations.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At least ten pine trees down four miles SSE of Perry Heights.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front sagged south into the Mid-South during the day on May 3, 2020. A potent,  quick-moving shortwave interacted with this front and convection developed across Missouri by noon. The airmass across the Mid-South was moderately unstable with fairly strong wind shear in place.  The convection formed into a bow echo and intensified as it raced across the northern Mid-South during the afternoon hours. Damaging winds were widespread. By early evening additional storms developed across West Tennessee and produced large hail.

Most locations did not receive any precipitation with this front, but a few favored upslope areas in the Sierra did record up to about 0.10 inches of liquid-equivalent precipitation. A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report via social media with photo of hail a little larger than quarter size. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lower Alloways Creek New Jersey Weathenet station.

Nonetheless, frontal forcing in the unstable air mass was sufficient to trigger scattered thunderstorms, some of which became strong to severe and produced a number of reports of damaging winds.

Showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon across northeast New Jersey ahead of an approaching backdoor cold front. With relatively weak flow aloft, these storms moved slowly, resulting in heavy rain across some areas. CoCoRaHS observations indicate a widespread 0.5-2 inches of rain in areas that received storms, with the ASOS at Teterboro Airport reporting 2.89 inches of rain. Much of this rain fell over a 1-2 hour time period, resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple mPING reports of streets flooded and vehicles stranded in Bogota.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms developed in a hot and humid airmass across north-central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of July 7th.  One of the cells produced gusty winds and minor damage in Eureka in Woodford County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few 2 to 4-inch diameter tree limbs were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving isolated thunderstorm dropped 1 to 2 inches of rain in a short amount of time across northeast Champaign County during the late afternoon of July 9th, leading to widespread flash flooding in Rantoul.  Meanwhile further west, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the Mississippi River ahead of an approaching cold front.  These storms pushed into the Illinois River Valley, producing scattered wind damage and flash flooding.  The line weakened as it tracked further eastward across the I-55 corridor later in the evening: however, one cell produced damaging downburst winds in northern Piatt County around midnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads were covered with water and impassable in Rantoul.  Up to 4 feet of water flowed across some roads.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The center of upper level high pressure continued moving west into Arizona by the end of July while moisture was recharged across the state behind a strong back door cold front. North to south steering flow with abundant shear and instability led to the development of numerous showers and storms during the early to mid afternoon hours. Several of these storms were strong to severe as they progressed southward across the eastern plains and through the Rio Grande Valley. A storm near Las Vegas dumped hail up to the size of golf balls with very heavy rainfall and strong winds. Another storm moved south across Interstate 25 near San Jose and produced quarter size hail. Storms that developed over the Jemez Mountains moved south through Cochiti Pueblo with quarter size hail before blasting through the Albuquerque metro area with damaging winds and heavy rainfall. Ruidoso also experienced severe weather with quarter size hail and heavy rainfall. Minor flooding was reported in many areas as well. Swift runoff into the urban drainage system in Albuquerque washed two individuals down the Embudo Arroyo. One individual was rescued however the other died in the flood waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A weather station near Tome-Adelino recorded a 59 mph wind gust as a severe thunderstorm continued to track south through the Rio Grande Valley.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep tap of monsoon moisture continued surging north into New Mexico on July 24, 2020, setting the stage for additional showers and thunderstorms with torrential rainfall, localized flash flooding, and strong microburst winds. Storms developed early in the afternoon then moved slowly north to northwest across most of New Mexico. Several of these thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall amounts over two inches along with small hail and strong microburst winds. The Clayton airport reported a peak wind gust up to 59 mph and the Roswell airport reported a peak wind gust up to 68 mph. Straight-line winds damaged power lines, power poles, roofs, fences, and trees in the area around Midway. Heavy rainfall around Alamo damaged culverts and roadways in the area. A flash flood near Lemitar washed a pickup truck into an arroyo and caused damage to roadways. Fortunately, no injuries occurred with these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Clayton airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from June 2020 continued in July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of northern Minnesota have seen rainfall deficits in excess of 5 inches for the year and by July areas of Severe Drought (D2) were observed across parts of the area. A wet middle part of July led to improving conditions that brought all areas into the Moderate Drought (D1) category by the end of the month, however, rainfall deficits persist and further dry conditions may reverse the improving trend.

However, it was enough to lift the area out of the Severe Drought category (D2), especially with the rainfall received on July 21, when around 1 to 1.50 inches fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex pulled a pair of fronts across the area during the afternoon and evening near the time of peak heating. Precipitable water values were between 1.75 and 2 inches, which resulted in torrential rainfall in concert with severe thunderstorm development.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.

The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind damaged the roof of a home, and destroyed a metal carport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Friday, July 24th, was one of the hottest and most humid days of 2020. Afternoon high temperatures ranged from the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the middle 70s to lower 80s. During the early evening, thunderstorms broke out along two lines, one from Bismarck to northwest of Grand Forks, and the other from Bismarck to west of Fargo. By the late evening, the strongest storms along both lines were converging toward Grand Forks. This brought a period of very strong winds to eastern Grand Forks and eastern Walsh counties, continuing up toward the Lake of the Woods region. Meanwhile, another cluster of storms over south central North Dakota moved east-northeast, tracking through the Fargo-Moorhead area and into west central Minnesota during the overnight hours. These storms also produced some strong wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were blown down between Kabekona and Benedict lakes.

During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front sagged south into the Mid-South during the day on May 3, 2020. A potent,  quick-moving shortwave interacted with this front and convection developed across Missouri by noon. The airmass across the Mid-South was moderately unstable with fairly strong wind shear in place.  The convection formed into a bow echo and intensified as it raced across the northern Mid-South during the afternoon hours. Damaging winds were widespread. By early evening additional storms developed across West Tennessee and produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on Sage Meadows Golf Course.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front stalled across the Mid-South started to lift north as low pressure tracked into southwest Missouri. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level disturbance tracked across the region and triggered thunderstorms across Missouri. The airmass across the Mid-South was ripe for severe storms with strong shear and instability in place. Clusters of severe storms moved into northern parts of the Mid-South by mid-afternoon and moved east-southeast through the evening hours producing damaging winds and hail. A macroburst occurred in the Missouri Bootheel producing widespread wind damage. This was the second day in a row that northern sections of the Mid-South suffered widespread severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A macroburst struck portions of Dunklin County with widespread wind damage from Campbell to Clarkton. Numerous trees and power lines were knocked down. There was significant damage to a building in Campbell.  A warehouse suffered major damage in Clarkton and a center pivot irrigation system was overturned. The Lynn Oak Church also suffered damage.  A train was derailed along Highway 62 near the Arkansas state line, closing the highway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported quarter-size hail in Canton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing warm front promoted heavy rain and thunderstorms during the afternoon of March 28th. Substantial breaks in the clouds south of the boundary, along with substantial warm air advection, resulted in around 1500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE,  and substantial (60kts+) effective shear was in place across the region. Hail growth increased into the evening as effective wind shear increased to 70kts over eastern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail reported through social media; picture provided.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid-level trough in split flow moved out of the southwestern U.S. on the morning of April 12, and phased with a strong northern stream trough across the northern Plains by April 13. Intense low pressure developed across the central Plains and moved into the Great Lakes, with a strong frontogenetic band of precipitation from Nebraska to Minnesota. Convective instability produced some spotty thunder along with the rain changing to snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 7.0 inches 2 miles southwest of Parker and 4.5 inches at Hurley. Winds near Davis and Freeman gusted from 30 to 40 mph, and as high as 45 mph between 0100 and 0900CST, with visibilities less than a mile, and frequently as low as one-half mile.

Winds gusted at 40 to 60 mph at many locations, and in few spots, exceeded 60 mph.  The winds knocked down trees, power lines, and produced other mostly minor structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down at CR 189 at CR 14 in Oakland.

A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report via social media with photos of hail to around quarter size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a Weatherflow gauge.

Nonetheless, frontal forcing in the unstable air mass was sufficient to trigger scattered thunderstorms, some of which became strong to severe and produced a number of reports of damaging winds.

The approach of the front also gradually increased wind shear values, though greater shear remained further north over New York and New England. Nonetheless, frontal forcing in the unstable air mass was sufficient to trigger scattered thunderstorms, some of which became strong to severe and produced a number of reports of damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were downed near Creek Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge of high pressure centered over the Southern Plains began to amplify and expand north-northeast into the Plains and Mississippi Valley through the middle portions of July, resulting in increased subsidence and hence, hotter temperatures as readings climbed into the mid to upper 90s across much of the Ark-La-Tex. The weak surface boundary that lingered across portions of Northeast Texas, Southern Arkansas, and North Louisiana gradually lifted north and dissipated by the 14th, allowing dewpoints to mix out and thus result in slightly less oppressive conditions. However, afternoon heat indices still ranged from 105 to 110 degrees each day through the 16th.

Showers and thunderstorms developed during the afternoon across northeast New Jersey ahead of an approaching backdoor cold front. With relatively weak flow aloft, these storms moved slowly, resulting in heavy rain across some areas. CoCoRaHS observations indicate a widespread 0.5-2 inches of rain in areas that received storms, with the ASOS at Teterboro Airport reporting 2.89 inches of rain. Much of this rain fell over a 1-2 hour time period, resulting in flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A woman drove into deep water near High Street and Benson Avenue in Passaic. After escaping the car, both the woman and the car were carried towards a viaduct opening. The woman traveled through the viaduct for about one mile before it emptied into the Passaic River, where she was able to swim to safety and exit the river, uninjured, along Carneer Avenue in Rutherford. Her car was later located in the viaduct under Brook Avenue near River Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving isolated thunderstorm dropped 1 to 2 inches of rain in a short amount of time across northeast Champaign County during the late afternoon of July 9th, leading to widespread flash flooding in Rantoul.  Meanwhile further west, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the Mississippi River ahead of an approaching cold front.  These storms pushed into the Illinois River Valley, producing scattered wind damage and flash flooding.  The line weakened as it tracked further eastward across the I-55 corridor later in the evening: however, one cell produced damaging downburst winds in northern Piatt County around midnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line was blown onto a road in Williamsfield.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 1-foot diameter tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low was situated over the Pacific Northwest on the 6th and 7th. This resulted in a southwest flow aloft across the Billings Forecast Area. This pattern is quite favorable for the development of severe thunderstorms. At the same time, a surface boundary stretched across northeast Wyoming northward through the southern portions of south central and southeast Montana. Dewpoints across this area were in the 50s. This, combined with strong daytime heating, resulted in CAPES around 1500j/kg. Midlevel flow was around 50kts which providing plenty of shear for rotating storms. This all resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms which resulted in large hail and some property damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A window was broken.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deeper moisture continued spreading into New Mexico as the center of upper level high pressure over the Four Corners region weakened further on July 19, 2020. Showers and thunderstorms developed during the mid to late afternoon hours along the central mountain chain before drifting southeast into nearby highlands and plains. Several of these thunderstorms produced a quick one to two inches of rain with minor flooding observed around Pojoaque, Santa Fe, Logan, and the Caprock region. The strongest thunderstorms generated torrential rainfall rates over two inches per hour with localized flash flooding in the high terrain west of Ruidoso and west of Corona.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rainfall caused flash flooding of arroyos along the southeast slope of the Gallinas Mountains west of Corona. A ranch owner observed trees falling into a nearby arroyo as the embankment gave way to flood waters. At least two cattle tank dams were also being over topped in the area. Damage amounts are estimated to repair infrastructure of two cattle tanks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep tap of monsoon moisture continued surging north into New Mexico on July 24, 2020, setting the stage for additional showers and thunderstorms with torrential rainfall, localized flash flooding, and strong microburst winds. Storms developed early in the afternoon then moved slowly north to northwest across most of New Mexico. Several of these thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall amounts over two inches along with small hail and strong microburst winds. The Clayton airport reported a peak wind gust up to 59 mph and the Roswell airport reported a peak wind gust up to 68 mph. Straight-line winds damaged power lines, power poles, roofs, fences, and trees in the area around Midway. Heavy rainfall around Alamo damaged culverts and roadways in the area. A flash flood near Lemitar washed a pickup truck into an arroyo and caused damage to roadways. Fortunately, no injuries occurred with these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding damaged several roadways and culverts around Alamo. Emergency management estimated damages between $60,000 and $100,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought conditions from June 2020 improved to severe drought in July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Portions of northern Minnesota have seen rainfall deficits in excess of 5 inches for the year and by July areas of Severe Drought (D2) were observed across parts of the area. A wet middle part of July led to improving conditions that brought all areas into the Moderate Drought (D1) category by the end of the month, however, rainfall deficits persist and further dry conditions may reverse the improving trend.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions worsened at the beginning of July as rainfall deficits for the year approached 6 to 8 inches. A few rainfall events during the middle of the month resulted in total rainfall for the month in the 1 to 3 inch range, which was still below normal. However, it was enough to lift the area out of the Severe Drought category (D2), especially with the rainfall received on July 18 and 21, when around 1 to 2 inches fell total.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. The most notable thing about these boundaries was the intersection of the boundary off of Lake Erie with a weaker one south of Lake Ontario. Thunderstorms developed and trained along this intersection for hours. The net result was some of the heaviest rains our area has ever seen in such a short duration with amounts of between 7 and 8 inches reported in Orleans County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ditches were overflowing and running across roads. In 3.5 hours, 5.10 inches of rainfall was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex pulled a pair of fronts across the area during the afternoon and evening near the time of peak heating. Due to cloud cover ahead of the MCV, instability was not very strong, however shear was impressive. Helicity values were impressive, and the presence of the MCV likely added to it locally over the western Southern Tier. Precipitable water values were between 1.75 and 2 inches, which resulted in torrential rainfall in concert with severe thunderstorm development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A barn was destroyed, trees were uprooted, and there was additional damage to a house and shop.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The summer of 2020 had more hot days than 2019, and July 17, 2020 was one of those hot days, with the exception of the Lake of the Woods region. Afternoon high temperatures ranged in the 80s to low 90s, with dew points in the mid 60s to mid 70s. During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado touchdown occurred in an open field just north of highway 2. The tornado continued to the east for less than a quarter of a mile. Peak winds were estimated at 70 mph. The tornado was wrapped in heavy rain and downburst wind, on the leading edge of a squall line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front stalled across the Mid-South started to lift north as low pressure tracked into southwest Missouri. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level disturbance tracked across the region and triggered thunderstorms across Missouri. The airmass across the Mid-South was ripe for severe storms with strong shear and instability in place. Clusters of severe storms moved into northern parts of the Mid-South by mid-afternoon and moved east-southeast through the evening hours producing damaging winds, hail, and flash flooding. This was the second day in a row that northern sections of the Mid-South suffered widespread severe weather.

A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported quarter-size hail four miles south of Canton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-lived complex of thunderstorms which originated over Kansas during the early morning hours, moved through southern Missouri, northern Arkansas and eventually into Tennessee and far north Alabama during the late afternoon and early evening hours.  The thunderstorms produced a gust front that pushed south and southeast away from the rain area into far north Alabama.  Winds gusted at 40 to 60 mph at many locations, and in few spots, exceeded 60 mph.  The winds knocked down trees, power lines, and produced other mostly minor structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm winds damaged the Bob Jones High School softball field dugout and netting poles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing warm front promoted heavy rain and thunderstorms during the afternoon of March 28th. Substantial breaks in the clouds south of the boundary, along with substantial warm air advection, resulted in around 1500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE,  and substantial (60kts+) effective shear was in place across the region. Hail growth increased into the evening as effective wind shear increased to 70kts over eastern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 911 Call Center from Brooke County reported large hail. Cars were damaged and windows were smashed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid-level trough in split flow moved out of the southwestern U.S. on the morning of April 12, and phased with a strong northern stream trough across the northern Plains by April 13. Intense low pressure developed across the central Plains and moved into the Great Lakes, with a strong frontogenetic band of precipitation from Nebraska to Minnesota. Convective instability produced some spotty thunder along with the rain changing to snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms formed over the northern Red River Valley during the early morning hours of Saturday, July 4th. A couple of the individual storm cells became fairly strong, but the main hazard shifted to heavy rain. The storms were slow moving, but kept back-building, which led to some areas picking up very heavy rainfall. The northern Valley into extreme northwest Minnesota was already saturated from heavy rain during June, which led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fields and farmyards filled with water after 4.50 inches of rain fell.

A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report via social media with photos of penny size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a CWOP station.

The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was split at a residence on Red Hill Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary which contributed to widespread severe weather on July 22 moved further north of the mid-Atlantic on July 23. However, another cold front began to approach from the northwest out of the Great Lakes, along with multiple fast moving upper level disturbances. The environment ahead of the front was characterized by moderate to strong instability, weak to moderate shear, and high moisture. The greatest forcing and lift from the approaching disturbances remained north of the region over southern New England, but thunderstorms still developed over the mid-Atlantic. With plenty of instability to work with some storms became severe mainly as clusters or line segments producing damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of downed power lines were received from the Stanton and Marshalltown areas. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary was draped in the area of southern New Jersey and Delmarva on July 30. Meanwhile, another cold front was approaching the region from the northwest. A warm and very humid air mass developed ahead of this second front, leading to the development of moderate to strong instability over much of the mid-Atlantic. The approach of the front also gradually increased wind shear values, though greater shear remained further north over New York and New England. Nonetheless, frontal forcing in the unstable air mass was sufficient to trigger scattered thunderstorms, some of which became strong to severe and produced a number of reports of damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were downed near Wood St in Burlington. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Fay tracked northward along the New Jersey coast before passing west of New York City. Several rounds of heavy rain occurred over the New York City metro area as the storm approached. This rain developed in a tropical airmass, with precipitable water values over 2 inches. Some of the highest rainfall totals occurred in New York City, where the ASOS in Central Park reported 2.43 inches of rain, and New York State Mesonet stations reported 2.96 inches in Midtown Manhattan, 2.44 inches in Brooklyn, 2.21 inches in Staten Island, 2.17 inches in the Bronx, and 2.08 inches in Queens.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Farragut Road was closed due to flooding east of Utica Avenue by Kings Highway in East Flatbush, Brooklyn.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving isolated thunderstorm dropped 1 to 2 inches of rain in a short amount of time across northeast Champaign County during the late afternoon of July 9th, leading to widespread flash flooding in Rantoul.  Meanwhile further west, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the Mississippi River ahead of an approaching cold front.  These storms pushed into the Illinois River Valley, producing scattered wind damage and flash flooding.  The line weakened as it tracked further eastward across the I-55 corridor later in the evening: however, one cell produced damaging downburst winds in northern Piatt County around midnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several streets were flooded and barricaded in Havana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low was situated over the Pacific Northwest on the 6th and 7th. This resulted in a southwest flow aloft across the Billings Forecast Area. This pattern is quite favorable for the development of severe thunderstorms. At the same time, a surface boundary stretched across northeast Wyoming northward through the southern portions of south central and southeast Montana. Dewpoints across this area were in the 50s. This, combined with strong daytime heating, resulted in CAPES around 1500j/kg. Midlevel flow was around 50kts which providing plenty of shear for rotating storms. This all resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms which resulted in large hail and some property damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A more traditional tap of monsoon moisture surged north into New Mexico on July 22, 2020, setting the stage for showers and thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall. The strongest thunderstorms impacted the area from Socorro County eastward through Lincoln County where recent heavy rainfall helped increase the risk for flash flooding. Heavy rainfall produced minor flooding around Magdalena where a couple arroyos neared bank full shortly before 5 pm. Another round of heavy rainfall over the Gallinas Mountains topped arroyo banks and led to flash flooding west of U.S. Highway 54. A section of county road A-019 was partially washed out as flood waters raged through the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding partially washed out a section of CR-A019 four miles west of U.S. Highway 54. Damage amounts are estimated for repairs to the county road and culverts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The richest plume of monsoon moisture of the entire season set up over New Mexico on the weekend of July 25-26, 2020. The center of upper level high pressure drifted west into the state from west Texas while a weak upper level disturbance moved slowly north from eastern Arizona. The combination of several days of heavy rainfall with widespread showers and thunderstorms set the stage for flash flooding across the region. Rainfall amounts over the 48-hour period averaged three to five inches in the area from Socorro County north and east across the Manzano Mountains into the high plains of eastern New Mexico. The remainder of the state also picked up heavy rainfall averaging one to three inches from the Continental Divide eastward across the Rio Grande Valley into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and northeast New Mexico. A quick burst of torrential rainfall around Madrid flooded several arroyos and damaged a couple roadways. Flash flooding occurred along parts of State Road 1 near Luis Lopez and washed one truck into the water. Another flash flood impacted the area around San Antonio resulting into the closure of U.S. Highway 380. Arroyos overflowed their banks between Bloomfield and Aztec, resulting in a few road closures and some minor damage to a couple homes. Minor flooding occurred in many other parts of the state including Aztec, Edgewood, Albuquerque, Gallup, and Dulce. Fortunately, there were no injuries from these heavy thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management and NMDOT officials reported flash flooding in the area between Luis Lopez and San Antonio. State Road 1 was closed between mile markers 51 and 60 due to flood waters and debris over the roadway. One vehicle was trapped in flood waters up to the mirrors near U.S. Highway 380 around San Antonio. U.S. Highway 380 was closed east of San Antonio. Damage amounts are a rough estimate for repairs to several roadways, culverts, low water crossings, and the flooded vehicle. Extent of injuries to the occupants of the flooded vehicle are unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from June 2020 worsened to extreme drought across central De Baca County in July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A hot and very moist air mass was in place across the region with dewpoints in the 70s and precipitable water values approaching 2 inches. Diurnal instability along a lake breeze boundary allowed for convection to develop. The most notable thing about these boundaries was the intersection of the boundary off of Lake Erie with a weaker one south of Lake Ontario. Thunderstorms developed and trained along this intersection for hours. The net result was some of the heaviest rains our area has ever seen in such a short duration with amounts of between 7 and 8 inches reported in Orleans County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A leading surface boundary sagged from lower Michigan across the Southern Tier and Genesee Valley. Ample moisture pooling evidenced by precipitable water values in excess of 1.5 inches and modest shear generated instability that allowed for thunderstorms to vertically develop into a layer of dry air aloft. This provided the first set of wind damage producing thunderstorms. Subsequent to those, the Lake Ontario lake breeze forced additional thunderstorms that keyed on much higher low level helicity that moved southeastward from Genesee to Ontario counties. These storms developed notable rotation, resulting in one tornado in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree and wires feel onto a house along State Route 394.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The summer of 2020 had more hot days than 2019, and July 17, 2020 was one of those hot days, with the exception of the Lake of the Woods region. Afternoon high temperatures ranged in the 80s to low 90s, with dew points in the mid 60s to mid 70s. During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured by a NDAWN mesonet sensor. A nearby north to south running irrigation system was flipped to the east.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Up-slope east to northeast flow associated with a weak frontal boundary across the area assisted in maintaining a moist and unstable atmosphere across the Texas Panhandle. Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening as an upper level disturbance in northwest flow aloft. The strongly sheared environment led to rotating storms, which supported the production of very large hail and damaging winds across western, northern and central parts of the Panhandle. A brief landspout tornado developed in the southwest Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very large hail fell up to 3.25 inches in diameter 3 miles east-southeast of Vega.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing warm front promoted heavy rain and thunderstorms during the afternoon of March 28th. Substantial breaks in the clouds south of the boundary, along with substantial warm air advection, resulted in around 1500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE,  and substantial (60kts+) effective shear was in place across the region. Hail growth increased into the evening as effective wind shear increased to 70kts over eastern Ohio.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan on the evening of April 7th to far-southwestern Ontario Province by very early morning of April 8th. The accompanying warm front initially extended east-southeastward from the low and across Lake Erie. This warm front moved northward to the northern lakeshore by very early morning of the 8th. Simultaneously, the low's trailing cold front moved southeastward to far-western Lake Erie. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward across Lake Erie during the late evening of the 7th. Elevated weak to primarily moderate most-unstable CAPE and strong vertical wind shear allowed the squall line to remain organized as it crossed the relatively-cool waters of Lake Erie. Despite a cool and stable marine boundary layer reducing the strength of downdrafts, gale force wind gusts occurred along or just behind the squall line's downshear gust front as it came ashore in northern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: C-MAN Station GELO1 at Geneva Light measured a 43 kt marine thunderstorm wind gust.

A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Penny size hail reported by CoCoRaHS observer NJ-MN-64. Hail fell for around 15 minutes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed on Deckerton Turnpike near the intersection with County Route 675. Time estimated from radar.

This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees and wires down in Stouchsburg. Time estimated from radar.
