EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A longwave trough and associated closed low pressure system extended from the Midwest/Mid Mississippi Valley southwest into Oklahoma during the afternoon hours of July 30th, with an attendant weak cool front mixing south into Northwest Arkansas, bisecting Eastern, Central, and Southern Oklahoma. As a shortwave trough rounded the base of the deeper trough near the front during the afternoon, showers and thunderstorms quickly developed during the late afternoon within a moderately unstable air mass, and intensified into a small mesoscale convective system (MCS) as it moved through far Southern and Southeast Oklahoma. Some of these storms were severe, with measured wind gusts up to 90 mph recorded by a couple of Oklahoma Mesonet stations, resulting in numerous reports of wind damage over these areas. These storms did weaken by the mid and late evening hours as they entered extreme Southeast Oklahoma and adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, but remained strong enough to down power lines in De Queen before weakening further below severe limits.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were downed in De Queen.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An abnormally deep longwave trough shifted south southeast through the Midwest  into Eastern Oklahoma and North Texas by the morning hours of July 31st, with an attendant cool front mixing southeast into Northwest Arkansas, Eastern Oklahoma, and North Texas. Showers and thunderstorms continued to develop along and ahead of this front along the longwave trough axis during the morning of the 31st, which organized into a broken line as it moved into a moderately unstable air mass by early afternoon during peak heating. Some of the storms became severe across the southern sections of Northcentral Louisiana, where trees and power lines were downed at various locations in Grant Parish, before exiting and weakening the area during the late afternoon hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were blown down on Lemoine Cutoff Road near Highway 71 just northeast of Colfax.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low was situated over the Pacific Northwest on the 6th and 7th. This resulted in a southwest flow aloft across the Billings Forecast Area. This pattern is quite favorable for the development of severe thunderstorms. At the same time, a surface boundary stretched across northeast Wyoming northward through the southern portions of south central and southeast Montana. Dewpoints across this area were in the 50s. This, combined with strong daytime heating, resulted in CAPES around 1500j/kg. Midlevel flow was around 50kts which providing plenty of shear for rotating storms. This all resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms which resulted in large hail and some property damage.

An upper level ridge of high pressure centered over the Southern Plains on July 10th, began to amplify and expand north-northeast into the Plains and Mississippi Valley through the middle portions of the month, resulting in increased subsidence and hence, hotter temperatures as readings climbed into the mid to upper 90s across much of the Ark-La-Tex. Very little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this time period, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105 to 110 degrees during the afternoons across portions of Northeast Texas through July 12th. However, a weak surface trough became stationary across portions of extreme Northeast Texas, extreme Southern Arkansas, and North Louisiana on the 13th, with low level moisture pooling along this boundary resulting in even more oppressive heat by this time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The richest plume of monsoon moisture of the entire season set up over New Mexico on the weekend of July 25-26, 2020. The center of upper level high pressure drifted west into the state from west Texas while a weak upper level disturbance moved slowly north from eastern Arizona. The combination of several days of heavy rainfall with widespread showers and thunderstorms set the stage for flash flooding across the region. Rainfall amounts over the 48-hour period averaged three to five inches in the area from Socorro County north and east across the Manzano Mountains into the high plains of eastern New Mexico. The remainder of the state also picked up heavy rainfall averaging one to three inches from the Continental Divide eastward across the Rio Grande Valley into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and northeast New Mexico. A quick burst of torrential rainfall around Madrid flooded several arroyos and damaged a couple roadways. Flash flooding occurred along parts of State Road 1 near Luis Lopez and washed one truck into the water. Another flash flood impacted the area around San Antonio resulting into the closure of U.S. Highway 380. Arroyos overflowed their banks between Bloomfield and Aztec, resulting in a few road closures and some minor damage to a couple homes. Minor flooding occurred in many other parts of the state including Aztec, Edgewood, Albuquerque, Gallup, and Dulce. Fortunately, there were no injuries from these heavy thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Arroyos overflowed their banks along U.S. 550 between Aztec and Bloomfield. The roadway was closed for several hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from June 2020 continued in July.

Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from June 2020 worsened in July with extreme drought developing across portions of southern and northern Chaves County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. Numerous reports of hail and wind damage were received along with one confirmed tornado near Brainerd that was on the ground for nearly 25 minutes before lifting, but caused little in the way of damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A supercell briefly produced a tornado in a rural area between Brainerd and Garrison. The tornado produced minor damage to one  property as well as damaging several trees along its path. The tornado was estimated to be on the ground for nearly 23 minutes |before dissipating as the parent storm became outflow dominant.

A nearby couple rescued all three swimmers and got them back to shore just as the Michigan State Police and U.S. Coast Guard arrived on the scene.  The two children were medically cleared at the scene.  The 38-year-old male was transported to a local hospital for further medical evaluation.  Winds were west at 15 to 20 mph based on nearby observations along the shoreline, and conditions were reported to be choppy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Nearly all of South Central Texas had less than 50% of normal precipitation in July. Some parts of Uvalde, Kinney, Zavala, and Maverick Counties had less than 10% of normal. Public water supply systems in Uvalde, Zavala, Dimmit, and Val Verde Counties had water restrictions in place. Lake Amistad was 47.1 feet below conservation pool elevation.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A leading surface boundary sagged from lower Michigan across the Southern Tier and Genesee Valley. Ample moisture pooling evidenced by precipitable water values in excess of 1.5 inches and modest shear generated instability that allowed for thunderstorms to vertically develop into a layer of dry air aloft. This provided the first set of wind damage producing thunderstorms. Subsequent to those, the Lake Ontario lake breeze forced additional thunderstorms that keyed on much higher low level helicity that moved southeastward from Genesee to Ontario counties. These storms developed notable rotation, resulting in one tornado in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree and wires were down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective vortex pulled a pair of fronts across the area during the afternoon and evening near the time of peak heating. Due to cloud cover ahead of the MCV, instability was not very strong, however shear was impressive. Helicity values were impressive, and the presence of the MCV likely added to it locally over the western Southern Tier. Precipitable water values were between 1.75 and 2 inches, which resulted in torrential rainfall in concert with severe thunderstorm development.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were reported down.

Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golf ball size hail was reported by media storm chasers. The hail damaged a few homes and vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The summer of 2020 had more hot days than 2019, and July 17, 2020 was one of those hot days, with the exception of the Lake of the Woods region. Afternoon high temperatures ranged in the 80s to low 90s, with dew points in the mid 60s to mid 70s. During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured by a NDAWN mesonet sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees down where Lincoln Way NW intersects 28th Street NW, 20th Street NW, and 17th Street NW. Large uprooted tree at Erie Street S and Forest Avenue SE. Considering the nearby tornado was no more than 100 yards wide, this tree damage in Massillon was likely related to straight-line winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

A stronger storm system moved across the Sierra Nevada mainly on the 16th, with lighter snow showers and icy roads lingering into the morning of the 17th. This storm produced strong winds, but it also produced more significant precipitation that previous storms, mainly as snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavenly Ski Resort reported 18 inches of snowfall in a 24-hour period from 16 January 0700PST to 17 January 0700PST at an elevation of 7499 feet MSL.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front sagged south into the Mid-South during the day on May 3, 2020. A potent, quick-moving shortwave interacted with this front and convection developed across Missouri by noon. The airmass across the Mid-South was moderately unstable with fairly strong wind shear in place. The convection formed into a bow echo and intensified as it raced across the northern Mid-South during the afternoon hours. Damaging winds were widespread. By early evening additional storms developed across West Tennessee and produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four trees were knocked down in Three Way.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing warm front promoted heavy rain and thunderstorms during the afternoon of March 28th. Substantial breaks in the clouds south of the boundary, along with substantial warm air advection, resulted in around 1500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE,  and substantial (60kts+) effective shear was in place across the region. Hail growth increased into the evening as effective wind shear increased to 70kts over eastern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported quarter size hail.

The thunderstorms produced a gust front that pushed south and southeast away from the rain area into far north Alabama.  Winds gusted at 40 to 60 mph at many locations, and in few spots, exceeded 60 mph.  The winds knocked down trees, power lines, and produced other mostly minor structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was knocked down at 3812 CR 533 in Anderson.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid-level trough in split flow moved out of the southwestern U.S. on the morning of April 12, and phased with a strong northern stream trough across the northern Plains by April 13. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lone weak cell appeared on radar at 430 pm CDT over northern Grant County, Minnesota. Numerous storm chasers had congregated in this area, hoping to see a good storm to chase. By 5 pm, the cell had blossomed into a strong thunderstorm. Weather spotters, law enforcement, and storm chasers then reported a funnel coming down toward the ground slightly after 505 pm. A tornado warning was issued at 508 pm (until 6 pm) for portions of south central Otter Tail and northeast Grant counties. This tornado tracked about 9 miles through the warned area, before dissipating. At its peak strength, it was rated as an EF-4 tornado. Another rotation was noted a little later, leading to a second tornado warning at 635 pm (until 7 pm), this time for southwest Wadena and southeast Otter Tail counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A persistent funnel cloud briefly touched down. Peak winds were estimated at 75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report via social media with photos of quarter size hail. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary which contributed to widespread severe weather on July 22 moved further north of the mid-Atlantic on July 23. However, another cold front began to approach from the northwest out of the Great Lakes, along with multiple fast moving upper level disturbances. The environment ahead of the front was characterized by moderate to strong instability, weak to moderate shear, and high moisture. The greatest forcing and lift from the approaching disturbances remained north of the region over southern New England, but thunderstorms still developed over the mid-Atlantic. With plenty of instability to work with some storms became severe mainly as clusters or line segments producing damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wires were downed near the intersection of Trenton Lakewood Rd and Red Valley Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours.  Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County.  Meanwhile, hailstones as large as 2 inches in diameter caused considerable damage to car dealerships in Savoy and numerous roofs on the east side of Urbana in Champaign County.  The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper low was situated over the Pacific Northwest on the 6th and 7th. This resulted in a southwest flow aloft across the Billings Forecast Area. This pattern is quite favorable for the development of severe thunderstorms. At the same time, a surface boundary stretched across northeast Wyoming northward through the southern portions of south central and southeast Montana. Dewpoints across this area were in the 50s. This, combined with strong daytime heating, resulted in CAPES around 1500j/kg. Midlevel flow was around 50kts which providing plenty of shear for rotating storms. This all resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms which resulted in large hail and some property damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Property damage was reported.

The richest plume of monsoon moisture of the entire season set up over New Mexico on the weekend of July 25-26, 2020. The center of upper level high pressure drifted west into the state from west Texas while a weak upper level disturbance moved slowly north from eastern Arizona. The combination of several days of heavy rainfall with widespread showers and thunderstorms set the stage for flash flooding across the region. Rainfall amounts over the 48-hour period averaged three to five inches in the area from Socorro County north and east across the Manzano Mountains into the high plains of eastern New Mexico. The remainder of the state also picked up heavy rainfall averaging one to three inches from the Continental Divide eastward across the Rio Grande Valley into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and northeast New Mexico. A quick burst of torrential rainfall around Madrid flooded several arroyos and damaged a couple roadways. Flash flooding occurred along parts of State Road 1 near Luis Lopez and washed one truck into the water. Another flash flood impacted the area around San Antonio resulting into the closure of U.S. Highway 380. Arroyos overflowed their banks between Bloomfield and Aztec, resulting in a few road closures and some minor damage to a couple homes. Minor flooding occurred in many other parts of the state including Aztec, Edgewood, Albuquerque, Gallup, and Dulce. Fortunately, there were no injuries from these heavy thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: U.S. Highway 64 was closed due to flood waters between U.S. Highway 550 and Jordan Court. Two homes were partially flooded at the intersection of East Broadway Avenue and Johnson Street. Damage amounts are a rough estimate to water damage to two homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions developed across the Glorieta Pass area during July 2020. Below normal precipitation amounts set the stage for deteriorating drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. Numerous reports of hail and wind damage were received along with one confirmed tornado near Brainerd that was on the ground for nearly 25 minutes before lifting, but caused little in the way of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A leading surface boundary sagged from lower Michigan across the Southern Tier and Genesee Valley. Ample moisture pooling evidenced by precipitable water values in excess of 1.5 inches and modest shear generated instability that allowed for thunderstorms to vertically develop into a layer of dry air aloft. This provided the first set of wind damage producing thunderstorms. Subsequent to those, the Lake Ontario lake breeze forced additional thunderstorms that keyed on much higher low level helicity that moved southeastward from Genesee to Ontario counties. These storms developed notable rotation, resulting in one tornado in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and power lines were down.

Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Oklahoma Mesonet station north of Vinita measured 66 mph thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The summer of 2020 had more hot days than 2019, and July 17, 2020 was one of those hot days, with the exception of the Lake of the Woods region. Afternoon high temperatures ranged in the 80s to low 90s, with dew points in the mid 60s to mid 70s. During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Metal roofing and siding were blown off a building.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A front stalled across the Mid-South started to lift north as low pressure tracked into southwest Missouri. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level disturbance tracked across the region and triggered thunderstorms across Missouri. The airmass across the Mid-South was ripe for severe storms with strong shear and instability in place. Clusters of severe storms moved into northern parts of the Mid-South by mid-afternoon and moved east-southeast through the evening hours producing damaging winds, hail, and flash flooding. This was the second day in a row that northern sections of the Mid-South suffered widespread severe weather.

A strong mid-level trough in split flow moved out of the southwestern U.S. on the morning of April 12, and phased with a strong northern stream trough across the northern Plains by April 13. Intense low pressure developed across the central Plains and moved into the Great Lakes, with a strong frontogenetic band of precipitation from Nebraska to Minnesota. Convective instability produced some spotty thunder along with the rain changing to snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snowfall totaled 6.3 inches 5 miles east of Yankton and 6.0 inches at Yankton. Winds at Yankton gusted as high as 40 mph between 0700CST and 1230CST, with visibilities frequently at one-half mile or less, and occasionally as low as one-quarter mile.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A squall line rolled through the region during the early morning hours of April 13, 2020.  Strong instability and shear led to numerous severe thunderstorm wind gusts along with several tornadoes. In total, across central SC, there were 5 EF-3 tornadoes, 1 EF-2 tornadoes, and 1 EF-1 tornado. Two fatalities, and several injuries, occurred with the tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sentinel Satellite Data from April 13, 2020 clearly showed a damage scar beginning at the western edge of Parr Pond in the Savannah River Site and ending near the intersection of Highway 278 and State Road 21. A tornadic debris signature detected by the KCAE radar aligns with the damage scar. A ground survey also indicated a few trees down just off a field on the eastern side of Fellowship Road as the tornado dissipated. Based off of the above information and correspondence with a Savannah River Site official, it is estimated that winds reached EF-3 strength, with speeds up to 138 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Higher flows from rainfall and snow melt were sustained by heavy rainfall again at the end of March and beginning of April. A drier period heading into mid-month allowed the river to fall below flood stage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A continuation of minor flooding from March, the Little Sioux River near Milford (gage site MIFI4) began the month 0.83 feet above flood stage, with a slow and steady fall to below flood stage on April 3. Main impacts occurred with flooding of crop and pasture land.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front sagged south into the Mid-South during the day on May 3, 2020. A potent, quick-moving shortwave interacted with this front and convection developed across Missouri by noon. The airmass across the Mid-South was moderately unstable with fairly strong wind shear in place. The convection formed into a bow echo and intensified as it raced across the northern Mid-South during the afternoon hours. Damaging winds were widespread. By early evening additional storms developed across West Tennessee and produced large hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Uprooted trees damaged six homes in Caruthersville.

The airmass across the Mid-South was ripe for severe storms with strong shear and instability in place. Clusters of severe storms moved into northern parts of the Mid-South by mid-afternoon and moved east-southeast through the evening hours producing damaging winds and hail. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lone weak cell appeared on radar at 430 pm CDT over northern Grant County, Minnesota. Numerous storm chasers had congregated in this area, hoping to see a good storm to chase. By 5 pm, the cell had blossomed into a strong thunderstorm. Weather spotters, law enforcement, and storm chasers then reported a funnel coming down toward the ground slightly after 505 pm. A tornado warning was issued at 508 pm (until 6 pm) for portions of south central Otter Tail and northeast Grant counties. This tornado tracked about 9 miles through the warned area, before dissipating. At its peak strength, it was rated as an EF-4 tornado. Another rotation was noted a little later, leading to a second tornado warning at 635 pm (until 7 pm), this time for southwest Wadena and southeast Otter Tail counties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A lightning strike ignited a wildfire 18 miles north of Grand Junction.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Pine Gulch Fire began at the end of July due to lightning 18 miles north of Grand Junction and grew to 139,007 acres before it was contained in mid September. The combination of drought-stressed vegetation, unseasonably hot weather and steep terrain led to weeks of active burning. Smoke columns were often visible from Grand Junction and the surrounding area as the wildfire exhibited extreme fire behavior. During the night of August 18, the fire grew quickly due to thunderstorm winds up to 40 mph for a three to four hour period. As a result, the fire increased by more than 30,000 acres that night. As of August 27, 2020 the Pine Gulch Fire became the largest wildfire in Colorado State history, surpassing the Hayman Fire that burned near Colorado Springs in the summer of 2002.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported quarter size hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail fell in Montague. Report via social media with photos.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  The first round developed along an outflow boundary from previous convection that had tracked across northern Illinois around midday.  These cells formed along the I-74 corridor and brought large hail and locally heavy rainfall during the late afternoon hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The richest plume of monsoon moisture of the entire season set up over New Mexico on the weekend of July 25-26, 2020. The center of upper level high pressure drifted west into the state from west Texas while a weak upper level disturbance moved slowly north from eastern Arizona. The combination of several days of heavy rainfall with widespread showers and thunderstorms set the stage for flash flooding across the region. Rainfall amounts over the 48-hour period averaged three to five inches in the area from Socorro County north and east across the Manzano Mountains into the high plains of eastern New Mexico. The remainder of the state also picked up heavy rainfall averaging one to three inches from the Continental Divide eastward across the Rio Grande Valley into the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and northeast New Mexico. A quick burst of torrential rainfall around Madrid flooded several arroyos and damaged a couple roadways. Flash flooding occurred along parts of State Road 1 near Luis Lopez and washed one truck into the water. Another flash flood impacted the area around San Antonio resulting into the closure of U.S. Highway 380. Arroyos overflowed their banks between Bloomfield and Aztec, resulting in a few road closures and some minor damage to a couple homes. Minor flooding occurred in many other parts of the state including Aztec, Edgewood, Albuquerque, Gallup, and Dulce. Fortunately, there were no injuries from these heavy thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A sudden torrent of rainfall filled several arroyos around Madrid and Cerrillos. Flood damage was reported to low water crossings, culverts, and driveways. Damage amounts are a very rough estimate for repairs to several roadways and culverts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep tap of monsoon moisture continued surging north into New Mexico on July 24, 2020, setting the stage for additional showers and thunderstorms with torrential rainfall, localized flash flooding, and strong microburst winds. Storms developed early in the afternoon then moved slowly north to northwest across most of New Mexico. Several of these thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall amounts over two inches along with small hail and strong microburst winds. The Clayton airport reported a peak wind gust up to 59 mph and the Roswell airport reported a peak wind gust up to 68 mph. Straight-line winds damaged power lines, power poles, roofs, fences, and trees in the area around Midway. Heavy rainfall around Alamo damaged culverts and roadways in the area. A flash flood near Lemitar washed a pickup truck into an arroyo and caused damage to roadways. Fortunately, no injuries occurred with these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A pickup truck crossing flood waters along CR-91 between Lemitar and Escondida was washed downstream. Occupants were able to safely abandon the vehicle before it was destroyed. Extent of injuries to the occupants of the vehicle are unknown. Damage amounts are estimated for loss of the truck.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions developed across northern portions of the Sandia/Manzano Mountains during July 2020. Below normal precipitation amounts set the stage for deteriorating drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of thunderstorms increased in coverage and intensity during the afternoon along an east to west corridor across southeast Missouri into western Kentucky. The storms produced very heavy rainfall, along with an isolated damaging wind gust or two. The storms formed along and ahead of a slow moving frontal boundary that extended generally along the Ohio River into southeast Missouri. The environment near and south of the front was characterized by dew points in the lower to middle 70s and precipitable water values of 1.75 inches. With daytime heating, instability increased substantially to around 3000 J/kg south of the front, with a sharp gradient along the surface front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few small trees and tree limbs were blown down. One tree limb punctured a hole through the roof of a house before striking the floor of the house.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. Numerous reports of hail and wind damage were received along with one confirmed tornado near Brainerd that was on the ground for nearly 25 minutes before lifting, but caused little in the way of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A leading surface boundary sagged from lower Michigan across the Southern Tier and Genesee Valley. Ample moisture pooling evidenced by precipitable water values in excess of 1.5 inches and modest shear generated instability that allowed for thunderstorms to vertically develop into a layer of dry air aloft. This provided the first set of wind damage producing thunderstorms. Subsequent to those, the Lake Ontario lake breeze forced additional thunderstorms that keyed on much higher low level helicity that moved southeastward from Genesee to Ontario counties. These storms developed notable rotation, resulting in one tornado in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree feels onto a parked car on Sandy Beach Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorm wind blew down trees onto homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree fell onto house near downtown Elyria and another tree fell onto another home one mile SSE of Elyria. 18 trees were downed at OH routes 10 and 57, four miles WNW of Eaton Estates.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system crossing through the state inflicted multiple rounds of severe weather across West Virginia. Starting on the 7th, a warm front draped across the Ohio Valley was the primary focus for convection to develop that evening. These storms produced large hail across portions of northern West Virginia. A brief lull in storms during the day of the 8th primed the atmosphere once more for severe thunderstorms to arise ahead of a cold front which passed through late that night. During which time, another round of thunderstorm wind damage, hail, and flash flooding occurred late that evening and into the early morning hours of the 9th. Local cooperative observers reported one to two inches of rainfall occurred with this second round of convection. Strong synoptic winds of 35-45 miles per hour on the backside of the disturbance remained in place before high pressure finally built into the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several blocks of 7th Avenue in St. Albans were closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level low pressure center moved east from southern Colorado across south central Kansas through the late afternoon on Tuesday, June 9, 2020. As it did, a surface low deepened and moved east across Kansas pushing a cold front south across the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles before moving into western Texas. The cold front moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle early in the morning and quickly swept south through through the Texas Panhandle, continuing to move across the region. A strong pressure gradient between the low over Kansas and high pressure surging southeast out of Colorado created very strong winds across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles behind the front, which lasted into the early evening.||Across the northern half of the Texas Panhandle, sustained winds increased into the 40 to greater than 50 MPH range out of the north to northwest, with gusts mainly in the 55 to 65 MPH range. Farther south, sustained winds generally ranged from 37 to 46 MPH with gusts mainly in the 50 to 60 MPH range. These strong winds lasted most of the day before finally diminishing from west to east beginning in the late afternoon. Although the relative humidity was only 15 to 35 percent across the northwestern two-thirds of the Texas Panhandle, the high winds and dry fuels associated with recent onset of moderate to extreme drought in the area led to a high wildfire danger across part of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station 4 miles west-northwest of Stratford measured sustained winds in the 40 to 54 MPH range during this time period. The highest sustained wind of 54 MPH occurred at 1200CST.

Slightly after midnight CDT, July 8th, storms out ahead of the main bowing segment entered the Barnes/Griggs county area. Eventually the main bowing segment tracked through Griggs and Steele counties before weakening. North of the main bowing segment, strong winds also tracked through portions of Benson and Ramsey counties. After 3 am CDT, a second bowing line of storms took shape over Richland County, North Dakota, which tracked through Otter Tail County, Minnesota. This segment also produced very strong winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported quarter to ping pong ball size hail.

Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of downed trees and wires were received on Mountain Rd. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of tree limbs and power lines down in Allamuchy Twp. Time estimated from radar.

Hail as large as tennis balls or 2.5 inches in diameter was reported in Bartonville in Peoria County. The second round of storms developed over eastern Iowa, then swept southeastward across much of the area during the evening bringing damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Excessive heat returned to the St. Lawrence Valley on what has already been a hot and dry early summer. In addition, high dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s created heat index values at or above 100 degrees in the St. Lawrence Valley on the 9th and 10th.||In fact, Massena's max temperature for the first 10 days of July has averaged 90.8 degrees, which broke the old record of 90.3 degrees set in 1973.||Some of this excessive heat migrated into the Champlain Valley on the 8th-10th with highs in the 90s and heat index values in the mid to upper 90s.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High temperatures in the mid to upper 90s with dew points in the 60s to around 70 created heat indices in the mid 90s to lower 100s. Massena reached 99 degrees on July 10th, 2nd hottest ALL-TIME since records kept in 1948.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge of high pressure centered over the Southern Plains on July 10th, began to amplify and expand north-northeast into the Plains and Mississippi Valley through the middle portions of the month, resulting in increased subsidence and hence, hotter temperatures as readings climbed into the mid to upper 90s across much of the Ark-La-Tex. Very little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this time period, resulting in heat indices ranging from 105 to 110 degrees during the afternoons across much of East Texas through July 12th. However, a weak surface boundary became stationary on the 13th across portions of Northeast Texas, Southern Arkansas, and North Louisiana, which resulted in low level moisture pooling near and south of this boundary. Thus, even more oppressive heat indices were observed across more of East Texas on the 13th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and eastern New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of July. Moderate to extreme drought worsened to about 94 percent of the state of which about 14 percent across northern and southeast New Mexico was deemed as extreme drought. Monsoon season got off to a slow start during the month of July as an area of high pressure strengthened over the state. Record heat and dry conditions were observed across the area for several days. A more traditional monsoon pattern developed toward mid-July with some areas receiving beneficial rainfall. Northeast New Mexico received above normal rainfall totals during the latter half of the month, and Clayton recorded their 6th wettest July on record with 5.84 of rainfall. Despite the more active pattern, storm tracks did not favor northwest and southeast New Mexico where below normal precipitation totals and worsening drought conditions were observed. Precipitation totals during the month of July generally ranged from two to three inches across southwest and south central New Mexico with one to three inches across central New Mexico and the Rio Grande Valley. Northeast New Mexico received the most amount of rainfall with CoCoRaHS observers in Union County receiving about five to seven inches. Southeast New Mexico and the Four Corners area received the least amount of precipitation with rain totals ranging from one to two inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions developed across the Central Highlands during July 2020. Below normal precipitation amounts set the stage for deteriorating drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The center of upper level high pressure continued moving west into Arizona by the end of July while moisture was recharged across the state behind a strong back door cold front. North to south steering flow with abundant shear and instability led to the development of numerous showers and storms during the early to mid afternoon hours. Several of these storms were strong to severe as they progressed southward across the eastern plains and through the Rio Grande Valley. A storm near Las Vegas dumped hail up to the size of golf balls with very heavy rainfall and strong winds. Another storm moved south across Interstate 25 near San Jose and produced quarter size hail. Storms that developed over the Jemez Mountains moved south through Cochiti Pueblo with quarter size hail before blasting through the Albuquerque metro area with damaging winds and heavy rainfall. Ruidoso also experienced severe weather with quarter size hail and heavy rainfall. Minor flooding was reported in many areas as well. Swift runoff into the urban drainage system in Albuquerque washed two individuals down the Embudo Arroyo. One individual was rescued however the other died in the flood waters.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A CoCoRaHS observer near San Pablo reported quarter size hail as a severe thunderstorm moved south through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving warm front lifted across the middle Ohio River Valley and central Appalachians on the 30th. Additional support was provided by several mid level shortwave troughs and a weak surface low. A high moisture atmosphere was in place, and slow moving showers and storms produced very heavy rainfall through the afternoon and evening. In the areas of heaviest rain, which stretched from Huntington northeastward to near Elkins, 2 to 4 inches of rain was common, and several gauges indicated more than 4 fell.  In fact, two gauges around Grantsville measured 5.12 and 5.04 of rain. A second, more localized, area of heavy rain fell in Tazewell County, VA northward into the headwaters of the Dry Fork of the Tug River in McDowell and Mercer Counties. Runoff from this heavy rain flowed down the Dry Fork of the Tug River overnight causing flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The intersection of Route 60 and 5th Avenue was closed due to rapidly flowing water. One car became stranded in the flood water. Highland Drive was also closed for a time due to high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Slow-moving thunderstorm cells over saturated ground caused localized flash flooding during the afternoon hours. An upper-level disturbance advancing quickly southeast across western Illinois promoted the growth of thunderstorms along an outflow boundary extending from southwest Illinois across western Kentucky. Very unstable air existed on the warm west side of the boundary, with dew points in the upper 70's. Weak low level inflow of this very unstable air ascended across the boundary, supporting active convection east of the boundary. Storm motions were nearly stationary at times, resulting in 2 to 3 inch totals over a 1 to 2 hour period. Since the ground was saturated, some flash flooding occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A secondary road was water-covered.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent storm system brought multiple rounds of severe storms to the Northland starting during the early morning hours of the 8th. Very little in the way of severe weather was observed with this initial round of storms. A warm front then lifted across the region through the day, bringing a very moist and unstable airmass to the area. Storms begin firing during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front bringing all modes of severe weather during the late afternoon and evening hours before transitioning to more of a low end hail and damaging wind threat through the overnight hours and into the morning of the 9th. Numerous reports of hail and wind damage were received along with one confirmed tornado near Brainerd that was on the ground for nearly 25 minutes before lifting, but caused little in the way of damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A leading surface boundary sagged from lower Michigan across the Southern Tier and Genesee Valley. Ample moisture pooling evidenced by precipitable water values in excess of 1.5 inches and modest shear generated instability that allowed for thunderstorms to vertically develop into a layer of dry air aloft. This provided the first set of wind damage producing thunderstorms. Subsequent to those, the Lake Ontario lake breeze forced additional thunderstorms that keyed on much higher low level helicity that moved southeastward from Genesee to Ontario counties. These storms developed notable rotation, resulting in one tornado in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down onto a parked car on Baycliff Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across southeastern Kansas and north central Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 11th, as a cold front moved southward into the area. The atmosphere became extremely unstable over eastern Oklahoma ahead of the storms. Wind fields above the ground were also unseasonably strong, which resulted in very strong deep layer wind shear across the region. The combination of the extreme instability and very strong wind shear resulted in organized severe thunderstorms that moved through eastern Oklahoma during the evening, producing widespread damaging wind and large hail. A very moist air mass combined with intense thunderstorm activity also resulted in very heavy rain rates, and localized flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were estimated to 75 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Saturday, July 25th was another hot and humid day, with highs in the 80s to around 90, and dew points in the 70s. By late in the afternoon, a cold front had moved into the Devils Lake region, helping to initiate a few thunderstorms. One severe storm tracked across portions of western Cavalier County, dropping large hail. There was a bit of a lull in thunderstorm activity until around sundown, when storms flared up again between Jamestown, Grand Forks, and Devils Lake. After midnight, another batch of strong storms tracked along the North and South Dakota border, from Oakes (ND) toward Elbow Lake (MN). These storms produced large and and strong wind gusts as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hail was mostly pea sized.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The summer of 2020 had more hot days than 2019, and July 17, 2020 was one of those hot days, with the exception of the Lake of the Woods region. Afternoon high temperatures ranged in the 80s to low 90s, with dew points in the mid 60s to mid 70s. During the early afternoon, a line of thunderstorms over north central North Dakota moved into the Devils Lake region. By the early evening, showers and storms covered most of the area north of Interstate 94 in North Dakota, and highway 10 in Minnesota. By mid to late evening, these showers and storms continued to sag southward, covering the rest of eastern North Dakota and west central Minnesota. These storms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts. In addition, most areas received from 1 to 4 inches of rain.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured at the Grand Forks airport.

A front stalled across the Mid-South started to lift north as low pressure tracked into southwest Missouri. Meanwhile, a potent upper-level disturbance tracked across the region and triggered thunderstorms across Missouri. The airmass across the Mid-South was ripe for severe storms with strong shear and instability in place. Clusters of severe storms moved into northern parts of the Mid-South by mid-afternoon and moved east-southeast through the evening hours producing damaging winds, hail, and flash flooding. This was the second day in a row that northern sections of the Mid-South suffered widespread severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree fell on a house on Sand Ridge Bargerton Road near Highway 412 west of Lexington.  Twenty-eight trees were knocked down on one property west of Lexington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved from west-central Lower Michigan during the evening of April 7th to near Long Island by daybreak on April 8th. The accompanying cold front extended west-southwestward from the low and swept south-southeastward through northern Ohio during the early morning of the 8th. Along and ahead of the cold front, clusters of thunderstorms, including supercells, formed over southern Lake Michigan and southern Lower Michigan by the early evening of the 7th. These storms grew upscale into a squall line, which then moved generally southeastward through northern Ohio from late evening of the 7th through the first hour of the 8th. Additional more discrete thunderstorms, including supercells, developed ahead of the squall line. These storms encountered primarily moderate instability amidst strong effective bulk shear within the warm sector. In addition to numerous reports of damaging straight-line winds and severe hail, three QLCS tornadoes occurred within the squall line and affected portions of northeast Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tweet reporting penny-size hail in Austintown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure moved into the Ohio Valley on the 23rd followed by another slightly stronger low on the 25th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Up-slope east to northeast flow associated with a weak frontal boundary across the area assisted in maintaining a moist and unstable atmosphere across the Texas Panhandle. Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening as an upper level disturbance in northwest flow aloft. The strongly sheared environment led to rotating storms, which supported the production of very large hail and damaging winds across western, northern and central parts of the Panhandle. A brief landspout tornado developed in the southwest Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This gust was measured at the West Texas Mesonet station 1 mile west-southwest of Boys Ranch.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A long-lived complex of thunderstorms which originated over Kansas during the early morning hours, moved through southern Missouri, northern Arkansas and eventually into Tennessee and far north Alabama during the late afternoon and early evening hours.  The thunderstorms produced a gust front that pushed south and southeast away from the rain area into far north Alabama.  Winds gusted at 40 to 60 mph at many locations, and in few spots, exceeded 60 mph.  The winds knocked down trees, power lines, and produced other mostly minor structural damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was uprooted and knocked over onto power lines. Video relayed via social media.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An advancing warm front promoted heavy rain and thunderstorms during the afternoon of March 28th. Substantial breaks in the clouds south of the boundary, along with substantial warm air advection, resulted in around 1500 J/kg of mean-layer CAPE,  and substantial (60kts+) effective shear was in place across the region. Hail growth increased into the evening as effective wind shear increased to 70kts over eastern Ohio.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail reported via social media; dents were made on cars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong mid-level trough in split flow moved out of the southwestern U.S. on the morning of April 12, and phased with a strong northern stream trough across the northern Plains by April 13. Intense low pressure developed across the central Plains and moved into the Great Lakes, with a strong frontogenetic band of precipitation from Nebraska to Minnesota. Convective instability produced some spotty thunder along with the rain changing to snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front pushed into the Mid-South during the evening hours of April 8, 2020, into the early morning hours of April 9, 2020. The front intersected an area of moderate instability and strong wind shear. As a result, storms developed across eastern Arkansas and the Missouri Bootheel then tracked across the Mid-South. Initially, storms were supercellular in nature with large hail and a couple of weak tornadoes. Storms eventually transitioned into clusters and line segments as they moved across the Mississippi River into West Tenessee and North Mississippi. These storms continued to produce large hail and damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Irregularly shaped hail up to 2 inches in diameter fell in Knob.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving backdoor cold front drifted southwest through the mid-Atlantic region on July 6. Meanwhile, a shortwave vorticity impulse, one of several in a series, moved across the region during the day. A very hot and humid air mass was present ahead of the backdoor cold front, leading to the development of strong to extreme instability over the region. The approaching upper level disturbance allowed for the development of moderate wind shear over the region. Combined with the front, it also acted as a trigger mechanism for convection. Severe thunderstorms developed by early afternoon over eastern PA and southern and central New Jersey. These storms produced strong outflow boundaries which served to initiate additional severe convection. The result was a ring of fire in which outflow steadily propagated outward in all directions. This caused severe weather to spread radially outward from its origin near Philadelphia to much of New Jersey, other portions of eastern Pennsylvania, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail occurred at Ginty Field in Morristown. Time estimated from radar and nearby hail reports.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary was draped across upstate New York and southern New England on July 22 with multiple waves of low pressure tracking along it. The mid-Atlantic was left in a warm sector air mass south of this front. This led to a very hot and humid day on July 22 with air temperatures rising into the 90s and dew point values near 70. This caused strong instability to develop. Shear values were not overly impressive, but an approaching shortwave disturbance from the Midwest did help to increase shear late in the day. This disturbance also served as forcing for convection to develop in the warm and unstable air mass. Widespread thunderstorm development occurred, with storms eventually developing into a mostly solid squall line. This line of storms produced numerous reports of wind damage across eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delmarva.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and wires were downed near Sycamore St and US-46 in Ramseysburg. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving frontal boundary which contributed to widespread severe weather on July 22 moved further north of the mid-Atlantic on July 23. However, another cold front began to approach from the northwest out of the Great Lakes, along with multiple fast moving upper level disturbances. The environment ahead of the front was characterized by moderate to strong instability, weak to moderate shear, and high moisture. The greatest forcing and lift from the approaching disturbances remained north of the region over southern New England, but thunderstorms still developed over the mid-Atlantic. With plenty of instability to work with some storms became severe mainly as clusters or line segments producing damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of downed wires in Middletown. Time estimated from radar.
