EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme drought (D3) conditions dominated the south to southeast portions of the county through the first half of the month with most of the rest of the county in severe drought (D2). The most beneficial rainfall from monsoonal moisture fell during the 3rd week of the month. 1.20 inches of the 1.82 inches that fell in for Borger, occurred on the 16th, 19th, and 20th of the month. A small portion or D3 to D2 still existed in the far southeast corner of the county going into August.  In July, a couple of wildfires were started by lightning due to the dryness of vegetation. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lightning ignited the Bighorn Fire on the west side of the Santa Catalina Mountains during the evening of June 5th. Two firefighters sustained minor injuries battling the fire during July, bringing the total number of injured personnel fighting the fire to nine. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna, the 2020 Atlantic season's first Hurricane, made landfall along the unpopulated Padre Island National Seashore on the mid-Kenedy County coastline as a Category 1 storm at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. The hurricane spun slowly but steadily into southern Kenedy and northern Hidalgo County through just after midnight on the 26th, then through Starr County as a Tropical Storm before moving into Tamaulipas before daybreak and eventually near Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, by noon before dissipating during the evening of the 26th. Following the passage of the inner eye wall, broad feeder bands of torrential rains and gusty tropical storm force winds continued through the mid to late morning hours of July 26th, slowly migrating from east to west across the populated Rio Grande Valley. ||Other than storm surge flooding, which peaked just north of Baffin Bay on the Kleberg and Nueces County coast near Corpus Christi, Hanna's memory for the Rio Grande Valley will be flooding rainfall, power outages, and an array of damage to poorly constructed buildings, from minor roof damage to complete demolition.  Between 8 and 15 inches of rain fell from Port Mansfield to Harlingen, and along Interstate Highway 2 out through Mission and Sullivan City. The combination of high rainfall, locally high rainfall rates, and poor drainage left between 18 inches and four feet of water depth in many areas, most commonly from western Cameron through southeastern Hidalgo County, as well as a separate pocket in the Mission/La Joya/Sullivan City area. The rainfall wiped out 95% of the region's cotton crop; the combination of crop loss and production loss was more than one third of a billion dollars alone ($366 million)...most of which was in the Rio Grande Valley region.  ||At the peak of the storm, 250 thousand electric customers were without power, including all of Willacy County. Though storm surge was cut short by strong westerly flow across Cameron County, radiating swells did produce a notable surge of 3 feet or greater (estimated) from near Port Mansfield through Kenedy County. When the damage and economic loss is counted to infrastructure and agriculture combined, it is likely that Hanna cost at least one billion dollars across the Rio Grande Valley and the Deep S. Texas ranch country.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Along Laguna Madre in northern coastal Willacy County, the approach of Hurricane Hanna just 15 miles north of the county line produced strong outbound tide on strong northwest winds. As the eye moved onshore and passed the longitude of Laguna Madre, winds quickly shifted to the south with strong tropical storm force gusts, and waters rose rapidly.  Peak tide (2.62 feet above Mean Sea Level) occurred at Port Mansfield at 1136 AM CST July 26th.  Based on these conditions, as well as survey results that showed return water about 25 yards into marsh grass along Laguna Madre in Port Mansfield, it was possible that 3 feet of water above normally high ground occurred at some point between 10 AM CST and 6 PM CST on July 26th, all associated with the backside circulation around Hanna, which had weakened to a tropical storm (but still with a large envelope) in northeast Mexico. ||Other than flattened marsh grass, no visible property damage was seen due to surge water in the town of Port Mansfield based on an NWS storm survey conducted on July 27th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level low pressure center moved east from southern Colorado across south central Kansas through the late afternoon on Tuesday, June 9, 2020. As it did, a surface low deepened and moved east across Kansas pushing a cold front south across the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles before moving into western Texas. The cold front moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle early in the morning and quickly swept south through through the Texas Panhandle, continuing to move across the region. A strong pressure gradient between the low over Kansas and high pressure surging southeast out of Colorado created very strong winds across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles behind the front, which lasted into the early evening.||Across the northern half of the Texas Panhandle, sustained winds increased into the 40 to greater than 50 MPH range out of the north to northwest, with gusts mainly in the 55 to 65 MPH range. Farther south, sustained winds generally ranged from 37 to 46 MPH with gusts mainly in the 50 to 60 MPH range. These strong winds lasted most of the day before finally diminishing from west to east beginning in the late afternoon. Although the relative humidity was only 15 to 35 percent across the northwestern two-thirds of the Texas Panhandle, the high winds and dry fuels associated with recent onset of moderate to extreme drought in the area led to a high wildfire danger across part of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station 9 miles north-northeast of Amarillo measured sustained winds in the 40 to 43 MPH range during this time period. The highest sustained winds of 43 MPH occurred at 1405CST.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A continuation of flooding from June, the James River at Mitchell (gage site JRMS2) started the month at moderate flood 3.23 feet above flood stage. Several county and township roads near the river remained under water at the start of the month, with inundation of agricultural land the primary threat thereafter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After two consecutive years with a wet winter, the desert wildland-urban interface north and east of Phoenix saw a boost in vegetative growth. Drying of the vegetation/fuels and extended periods of high to extreme fire weather conditions helped support the rapid growth of a wildfire that developed in mid-June when a car caught fire on Hwy-87, northeast of the Phoenix metro area in eastern Maricopa. The fire was named the Bush fire and ended up becoming one of the largest fires in AZ history after spreading across the Four Peaks wilderness, into parts of Gila county, and was not fully contained until early-July.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Bush fire began after a car caught fire near the intersection of Bush Hwy and Hwy-87. Hwy-87 was closed between Bush Hwy and Hwy-188 for an extended period of time. A portion of Bush Hwy was also closed for a time. Multiple communities were given evacuation orders, including Sunflower and the Apache Lake area in Maricopa county and Punkin Center and Tonto Basin in Gila county. High to extreme fire danger through much of June, with hot, dry, and windy weather conditions, supported the wildfire's rapid spread. No rain fell over the fire area through the duration of the burn and one Red Flag Warning was issued for June 28th and 29th. The Bush fire finally became 100% contained on July 4th and ended up burning 193,455 acres, making it the 5th largest wildfire in Arizona history. Fortunately, no homes or structures were destroyed and no one was injured or killed as firefighters were able to mostly contain the fire between Hwy-87, Hwy-188, and the Salt river. The fire did damage portions of Hwy-87 and Hwy-188 according to Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT), including guardrails. For information only, ADOT estimated repair, cleanup, labor, and other miscellaneous costs at around $6 million for this wildfire.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

With one to four inches of liquid residing in the snowpack near and north of Interstate 90 at the start of the month, a more or less ideal melting of the winter snowpack in early March combined with high base flows and wet antecedent conditions to produce minor to major flooding along middle portions of the James River Basin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The James River at Mitchell (gage site JRMS2) began the month in minor flood, then crested on March 13 in moderate flood, 4.86 feet above flood stage. Impacts were generally limited to flooding of agricultural lands near the river, but flood waters did cause the closing of Shanard Road, east of Mitchell. The river remained at moderate flood stage at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna was the first hurricane of the 2020 Atlantic Basin hurricane season and made landfall on the lower Texas coast north of Port Mansfield on the afternoon of the 25th. Hanna was the first hurricane to make landfall in Texas since Hurricane Harvey.||Hanna began as a tropical wave, first noted for possible development when it was near Hispaniola on the 19th. The tropical wave moved northwest across Cuba into the central Gulf of Mexico where it became a tropical depression on the morning of the 22nd. Tropical Storm Hanna formed late in the evening on the 23rd as it moved west-northwest over the central Gulf of Mexico. Hanna continued to strengthen and became a hurricane on the morning of the 25th around 100 miles east of the Middle Texas coast. Hurricane Hanna turned to the southwest and made landfall north of Port Mansfield, late in the afternoon on the 25th with a peak intensity of 90 mph and a central pressure of 973 millibars.||Hurricane force winds moved across the coastal waters south of Port Aransas while tropical storm force winds occurred over the coastal waters north of Port Aransas. Wave heights rose to 20 feet over the Gulf waters according to offshore buoys. Surge damaged the navigation markers and aids along the Corpus Christi ship channel.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet data and radar data indicated tropical storm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed over the northern Detroit Metro Area, with some wind damage and heavy rain reported. Rainfall totals of 3 to 4 inches in and around Ferndale lead to flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Eight mile road near Ferndale and Detroit was flooded, along with many side streets. Basements were also reported flooded in Ferndale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms moving through the area caused extreme water level fluctuations on Lake St. Clair, St. Clair River, and southern Lake Huron, which lead to lakeshore flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The water level rapidly rose 10 inches at the mouth of the St. Clair River, peaking out just over 70 inches above LWD at Algonac early in the afternoon. Emergency management reported a number of homes and secondary roads were impacted due to the flooding in Algonac. Standing water was also observed on roadways in Clay and Ira townships. Many homes and yards along the various canals also experienced minor flooding. In addition, the water level at Fort Gratiot peaked out a little over 73 inches above LWD around noon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of Friday, July 17th, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms that developed across northwest Minnesota, propagated south-southeast across central Minnesota and became a well defined bow echo segment. There were two areas that had the worst damage. One occurred in Stevens County where a swath of wind damage extended 3/4 of a mile to the southeast of Chokio, and about 1/4 of a mile wide. Many trees were snapped off just above the base, while others were uprooted. The second area was associated with straight-line winds, occasional downbursts, and two tornadoes that hit northern Isanti, and northern Chisago Counties. ||There was ample instability and wind shear during the evening to hold supercell characteristics along this bow echo segment. As the storm bowed out to the southeast late in the evening, less instability and wind shear diminished the organized nature of the bow segment. However, a one bow echo segment allowed for two tornadic storms near Day and Rush City.  ||There was continued weakening of this bow echo overnight, with more individual line segments which caused brief, and isolated wind damage. Even local airport wind sensors, and private wind sensors were measuring wind gusts in the 40 to 50 mph range past midnight LST. The exception was in the Twin Cities metro area where the Flying Cloud airport measured a wind gust of 59 mph, and the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport measured a wind gust of 55 mph.

Scattered thunderstorms developed over west central Wisconsin, ahead of a cold front across eastern Minnesota early Thursday morning. The storms over eastern Minnesota developed an outflow boundary which led to additional thunderstorms development over western Wisconsin. Although a few large hail stones occurred and minor wind damage reported, most of the storms were sub-severe.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A downburst likely occurred in the city of Menomonie as a few power lines were blown down, and a large tree was snapped off 10 feet above the ground on the north side of Menomonie.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved into the region on the 26th and meandered across the region through the 31st before an unseasonably strong upper level low pressure system moved east of the region. A very moist airmass and slow movement of the upper level system led to periods of very heavy rainfall each day. The most notable heavy rain event occurred across St. Clair County between Osceola and Lowry City. Over 7 inches of rain fell in a period of a few hours during the early morning of the 31st and led to flash flooding which washed out several roads and bridges and shut down the south bound lane of Highway 13. One public observer from Osceola measured over 11 inches of rain from 3 AM to 9 AM.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous locations across Morgan County received more than 2 inches of rain over a 24 hour period. The heaviest rains fell in the Stover and Versailles areas with between 2.00 and 4.51 inches of rainfall measured by Co-op observers, Mesonet stations and the public.

Extensive line of thunderstorms brought widespread severe wind to much of south central Nebraska and portions of north central Kansas on this date. This event will likely go down as the most widespread severe weather event of the spring and summer of 2020 for the Hastings County Warning Area (CWA). Thunderstorms developed along a cold front across north central Nebraska, and also within a zone of low level upslope flow over western Nebraska and northeast Colorado, during the early evening hours of July 8th. Both areas of development initially contained line segments and embedded supercells, posing risks for all severe hazards, but quickly organized into two separate lines of convection, or quasi linear convective systems (QLCSs). By 9pm CDT, one line extended roughly west to east from Thedford, NE to O'Neill, NE and was moving southeast, while the other line extended roughly north to south from near Thedford, NE to just west of McCook, NE and was moving mainly east. Shortly thereafter, both lines began to merge together into one coherent line and produced several instances of 60-75 mph wind gusts and isolated severe hail north/northwest of the CWA. Thunderstorms increased in organization into a bow echo over Furnas and Gosper Counties in Nebraska, then entered far western/northwestern portions of north central Kansas between 10:30-11pm CDT. By 11pm CDT, the QLCS had taken on an ���S��� shape, slanting southwest to northeast. The greatest concentration of severe wind reports occurred north of the state line, however, several severe wind reports were also reported roughly along and north of Highway 36 between 11pm CDT on July 8th and 1am CDT on July 9th as forward speed increased dramatically. Peak wind gusts across north central Kansas generally remained 60-65mph. The only known damage was to a roof of a mobile home in Mitchell County, though at least minor tree and crop damage likely occurred across at least portions of the area as well. The leading edge of the QLCS, and associated peak wind threat, shifted east and southeast of the CWA by 1AM CDT, though lingering stratiform rain as well as a northwest to southeast band of thunderstorms near the state line continued for a few more hours. Severe hail associated with this activity remained just north of the state line, over Furnas County, where regenerating thunderstorms were most intense.||Meteorologically speaking, this severe wind event was driven largely by a cold front interacting with a strongly unstable airmass due to steep mid level lapse rates, strong heating, and moist boundary layer. Initially cellular activity quickly grew upscale into line segments owing to the linear forcing along the cold front and generally outflow dominated activity, with peak DCAPE values in excess of 1500 J/kg. The primary shortwave trough responsible for the cold front remained well north of the area, near the Montana/Canadian border, but several weak perturbations moving west to east over the cold front likely aided in thunderstorm development as well. A distinct mesoscale convective vortex, modest deep layer shear of 30-35 knots, and an intensifying southerly low level jet up to 45 knots sustained the severe convection well past sunset. Finally, it's worth noting that an impressive surface pressure rise/fall couplet of at least 3mb/2hr accompanied the QLCS across the CWA between 05Z and 07Z.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extensive line of thunderstorms brought widespread severe wind to much of south central Nebraska and portions of north central Kansas on this date. This event will likely go down as the most widespread severe weather event of the spring and summer of 2020 for the Hastings County Warning Area (CWA). Thunderstorms developed along a cold front across north central Nebraska, and also within a zone of low level upslope flow over western Nebraska and northeast Colorado, during the early evening hours of July 8th. Both areas of development initially contained both line segments and embedded supercells, posing risks for all severe hazards, but quickly organized into two separate lines of convection, or quasi linear convective systems (QLCSs). By 9pm CDT, one line extended roughly west to east from Thedford, NE to O'Neill, NE and was moving southeast, while the other line extended roughly north to south from near Thedford, NE to just west of McCook, NE and was moving mainly east. Shortly thereafter, both lines began to merge together into one coherent line. Thunderstorms began to enter far northern and western portions of the CWA around 10pm CDT. By this time, thunderstorms already had a history of producing 60 to 75 mph wind gusts and a few instances of large hail just northwest and west of the CWA. The line of thunderstorms strengthened and organized further as they shifted southeast into the CWA between 10-11pm CDT. In fact, an impressive bow echo developed over Gosper and Furnas Counties during this time and raced eastward, affecting areas primarily between Interstate 80 in south central Nebraska and Highway 36 in north central Kansas. Severe wind gusts remained the primary threat. The QLCS had taken on an ���S��� shape by 11pm CDT, slanting southwest to northeast. The greatest concentration of severe wind reports occurred over central and eastern portions of the CWA, roughly from Grand Island and Hastings eastward to York and Hebron, between 11pm CDT on July 8th and 1am CDT on July 9th as forward speed increased dramatically. Several wind gusts were measured between 70-75mph in this area, including a peak wind gust of 75mph in Thayer County. Not surprisingly, widespread wind damage was reported, as well, especially to trees, power lines, and crops. Downed tree limbs (medium to large size) and snapped small trees were fairly common. Power outages were also common across many small towns during the overnight and into the early morning hours, though an exact estimation of peak power outages is unknown. A few buildings also sustained damage, such as blown in doors and roof damage from fallen trees and lost shingles. Finally, a brief EF-0 tornado was determined to have occurred in Merrick County, with peak winds estimated to be around 85mph. Damage was limited. The leading edge of the QLCS, and associated peak wind threat, shifted east and southeast of the CWA by 1AM CDT, though lingering stratiform rain as well as a northwest to southeast band of thunderstorms near the state line continued for a few more hours. The only severe hail reported with this event was along the southwest flank of the QLCS over Furnas County, where thunderstorms continued to regenerate. A few instances of quarter to golf ball size hail was reported.||Meteorologically speaking, this severe wind event was driven largely by a cold front interacting with a strongly unstable airmass due to steep mid level lapse rates, strong heating, and moist boundary layer. Initially cellular activity quickly grew upscale into line segments owing to the linear forcing along the cold front and generally outflow dominated activity, with peak DCAPE values in excess of 1500 J/kg. The primary shortwave trough responsible for the cold front remained well north of the area, near the Montana/Canadian border, but several weak perturbations moving west to east over the cold front likely aided in thunderstorm development as well. A distinct mesoscale convective vortex, modest deep layer shear of 30-35 knots, and an intensifying southerly low level jet up to 45 knots sustained the severe convection well past sunset. Finally, it's worth noting that an impressive surface pressure rise/fall couplet of at least 3mb/2hr accompanied the QLCS across the CWA between 05Z and 07Z.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorms. Broad high pressure remained in control, though a weak low pressure lingered around the MS/AL coastline with an associated surface boundary stretching from east TX through the FL panhandle and into the western Atlantic. This allowed for an increase in thunderstorms along the east coast that brought gusty winds and hail to portions of Broward County.

Estimated wind gusts near 60 mph based primarily on magnitude of damage as well as strength of storm observed on radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Lightning West wildfire began about twelve miles east southeast of Plemons Texas in Hutchinson County around 1650CST. The wildfire consumed six thousand five hundred and ten acres. The cause of the wildfire was determined to be from lightning. There were two homes and two other structures threatened by the wildfire but were saved. There were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The Texas A&M Forest Service along with the Booker VFD, the Fritch VFD, Hardin County ESD #5, the Skellytown VFD, Borger Fire Department, Crutch Ranch VFD, the Hoover VFD, Miami/Roberts County VFD, Panhandle Fire Department, Perryton Fire Department, and White Deer VFD responded to the wildfire. The wildfire was contained around 2000CST on July 12 and brought under control around 1500CST on July 16.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought (D2) to extreme drought (D3) existed in the southwest half of the county going into the first week of July. Some beneficial monsoonal rainfall fell in the northern half of the county eroding the the D2 conditions in the portions of the northwest while D2 and D3 conditions began to appear in all of the southern areas along the county line into Gray County.  Wells were struggling to keep up with irrigation demand. Pasture and rangeland conditions were reported as very poor to fair. Reports were made of very short to short topsoil and subsoil moisture levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of tropical storm Cristobal moved north-northeast across eastern Iowa, and into southwest and central Wisconsin during the evening of Tuesday, June 9th. The circulation associated with the system brought record high precipitable water values across parts of the Upper Midwest. These high values combined with a nearly stationary area of showers and embedded thunderstorms that moved from southeast Minnesota, northeast into west central Wisconsin, produced high rainfall rates and amounts. By the time the system moved out of the area, two to four inches of rainfall occurred in less than 3-6 hours. These high rainfall values caused several roads to become impassable in portions of Eau Claire and Chippewa Counties of west central Wisconsin. One road near Cadott was washed out, and another road was closed for several hours near Allen, or south of Eau Claire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads became impassable during this flash flooding event, including County Road D by Marshall Road where the Beaver Creek went out of its banks.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong storm system moved across the area the afternoon of the 8th into the morning of the 9th.  This system produced severe thunderstorms and high winds, across northeast Colorado, with snow across the mountains, valley areas and higher foothills.  In addition rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches occurred across the plains.   Storm totals included:  15 inches, 9 miles south-southeast of Gould and 7 miles northwest of Red Feather Lakes; 11 inches near Cameron Pass; with 4 to 10 inches elsewhere.  Strong northwest winds developed across the northeast plains on the evening of the 8th into the early morning hours of the 9th, with peak gusts from 58 to 71 mph.  ||Severe thunderstorms  on the evening of the 8th, produced powerful and destructive wind gusts along with nickel to quarter size hail, over portions of northeast Colorado.  Peak wind gusts up to 80 mph occurred, with localized gusts from 100 to 113 mph, in and near Akron.  The swath of damaging winds extended from central Washington County into Logan County and across western areas of Phillips and Sedgwick counties.  Widespread crop and property damage was observed.

Several county and township roads near the river remained under water at the start of the month, with inundation of agricultural land the primary impact thereafter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A vigorous upper-level low pressure center moved east from southern Colorado across south central Kansas through the late afternoon on Tuesday, June 9, 2020. As it did, a surface low deepened and moved east across Kansas pushing a cold front south across the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles before moving into western Texas. The cold front moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle early in the morning and quickly swept south through through the Texas Panhandle, continuing to move across the region. A strong pressure gradient between the low over Kansas and high pressure surging southeast out of Colorado created very strong winds across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles behind the front, which lasted into the early evening.||Across the northern half of the Texas Panhandle, sustained winds increased into the 40 to greater than 50 MPH range out of the north to northwest, with gusts mainly in the 55 to 65 MPH range. Farther south, sustained winds generally ranged from 37 to 46 MPH with gusts mainly in the 50 to 60 MPH range. These strong winds lasted most of the day before finally diminishing from west to east beginning in the late afternoon. Although the relative humidity was only 15 to 35 percent across the northwestern two-thirds of the Texas Panhandle, the high winds and dry fuels associated with recent onset of moderate to extreme drought in the area led to a high wildfire danger across part of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The West Texas Mesonet station  3 miles north-northeast of Umbarger measured sustained winds in the 40 to 46 MPH range during this time period. The highest sustained wind of 46 MPH occurred at 1254CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of Sunday, June 28th, a complex of thunderstorms that developed across Iowa previously, moved slowly northward across southern Minnesota before stalling in central Minnesota Monday morning. Before the torrential rain began in south central Minnesota, a few of the storms caused minor damage to a home in Sibley County. ||Deep moisture convergence along the axis of thunderstorms, training along the periphery of the the numerous boundaries, combined with PWAT values of 1.7 to 1.9 inches which is over the 99th percentile value, caused extreme rainfall rates. ||There were two specific areas that the storms trained for a few hours and caused rainfall amounts of 4 of 8 inches. The first started around midnight just north of the Minnesota River Valley from Olivia, east-southeast to Winthrop, and Gaylord. Based on the return period from precipitation amounts in a specific time frame, the values were a 100-200 year event. Flash flood guidance values were 2 to 3 times above normal. As this area began to diminish, another area formed southeast of this area. The main area that received rainfall rates as high as 2 inches per hour occurred from southwest of New Ulm, northeast to St. Peter, and south of Montgomery. Other areas also received very heavy rainfall amounts in the south and southeast part of the Twin Cities metro area where locally 3 to 6 inches fell, with the heavier amounts of 6.04 inches over Afton, 5.55 inches near Burnsville, and 5.43 inches over Cottage Grove. ||As the runoff continued through the morning, the flash flood event become more areal flooding as the flood waters receded into creeks, streams, and eventually the mainstem rivers. ||Some of the highest rainfall totals around the area are as follows.||7 miles south of Bird Island, 7.56 inches. |5 miles north of Lake Crystal, 7.45 inches.|3 miles southwest of Kasota, 6.74 inches. |4 miles north of Miesville, 6.37 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a 12 hour rainfall report near Miesville of 5.86 inches.

As convection grew upscale and moved into southern Iowa the severe threat diminished, though heavy rain continued to fall through the evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms developed across eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Saturday, July 11, producing widespread wind damage and very large hail. The first line of storms came through during the morning, producing damaging wind gusts and reports of quarter to ping pong ball size hail from Independence to Tipton Iowa. A wind gust of 65 MPH was measured just west of Independence. The second round of thunderstorms developed as a result of an upper level disturbance interacting with an atmosphere characterized by extremely high instability with modest vertical wind shear. Activity initially formed in north central Iowa, producing golf ball to two inch hail from Fort Dodge to Waterloo Iowa. Eventually, storms made their way towards the Cedar Rapids/Iowa City metro areas, producing widespread wind damage and hail up to baseball size. These storms continued through the Quad Cities metro east towards Princeton, Sterling, and Hennepin Illinois, producing additional reports of wind damage and winds of 70 to 90 mph. Numerous power outages were also reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated 60 mph winds also reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna, the 2020 Atlantic season's first Hurricane, made landfall along the unpopulated Padre Island National Seashore on the mid-Kenedy County coastline as a Category 1 storm at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. The hurricane spun slowly but steadily into southern Kenedy and northern Hidalgo County through just after midnight on the 26th, then through Starr County as a Tropical Storm before moving into Tamaulipas before daybreak and eventually near Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, by noon before dissipating during the evening of the 26th. Following the passage of the inner eye wall, broad feeder bands of torrential rains and gusty tropical storm force winds continued through the mid to late morning hours of July 26th, slowly migrating from east to west across the populated Rio Grande Valley. ||Other than storm surge flooding, which peaked just north of Baffin Bay on the Kleberg and Nueces County coast near Corpus Christi, Hanna's memory for the Rio Grande Valley will be flooding rainfall, power outages, and an array of damage to poorly constructed buildings, from minor roof damage to complete demolition.  Between 8 and 15 inches of rain fell from Port Mansfield to Harlingen, and along Interstate Highway 2 out through Mission and Sullivan City. The combination of high rainfall, locally high rainfall rates, and poor drainage left between 18 inches and four feet of water depth in many areas, most commonly from western Cameron through southeastern Hidalgo County, as well as a separate pocket in the Mission/La Joya/Sullivan City area. The rainfall wiped out 95% of the region's cotton crop; the combination of crop loss and production loss was more than one third of a billion dollars alone ($366 million)...most of which was in the Rio Grande Valley region.  ||At the peak of the storm, 250 thousand electric customers were without power, including all of Willacy County. Though storm surge was cut short by strong westerly flow across Cameron County, radiating swells did produce a notable surge of 3 feet or greater (estimated) from near Port Mansfield through Kenedy County. When the damage and economic loss is counted to infrastructure and agriculture combined, it is likely that Hanna cost at least one billion dollars across the Rio Grande Valley and the Deep S. Texas ranch country.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna moved across the western Gulf of Mexico and made landfall on the mid-Kenedy County coastline at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. While there aren't many observations in Kenedy County during this event, Buoy RSJT2 is just off the coastline in the Laguna Madre that borders this county and can be used as a reasonable proxy. Peak winds reached 71 mph with a gust to 103 mph. With observations from RSJT2, along with radar analysis, it is reasonable to assume that portions of Kenedy County experienced hurricane-force winds around 14:00 CST to 16:30 CST. At this time, impacts/loss to livestock costs are unknown for this area.||An NWS employee and a national storm chaser each reported hundreds of trees and large limbs blown down along U.S. 77 in central/west central Kenedy County immediately after and during the week following the hurricane. It was unknown what type of damage was done to ranch buildings across the county.

Temperatures soared into the 90s throughout much of eastern New York on July 19th, reaching as high as the mid to upper 90s in the Hudson and Mohawk Valleys. The combination of the heat and a humid airmass brought heat indices into the 95 to 105 degree range. The heat prompted the opening of cooling centers and pools, but with reduced capacity due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic. In addition, a line of thunderstorms moved in from the west during the evening, resulting in a few reports of wind damage in the Schoharie and Mid-Hudson Valleys. Heat indices exceeded 95 degrees again in some of the lower elevations of the Hudson Valley again on July 20th, but were not quite as high as the previous day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across southern Pennsylvania during the afternoon and early evening hours on July 21, 2020 in a low-CAPE, and relatively modest shear environment. These storms produced sporadic wind damage as they pushed eastward across southern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm microburst produced straight line wind damage near the town of Ashtola, Pennsylvania, which is about 4 miles SE of Windber. Approximately 75-100 trees on private property just west of the Gallitzin State Forest and east of Crum Rd were downed by strong winds. Most of the damage was confined to an area about 100 yards wide and 500 yards long. Winds were estimated at 85-95 mph. We thank Somerset County and Ogle Township Emergency Management for providing aerial imagery for the damage analysis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed across southern Pennsylvania during the afternoon and early evening hours on July 21, 2020 in a low-CAPE, and relatively modest shear environment. These storms produced sporadic wind damage as they pushed eastward across southern Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm microburst produced straight line wind damage in Fayetteville, PA. Approximately 100 trees were downed by strong winds along a path approximately 700 yards long and 100 yards wide. Most of this damage occurred in a forested area alongside the road between 1640 and 1350 Woodstock Rd. In addition to this concentrated swath of damage, peripheral wind damage was scattered between Fayetteville and Chambersburg, including several isolated instances of trees down and damage to roofs of buildings. Wind in this area was estimated at 70-80 mph. A roof was ripped off a warehouse building on the 1600 block of Lincoln Highway. Another roof was partially removed from a building on the 1700 block of Lincoln Highway. A roof was partially removed from a barn and a shed was destroyed on the 2500 block of Grant Point Rd. One person was injured when a tree fell onto a person in Chambersburg. We thank the Civil Air Patrol for providing aerial imagery that was used in this damage analysis.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low moved northeastward across James Bay during the early afternoon through early evening of the 19th. Simultaneously, the trailing cold front swept southeastward from northern Lower Michigan and central Illinois to Lake Huron, far-northwest Ohio, and west-central Indiana. Ahead of the front, scattered thunderstorms with damaging wind gusts occurred within a humid warm sector across northern Ohio. The warm sector exhibited primarily moderate to strong instability and moderate DCAPE amidst moderate vertical wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and branches down in Perrysburg.

This thunderstorm continued southeast and impacted Kearney with 60-70mph winds, including a 61mph gust at the Kearney Airport. Additional severe wind reports, and even some quarter to half dollar size hail, occurred in Kearney County before the system weakened as it neared the state line during the late evening. These thunderstorms were supported by MLCAPE values of 2000-3000 J/kg, steep mid level lapse rates, and very strong effective shear of 50-60kt. ||The next round of thunderstorms brought high winds to central and northern portions of the area between 11PM CDT on the 10th, and 1AM CDT on the 11th. This round of severe weather actually stemmed from thunderstorms that developed well northwest of the area, across southeast Montana and northeast Wyoming, during the afternoon hours of July 10th. Weakening had been noted around midnight as the leading edge shifted into the northwest CWA, likely impacted by the remnant cool, drier outflow from the first wave resulting in decreasing surface based instability and increasing inhibition. However, a mesohigh quickly developed over north central Nebraska, which resulted in a rapidly increasing low level pressure gradient force and strong pressure rises. In fact, pressure rises on the order of 8-9mb/2 hr were noted at both Ord and Grand Island ASOSs. The pressure rises allowed strong wind to develop, despite an overall weakening trend within the convection itself. Multiple reports of 55-65mph wind gusts occurred with this second round of activity, impacting areas from Ord to Hastings, including Grand Island, east to the York area. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After almost a two year hiatus, drought conditions returned to the South Plains of West Texas in July. Some areas of the South Plains experienced much below normal rainfall in the spring months. The most extreme deficits occurred in both Yoakum and Terry Counties which saw rainfall amounts between four and five inches below normal. Much of the area in these counties were raised to D2 (Severe Drought) or D3 (Extreme Drought) by the end of July. These same drought levels also covered the extreme southwestern and south-central Texas Panhandle southward into the northern South Plains. These additional areas of drought experienced rainfall deficits around 1.5 inches. The lack of rainfall contributed to the extreme heat that was observed in July. At Lubbock Preston Smith International Airport, an all-time July temperature record was set on the 14th of 111 degrees Fahrenheit. The mean temperature for July was 85.5 degrees Fahrenheit. This value was the second warmest July on record only to the year 2011 when the last D4 (Exceptional Drought) occurred.||Dryland crops had mostly failed by June with the lack of significant rainfall in addition to isolated hail storms destroying crops. Some irrigated crops were generally in poor to very poor condition due to deteriorating soil moisture. Despite the very dry conditions across the South Plains and extreme southern Texas Panhandle, there was a lack of significant wildfire activity. No known estimates of crop losses were known at this time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge that had been dominant over the Southern Plains and Ark-La-Tex region to start the first couple of days of July had weakened by July 3rd, with a weak upper level disturbance sliding south into Southeast Oklahoma, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. A complex of showers and thunderstorms that developed over Central and Southern Arkansas during the evening of the 2nd reinforced a weak surface trough southwest into extreme Southeast Oklahoma, Northeast Texas, and North Louisiana during the morning hours of the 3rd, with this boundary focusing an area of compressional heating and moisture pooling throughout the day. As a result, afternoon temperatures climbed into the lower to middle 90s, with limited mixing of dewpoints resulting in oppressive heat indices of 105-110 degrees across extreme Southeast Oklahoma, adjacent sections of Southwest Arkansas, extreme Northeast Texas, and Western Louisiana from late morning through the mid afternoon hours. However, showers and thunderstorms developed along this boundary by early afternoon, with this complex of storms shifting west southwest across the region during the afternoon, resulting in much cooler conditions and relief to the oppressive heat.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: With one to four inches of liquid residing in the snowpack at the start of the month near and north of Interstate 90, a more or less ideal melting of the winter snowpack in early March combined with high base flows and wet antecedent conditions to produce minor to major flooding along middle and lower portions of the James River Basin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The James River near Yankton (gage site YNNS2) returned to flood around 0300CST on March 8, and crested in major flood stage on March 20, 4.09 feet above flood stage.  Significant flooding of agricultural lands near the river was the largest impact, with the water encroaching on southwest Jim River Rd. near 301st St.  The river remained at moderate flood stage at the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of wintry precipitation impacted portions of eastern New York on the 6th and 7th. The first was a round of light to moderate snow after midnight on 6th to around sunrise, which resulted in one to five inches of snow along and north of the I-88/I-90 corridor. Then, periods of freezing rain occurred from the afternoon of the 6th into the morning of the 7th mainly along and north of I-90. Reports of a quarter to a half an inch of ice accretion were received in the western Mohawk Valley and southern Adirondacks into Washington County. The freezing rain quickly turned to heavy snow during the afternoon of the 7th as a strong low pressure system passed south of the area. This round of snow resulted in a quick 6-12 inches of accumulation in the Mohawk Valley, southern Adirondacks, and Lake George Saratoga Region, with snowfall rates of one to two inches per hour were common. In the wake of the snowfall, westerly winds gusted to 40-55 miles per hour in the afternoon and evening of the 7th, highest south of I-90.||The weight of the heavy snow and ice on trees along with strong winds resulted in numerous reports of downed trees and powerlines. Nearly 90,000 customers lost power, with Saratoga (46,000) and Warren (22,000) Counties being hit the hardest. Over half of Warren County was without power, prompting warming shelters to be opened. Several accidents occurred due to the snowy and icy roads across the southern Adirondacks and Lake George Saratoga Region, including one fatality in Mayfield, and major damage to a fire engine in Chester. A man in Lake Luzerne was injured when he was pierced in the leg while driving a vehicle, and a Thurman Highway Department truck was damaged when a tree fell onto it. Travel was discouraged due to the conditions in Saratoga Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna was the first hurricane of the 2020 Atlantic Basin hurricane season and made landfall on the lower Texas coast north of Port Mansfield on the afternoon of the 25th. Hanna was the first hurricane to make landfall in Texas since Hurricane Harvey.||Hanna began as a tropical wave, first noted for possible development when it was near Hispaniola on the 19th. The tropical wave moved northwest across Cuba into the central Gulf of Mexico where it became a tropical depression on the morning of the 22nd. Tropical Storm Hanna formed late in the evening on the 23rd as it moved west-northwest over the central Gulf of Mexico. Hanna continued to strengthen and became a hurricane on the morning of the 25th around 100 miles east of the Middle Texas coast. Hurricane Hanna turned to the southwest and made landfall north of Port Mansfield, late in the afternoon on the 25th with a peak intensity of 90 mph and a central pressure of 973 millibars.||Hurricane force winds moved across the coastal waters south of Port Aransas while tropical storm force winds occurred over the coastal waters north of Port Aransas. Wave heights rose to 20 feet over the Gulf waters according to offshore buoys. Surge damaged the navigation markers and aids along the Corpus Christi ship channel.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Offshore buoy and radar data indicated tropical storm winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A bowing line of severe thunderstorms tracked from western into central North Dakota during the evening of Tuesday, July 7th. Slightly after midnight CDT, July 8th, storms out ahead of the main bowing segment entered the Barnes/Griggs county area. Eventually the main bowing segment tracked through Griggs and Steele counties before weakening. North of the main bowing segment, strong winds also tracked through portions of Benson and Ramsey counties. After 3 am CDT, a second bowing line of storms took shape over Richland County, North Dakota, which tracked through Otter Tail County, Minnesota. This segment also produced very strong winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado began in Wilkin County, but ended in Otter Tail County, on the north side of Fergus Falls. The tornado was wrapped in downburst winds and rain, with a total track length of about 11 miles. The tornado uprooted or snapped numerous trees in shelterbelts along its path. It also snapped a few power poles and tore the roof off and collapsed the walls at a welding and manufacturing shop near the Fergus Falls airport. Peak winds were estimated at 100 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of Friday, July 17th, a line of strong to severe thunderstorms that developed across northwest Minnesota, propagated south-southeast across central Minnesota and became a well defined bow echo segment. There were two areas that had the worst damage. One occurred in Stevens County where a swath of wind damage extended 3/4 of a mile to the southeast of Chokio, and about 1/4 of a mile wide. Many trees were snapped off just above the base, while others were uprooted. The second area was associated with straight-line winds, occasional downbursts, and two tornadoes that hit northern Isanti, and northern Chisago Counties. ||There was ample instability and wind shear during the evening to hold supercell characteristics along this bow echo segment. As the storm bowed out to the southeast late in the evening, less instability and wind shear diminished the organized nature of the bow segment. However, a one bow echo segment allowed for two tornadic storms near Day and Rush City.  ||There was continued weakening of this bow echo overnight, with more individual line segments which caused brief, and isolated wind damage. Even local airport wind sensors, and private wind sensors were measuring wind gusts in the 40 to 50 mph range past midnight LST. The exception was in the Twin Cities metro area where the Flying Cloud airport measured a wind gust of 59 mph, and the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport measured a wind gust of 55 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A measured wind report of 53 knots from a private weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms that developed over the Dakotas Tuesday evening moved eastward across western Minnesota after midnight. Gusty winds accompany the strongest storms as they moved out of the Dakotas with numerous measured surface observations of 40 to 50 mph. The highest measured wind speed near Donnelly occurred at Graceville where a Minnesota Department of Transportation wind sensor measured 42 mph. There was another wind gust of 53 mph at Big Stone RAWS station near the Minnesota/South Dakota border. A few stronger storms did develop in Stevens county where the wind damage occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm survey that was conducted by the local emergency manager, and storm chasers, concluded that a downburst caused wind damage from 4 miles southwest of Donnelly, to 2 miles northeast of Donnelly. The damage field was 1/2 mile wide and all the damage was to the east/northeast. All the damage outside of Donnelly was scattered trees blown down and some crop damage. There were multiple buildings in the town of Donnelly that had damage. Some siding and many shingles were blown off downtown structures. Some trees fell onto houses and buildings. Two metal buildings had their tin roofs partially removed and one had a steel garage door blown in.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed across extreme southeast Kansas before moving into southwest Missouri during the mid-afternoon and late afternoon hours as a very unstable airmass interacted with a stalled front. Severe straight-line winds caused damage to a couple barns near Baxter Springs in Cherokee County, Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two barns suffered minor to moderate damage on Ballard Avenue southwest of Baxter Springs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm developed over the eastern Twin Cities Metro area during the afternoon of Sunday, July 5th. This storm was nearly stationary for an hour and produced up to 2 inches of rainfall in a short period of time. Four separate flood reports were noted with roads temporarily closed around Maplewood.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were several reports of roads flooded due to rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches in a very short period of time. These heavy rainfall rates, combined with the urban area (mostly runoff from the streets), led to several flooded roads and a couple closures. Specifically, White Bear Avenue, Lakewood, and Maryland Streets were flooded at one point with stalled vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very intense storms developed across northeast Kansas during the early afternoon and moved through southeast Kansas during the late afternoon. Hail to the size of golf balls and wind gusts estimated at 70 mph occurred over Cherokee County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of thunderstorms developed across northwest Minnesota during the afternoon of Monday, July 13th. These storms developed and moved southeast toward central Minnesota during the late evening and produced large hail in Morrison County. ||Although there were no reports of large hail across Todd County from this same storm that produced half dollar size hail in Morrison County, there was a band, based on MRMS hail algorithm, from west of Browerville to east of Browerville earlier that likely produced half dollar size hail or larger.

A large area of showers and thunderstorms developed across southwest Minnesota during the early morning hours of Tuesday, July 14th. These storms moved northeast across southern Minnesota during the morning. One of the storms became severe in Dakota County and produced golf ball size hail east of Vermillion. Although hail wasn't reported southwest of Vermillion, based on radar, severe hail likely fell between Empire and Hampton before moving east of Vermillion where golf ball size hail fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed in the afternoon of Tuesday, July 14th across west central Wisconsin. These storms developed along a cold front with steep lapse rates and modest instability. Several storms merged over Eau Claire County and developed a small bow segment that produced wind damage in Augusta.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees and large tree branches were blown down on the northwest part of Augusta. A few trees also landed on power lines elsewhere in Augusta.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extensive line of thunderstorms brought widespread severe wind to much of south central Nebraska and portions of north central Kansas on this date. This event will likely go down as the most widespread severe weather event of the spring and summer of 2020 for the Hastings County Warning Area (CWA). Thunderstorms developed along a cold front across north central Nebraska, and also within a zone of low level upslope flow over western Nebraska and northeast Colorado, during the early evening hours of July 8th. Both areas of development initially contained both line segments and embedded supercells, posing risks for all severe hazards, but quickly organized into two separate lines of convection, or quasi linear convective systems (QLCSs). By 9pm CDT, one line extended roughly west to east from Thedford, NE to O'Neill, NE and was moving southeast, while the other line extended roughly north to south from near Thedford, NE to just west of McCook, NE and was moving mainly east. Shortly thereafter, both lines began to merge together into one coherent line. Thunderstorms began to enter far northern and western portions of the CWA around 10pm CDT. By this time, thunderstorms already had a history of producing 60 to 75 mph wind gusts and a few instances of large hail just northwest and west of the CWA. The line of thunderstorms strengthened and organized further as they shifted southeast into the CWA between 10-11pm CDT. In fact, an impressive bow echo developed over Gosper and Furnas Counties during this time and raced eastward, affecting areas primarily between Interstate 80 in south central Nebraska and Highway 36 in north central Kansas. Severe wind gusts remained the primary threat. The QLCS had taken on an ���S��� shape by 11pm CDT, slanting southwest to northeast. The greatest concentration of severe wind reports occurred over central and eastern portions of the CWA, roughly from Grand Island and Hastings eastward to York and Hebron, between 11pm CDT on July 8th and 1am CDT on July 9th as forward speed increased dramatically. Several wind gusts were measured between 70-75mph in this area, including a peak wind gust of 75mph in Thayer County. Not surprisingly, widespread wind damage was reported, as well, especially to trees, power lines, and crops. Downed tree limbs (medium to large size) and snapped small trees were fairly common. Power outages were also common across many small towns during the overnight and into the early morning hours, though an exact estimation of peak power outages is unknown. A few buildings also sustained damage, such as blown in doors and roof damage from fallen trees and lost shingles. Finally, a brief EF-0 tornado was determined to have occurred in Merrick County, with peak winds estimated to be around 85mph. Damage was limited. The leading edge of the QLCS, and associated peak wind threat, shifted east and southeast of the CWA by 1AM CDT, though lingering stratiform rain as well as a northwest to southeast band of thunderstorms near the state line continued for a few more hours. The only severe hail reported with this event was along the southwest flank of the QLCS over Furnas County, where thunderstorms continued to regenerate. A few instances of quarter to golf ball size hail was reported.||Meteorologically speaking, this severe wind event was driven largely by a cold front interacting with a strongly unstable airmass due to steep mid level lapse rates, strong heating, and moist boundary layer. Initially cellular activity quickly grew upscale into line segments owing to the linear forcing along the cold front and generally outflow dominated activity, with peak DCAPE values in excess of 1500 J/kg. The primary shortwave trough responsible for the cold front remained well north of the area, near the Montana/Canadian border, but several weak perturbations moving west to east over the cold front likely aided in thunderstorm development as well. A distinct mesoscale convective vortex, modest deep layer shear of 30-35 knots, and an intensifying southerly low level jet up to 45 knots sustained the severe convection well past sunset. Finally, it's worth noting that an impressive surface pressure rise/fall couplet of at least 3mb/2hr accompanied the QLCS across the CWA between 05Z and 07Z.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were estimated to be near 60 MPH.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Campbell Road wildfire began around 1801CST about twelve miles north northeast of Skellytown Texas in Hutchinson County. There was a report that one home was threatened by the wildfire but was saved, otherwise there were no reports of any homes or other structures threatened. There was a report of one injury, however no fatalities were reported. The wildfire consumed thirty-one hundred acres and spread into western Roberts County where the Texas A&M Forest Service received a request for assistance. The cause of the wildfire was determined to be from lightning. The Skellytown VFD, the Booker VFD, the Hoover VFD, the Miami/Roberts County VFD, the Panhandle Fire Department, the Perryton Fire Department, the White Deer VFD, and the Texas A&M Forest Service responded to the wildfire. The wildfire was contained and controlled by 1500CST on July 13.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At least some portion of the western Oklahoma Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since November of 2019. After the drought worsened and peaked in June, significant improvement occurred across the central and eastern portions of the Oklahoma Panhandle in July where monsoon rainfall led to 150 to 300 percent above normal rainfall. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 4 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement in those areas. However, some of the western Oklahoma Panhandle experienced only 50 to 75 percent of normal rainfall in July which lead to additional deficits of 1-2 inches for the month of July. Given this, Extreme Drought (D3) persisted in parts of the far western Oklahoma Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The western half of Beaver County was severe drought (D2) with small areas in the northwest and southwest in extreme drought (D3) going into July. The eastern half was only in moderate drought (D1) going into the month of July. For the first part of July most of the county degraded into severe drought (D2), although the D3 in the northwest did improve with some beneficial rainfall in the beginning of the month. During the third week of July, the county started to get enough rainfall to eliminate D2 conditions across the entire county. Abnormally dry (D0) to moderate drought (D1) conditions remained with the worse conditions noted across the northwest quarter of the county as Beaver and Slapout ended the month with just under 2 inches of rainfall which is just below normal.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The far northwest Texas Panhandle had been in Severe Drought (D2) since May, 2020. After the drought worsened and spread in June, significant improvement occurred especially across the northwest half of the Texas Panhandle in July as monsoon rainfall led to 125 to 200 percent above normal rainfall for many areas. This equated to rainfall of 1 to 2 inches above normal for the month and significant drought improvement if not drought removal in those areas. Meanwhile, portions of the southeast Texas Panhandle received below normal rainfall up to around 50 percent of normal, which equated to 1 to 2 inch deficits in July. This led to drought worsening and spread in these areas. By the end of the month, the Severe Drought (D2) continued across portions of the far southern and southeastern Texas Panhandle and pockets of Extreme Drought (D3) remained as well.||Some of the impacts to agriculture included but were not limited to the following. Corn especially, was largely harvested for silage in order to plant a secondary crop. Cotton crop had already been stunted even in areas that received meaningful rain towards the end of the month.  Irrigation was in full use especially in West Texas to include Oldham, Deaf Smith, Randall, and Armstrong County in the Texas Panhandle where drought conditions continue to persist.  Water supply for livestock continued to be low for much of the area in persistent D1 to D3 categories.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hemphill County were not so lucky in receiving monsoonal rainfall during the month of July as some nearby counties did. Just enough rain fell to roughly maintain severe drought (D2) in the southern portion of the county while only seeing a slight improvement in the north to the moderate drought (D1) conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Lift associated with a jet streak across southern North Dakota interacted with an unstable and weakly capped environment with 30 to 40 knots of deep-layer shear to produce a couple of smaller clusters of thunderstorms with large hail and damaging wind during the evening and overnight which progressed east and southeast across southeast South Dakota.  The final cluster was a larger-scale bowing segment which produced damaging wind gusts across south central South Dakota.  Repeated storms with heavy rainfall resulted in spotty flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roads were flooded over the curb in Armour, with water encroaching on several buildings. Numerous intersections along SD Highway 44 had standing water. Rainfall totaled 3.88 inches 3 miles south southwest of Corsica and 3.16 inches 5 miles west of Armour. Property damage costs are rough estimates.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracked from near Kansas City on the morning of July 15th to southern Lake Michigan by midnight on July 16th.  The low interacted with an unstable and very moist environment to produce a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) over eastern Kansas into Missouri, which then pushed into west-central Illinois by the mid to late morning of July 15th.  Several rounds of convection moved across the Illinois River Valley through the afternoon, producing heavy rain and isolated wind damage.  The heaviest rainfall of 5 to 7 inches was focused across Tazewell, Woodford, and far eastern Peoria counties where significant flash flooding occurred.  In addition, 5 weak tornadoes touched down...including 2 in Tazewell County, 1 in McLean County, 1 in Morgan County, and 1 in Montgomery County which then crossed into southern Sangamon County.  Minor damage was reported with some of the tornadoes: however, no injuries or deaths occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two inches of rain fell in about an hour, resulting in numerous flooded streets across Pekin.  Due to additional rainfall, water continued to rise through the afternoon and early evening with up to one foot of water reported on many roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Hanna, the 2020 Atlantic season's first Hurricane, made landfall along the unpopulated Padre Island National Seashore on the mid-Kenedy County coastline as a Category 1 storm at around 5 PM Central Time Saturday, July 25th, carrying sustained 90 mph winds with gusts over 100 mph in a small portion of the inner eye wall. The hurricane spun slowly but steadily into southern Kenedy and northern Hidalgo County through just after midnight on the 26th, then through Starr County as a Tropical Storm before moving into Tamaulipas before daybreak and eventually near Monterrey, Nuevo Leon, by noon before dissipating during the evening of the 26th. Following the passage of the inner eye wall, broad feeder bands of torrential rains and gusty tropical storm force winds continued through the mid to late morning hours of July 26th, slowly migrating from east to west across the populated Rio Grande Valley. ||Other than storm surge flooding, which peaked just north of Baffin Bay on the Kleberg and Nueces County coast near Corpus Christi, Hanna's memory for the Rio Grande Valley will be flooding rainfall, power outages, and an array of damage to poorly constructed buildings, from minor roof damage to complete demolition.  Between 8 and 15 inches of rain fell from Port Mansfield to Harlingen, and along Interstate Highway 2 out through Mission and Sullivan City. The combination of high rainfall, locally high rainfall rates, and poor drainage left between 18 inches and four feet of water depth in many areas, most commonly from western Cameron through southeastern Hidalgo County, as well as a separate pocket in the Mission/La Joya/Sullivan City area. The rainfall wiped out 95% of the region's cotton crop; the combination of crop loss and production loss was more than one third of a billion dollars alone ($366 million)...most of which was in the Rio Grande Valley region.  ||At the peak of the storm, 250 thousand electric customers were without power, including all of Willacy County. Though storm surge was cut short by strong westerly flow across Cameron County, radiating swells did produce a notable surge of 3 feet or greater (estimated) from near Port Mansfield through Kenedy County. When the damage and economic loss is counted to infrastructure and agriculture combined, it is likely that Hanna cost at least one billion dollars across the Rio Grande Valley and the Deep S. Texas ranch country.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The slowly weakening inner eyewall of Hurricane Hanna slid across southern and central Brooks County during the evening of July 25th, producing peak sustained winds (though incomplete) of 34 mph with a peak gust of 53 mph at the Brooks County Airport east of Falfurrias. Stronger winds, likely sustained at 40 to 45 mph with estimated gusts to 55 or 60 mph, were likely over the southern third of the county which experienced the more persistent rains and wind in the eyewall.  A storm survey conducted in southern Brooks County found dozens of large tree limbs down, but no significant structural damage, near Encino.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A sharp cold front lied across far southern Minnesota during the afternoon of Tuesday, June 2nd. Temperatures ahead of this front rose into the mid to upper 90s with 70s and 80s behind it. In addition, dew points dropped significantly behind the front across central Minnesota. ||During the late morning, and early afternoon, elevated convection developed across central Minnesota and moved eastward but continued to develop on the southwest flank. Numerous hail stones were reported, but most were sub-severe. A few stronger updrafts contributed to a few hail stones as large as golf ball size near Alexandria. As the storms moved farther to the southeast, reports of large hail was observed near Elk River. ||By the mid-late afternoon, severe thunderstorms developed along a cold front across far southern Minnesota. Initially, most of the reports were very large hail, south of the Minnesota River, from around Lake Crystal, Garden City, Vernon Center and Good Thunder. There was a measured hail stone of 2.5 inches in diameter near Garden City. There was another measured report of 2.0 inches near Waldorf.  ||All of the significant wind damage reports were from the areas around New Richland, Waldorf, Hollandale, Myrtle, Albert Lea, Lewisville, and other areas of south central Minnesota due to severe thunderstorm outflow winds.  The storms were |highly visible from miles away and dozens of people took pictures and video.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A semi truck was overturned east of Albert Lea on County Road 21.
