EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Beta initially developed as a disturbance in the Bay of Campeche early on September 10th. The system drifting around the Bay of Campeche for several days as development was unlikely due to unfavorable upper-level winds produced by nearby Hurricane Sally. This system eventually began to organize and became Tropical Depression Twenty-Two on September 17th and became Tropical Storm Beta on September 18th. The storm continued to intensify reaching a peak of 60mph winds and a central pressure of 994mb (29.36 inHg) on September 19th as the storm became nearly stationary after turning westward over the Gulf of Mexico. Tropical Storm Beta approached the Texas coast and weakened before making landfall on the Matagorda Peninsula on September 22nd with maximum sustained winds of 45mph and a pressure of 999mb (29.50 inHg).||A tight pressure gradient between Beta and an area of high pressure to the northeast resulted in persistent moderate to strong onshore east and northeast winds across the area. This caused an extended duration of impacts to the area between the days of September 19th and September 23rd. The strongest winds and highest water levels occurred when Beta's center of circulation was well removed from the local area and thus much of the local impacts were mainly confined to marine and coastal areas where tropical storm watches and warnings were in effect.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of minor storm surge inundation across coastal Jackson County, MS with observations ranging from 2.16 MHHW at the NOS site PNLM6 in Pascagoula on the 22nd at 02:24 CDT to 3.25 NAVD88 on the 22nd at 03:00 CDT at the USGS site OFBM6 Ocean Springs, MS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Sally initially formed as an area of disturbed weather over the Bahamas late on September 10th, 2020. Over the next few days, the system became better organized and became Tropical Depression Nineteen in the afternoon hours on September 11th. Later that night around midnight CDT on September 12th, TD Nineteen made landfall at Key Biscayne with peak winds of 35 mph and a central pressure of 1007mb (29.74 inHg). The system continued west emerging into the east-central Gulf of Mexico and quickly strengthened into a Tropical Storm later in the day on the 11th. This system continued to drift northwestward with time and strengthened into a hurricane in the morning hours on September 14th with maximum sustained winds of 85 mph and a central pressure of 985 mb (29.09 inHg) and continued to strengthen becoming a category 2 hurricane shortly after. Sally would then eventually weaken some, and slow down in forward speed before turning very slowly northwards making landfall near Gulf Shores, Alabama as a strong Category 2 hurricane with peak winds of 105 mph and a central pressure of 965mb (28.50 inHg) early in the morning hours on September 16th.||Impacts to southeastern Louisiana and southern Mississippi was mostly confined to coastal counties of southern Mississippi, southeastern Louisiana and adjacent marine areas. Main impacts included storm surge inundation for coastal areas, as well as some wind damage across portions of Jackson and Harrison County, MS while Hurricane Sally was making landfall east across Gulf Shores, AL. Rainfall was of little impact across coastal MS and westward with only small areas of rainfall totaling around 3 inches reported in eastern Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Areas impacted by flooding include Pass Christian, with several roadways flooded. Surge around Point Cadet in Biloxi with the bottom level of a parking garage flooded. Storm surge washed over parts of beach blvd near Bay St. Louis. Flooding of roadways occurred in Orange Grove, MS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level system impacted southern Colorado from September 8th through the 10th. This system brought an end to the above normal warmth, and provided the region with winter like weather. Strong northerly winds, heavy snow across the mountains and mountain valleys, and a wintry mix of rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain across parts of the I-25 corridor were all observed during this time. Additionally, well below normal temperatures brought an end to the growing season over much of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total of 11.9 inches of snow. Maysville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record breaking heatwave during the first week of September took a dramatic turn toward winter as a powerful storm system moved south through the Rocky Mountains on September 8, 2020. A powerful cold front shifted south and west through eastern New Mexico and plowed through gaps in the central mountain chain into the Rio Grande Valley on the morning of September 9, 2020. Canyon winds peaked during the late afternoon and evening hours when gusts of 70 to 80 mph were reported. These powerful winds affected the east side of the Albuquerque metro area for several hours before slowly tapering off through September 10, 2020. Dozens of trees, power lines, power poles, fences, and walls were blown down. Roof damage was also reported across the city. At least 15,000 customers were without power, and as many as a 1,000 customers had no power for three days after the event. Record breaking early snowfall also impacted the high terrain with this event. Many locations in the northern mountains reported two to six inches of snow while one to two inches fell at lower elevations of northern New Mexico. Fire and rescue personnel evacuated the Rio Chama RV Park as the combination of heavy snow and strong winds downed several large tree limbs onto at least two recreational vehicles. Several locations also set daily record low minimum and record low maximum temperatures on both September 9th and September 10th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust up to 89 mph was measured at the top of the Sandia Peak Tramway. The tram was closed for the day due to high winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Many areas across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw improvements in drought going into August. A couple of rain events help keep those areas from degradation during the month with some even improving by the end of the month. Northwest Cimarron County in Oklahoma was in extreme drought (D3) for the longest time until the end of the month after the August 29th event. An area in extreme drought in east central Texas Panhandle managed to leave the extreme drought category as well. However, the southwest Texas Panhandle kept missing out on rain with all storms passing to the north and northwest. Areas in severe drought and extreme drought are looking at a 6 to 12 inches deficit for rainfall year today. Many ranchers are either selling their cattle or buying feed as there are no rangeland grasses. Many dryland crops have failed thus far, even with the July and August rains that came just too late.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southern third of Hemphill County began the month in severe (D2) drought with less dire conditions across the north. In August,  slightly below average rainfall was received and enought to lead to removal of D2 drought conditions.  However, some moderate drought (D1) did persist across the south.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias was the first tropical storm to impact New Hampshire since 2011.  The center of the storm tracked west of the state, keeping the flooding rain associated with the storm across New York.  The primary impacts the storm brought to New Hampshire were gusty winds with widespread reports of wind gusts in the mid to upper 40s.  Numerous trees and branches were brought down with scattered power outages across the state.  An area of enhanced damage was concentrated in Carroll County as a squall line pushed through the region.  Concentrated tree damage toppled 100s of trees with one fatality being reported as a large crashed into the home. Overall storm impacts were brief with a period of gusty winds from the south to southeast on the evening of August 4th causing most of the damage.  There was no coastal flooding reported as the relatively minor storm surge of around a foot coincided at the time of low tide on the New Hampshire coast.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias brought moderate impacts to Sullivan County with scattered reports of trees and branches down leading to scattered power outages. Some damage occurred within an outer feeder band during the early and middle afternoon across the western half of the county. Isolated wind damage occurred during the evening hours when Isaias made its closest approach. Overall power outages for the county remained low with  15% of the county without power. No flooding was reported.

The center of the storm tracked well west of the state, keeping all the heavy rain associated with the storm across New York.  The primary impacts the storm brought to southwest Maine were gusty winds with widespread reports of wind gusts in the mid to upper 40s. Additional boat damage was also reported on some area lakes due to the strong winds.  Overall storm impacts were brief with a period of gusty winds from the south to southeast on the evening of August 4th causing most of the damage. A number of boats were grounded or sunk on Sebago lake, with a unverified home weather station reported wind gust on the lakefront of 66 mph.  Hundreds of trees were uprooted on the northern end of the lake. No flooding was reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Deep moisture returned to the lower mid-Atlantic region during the period August 12th - 15th, with precipitable water values ranging from 1.6 to 1.9 inches each day.  A frontal boundary stalled near the Interstate 64 corridor provided a trigger for convection, supported aloft by passing upper level disturbances. Strong daytime heating contributed to deep instability, resulting in thunderstorms with high rainfall rates.  Light winds aloft resulted in mean wind speeds generally 10 knots or less, indicating slow cell movement. Considering the moist antecedent conditions, flash flood watches were in effect each day through this period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Runoff due to heavy rain from a thunderstorm caused an unnamed creek to overflow its banks, and cause flooding of buildings nearby the intersection of 2nd Street and Statesville Road (Highway 115) in the town of North Wilkesboro.  The road reopened after flood waters receded.

An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico began to slowly slide back to the west on August 16th, as a weak cold front began to slide southeast across Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana. However, the combination of the upper ridge providing strong sinking motion, and compressional heating just ahead of the front over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulted in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during the 16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time as low level moisture pooled just ahead of the front, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly behind the weak mid-August cool front during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late morning through the afternoon of Monday August 10th, a line of intense thunderstorms known as a derecho brought widespread severe wind damage across Iowa, northern Illinois and northern Indiana.||In north central and northeast Illinois alone, the severe winds of 60 to 100 mph downed or damaged tens of thousands of trees, as well as caused severe damage to homes, businesses, and infrastructure.  There were 10 injuries reported in north central and northeast Illinois within the NWS Chicago/Romeoville County Warning Area (CWA).  Local officials estimated that nearly one million customers lost power across northern Illinois at the height of the derecho and some people were without power for several days.  Damage was estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars in north central and northeast Illinois, with several billions of dollars in damages across the entire Corn Belt region including significant damage to crops and agriculture infrastructure.  While much of the damage was due to straight line winds, there were also 14 tornadoes documented in north central and northeast Illinois.||The combination of high moisture, explosive instability and very strong atmospheric wind flow for mid-summer had developed quickly over the Corn Belt region on the morning of August 10th.  This resulted in a progressive, well-organized complex of storms for hundreds of miles and at times traveling nearly 70 mph.  After bringing extensive damage from extreme wind speeds in Iowa that morning, the damage transitioned across northern Illinois from widespread wind damage to narrow, brief and intense swaths associated with compact circulations within the thunderstorm line, some of which were associated with tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree limbs were blown down west of Roselle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico continued to provide strong sinking motion and thus compressional heating over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulting in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during August 15th-16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly as a weak mid-August cold front moved through the region during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front moved across the ArkLaMiss region during the afternoon and evening of August 16th. Ahead of the front, temperatures in the mid to upper 90s helped to create a very unstable airmass. Storms that developed across the Golden Triangle quickly became better organized and plowed across central Mississippi, affecting locations generally along and east of the I-55 corridor during the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms brought damaging winds to the region, which resulted in downed trees and power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Laura made landfall along the Louisiana coast near Lake Charles in the early morning hours of August 27. It moved north into Central Louisiana during the morning and afternoon before turning to the northeast and tracking through Arkansas. Impacts from Laura were felt far from the center of the storm, which was mainly in the form of tropical storm force winds across portions of northeast Louisiana and southeast Arkansas. Farther east, into Mississippi, the tight pressure gradient that resulted from Laura was the cause for gusty winds across portions of western Mississippi. Winds were sustained 30 to 35 mph, gusting to 45 to 49 mph across portions of northeast Louisiana, southeast Arkansas and the northwest portion of Mississippi. This resulted in downed trees and power lines across the region. Since Laura moved inland fairly quickly, rainfall totals were not high. Rainfall amounts up to four inches occurred along and west of the Mississippi River and this resulted in some minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor street flooding occurred in Collins. Minor flooding also occurred on Knights Road southwest of Collins.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon/early evening of August 10th, 2020, scattered severe thunderstorms created damage across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms eventually congealed into a line as they exited the eastern Panhandles. Several reports of hail between the size of Pennies and Quarters were reported across the area and a few storms produced up to golf ball size hail. Thunderstorm wind damage was reported along with a network of weather equipment measuring wind gusts near 70 MPH. Some of the more significant damage included a couple trailers which were completed totaled near Perryton, TX as well as 2 miles of power poles downed near Spearman, TX. In eastern Oklahoma Panhandle there was also some rural flooding reported near Knowles, OK from heavy rains.

An upper level disturbance high instability and moderate wind shear led to severe storm development across the Texas Panhandle. The strongest storm produced a swath of thunderstorm wind damage around 2 miles wide and 4 miles long occurred along the Fritch Highway near Webb Rd. Damage within the area included numerous broken or leaning power poles, downed power lines and damage to roofs, porches, and awnings at local residences, especially those facing west. In addition, many large tree limbs in the area were snapped and some out outbuildings and old barns in the area were destroyed. One single wide trailer was pushed off its blocks. Damage was consistent with straight line winds. All while this was going some places in north Amarillo saw large hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter and even some areas of accumulating hail up to 5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Late picture received of hail covering the ground up to 5 inches deep. Time estimated from radar and nearby reports.

A cluster of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa during the pre-dawn hours of August 10th.  As a moist and highly unstable airmass fed into the system, the storms quickly intensified and began racing eastward  as a derecho across Iowa into northern Illinois along a pre-existing boundary.  While the greatest damage and highest wind speeds remained along and north of the I-80 corridor, a trailing boundary sank southward into central Illinois creating wind gusts of 60-75 mph.  As a result, widespread wind damage was reported along and north of a Macomb...to Springfield...to Paris line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown over in Kickapoo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and central New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of September 2020. As one of the worst monsoon seasons on record came to end, moderate to extreme drought worsened to nearly 100 percent of the state of which 40 percent was deemed as extreme to exceptional drought. An anomalous early season winter storm brought high terrain snow and rain to most of the area during the first week of September. Precipitation totals across central and western New Mexico generally ranged from half an inch to three quarters an inch while precipitation totals neared an inch across north central and northeast New Mexico. Portions of the higher terrain of south central New Mexico fared better with totals generally near an inch and a half. Despite this, the second half of the month was mostly dry with more record heat which contributed to the worsening drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions from August 2020 continued in September.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled weak front extending across inland SE GA with a mid/upper level short wave trough moving over the boundary in the afternoon. Southerly steering over a very  moisture airmass with PWATs near 2.25 inches. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Sally initially formed as an area of disturbed weather over the Bahamas late on September 10th, 2020. Over the next few days, the system became better organized and became Tropical Depression Nineteen in the afternoon hours on September 11th. Later that night around midnight CDT on September 12th, TD Nineteen made landfall at Key Biscayne with peak winds of 35 mph and a central pressure of 1007mb (29.74 inHg). The system continued west emerging into the east-central Gulf of Mexico and quickly strengthened into a Tropical Storm later in the day on the 11th. This system continued to drift northwestward with time and strengthened into a hurricane in the morning hours on September 14th with maximum sustained winds of 85 mph and a central pressure of 985 mb (29.09 inHg) and continued to strengthen becoming a category 2 hurricane shortly after. Sally would then eventually weaken some, and slow down in forward speed before turning very slowly northwards making landfall near Gulf Shores, Alabama as a strong Category 2 hurricane with peak winds of 105 mph and a central pressure of 965mb (28.50 inHg) early in the morning hours on September 16th.||Impacts to southeastern Louisiana and southern Mississippi was mostly confined to coastal counties of southern Mississippi, southeastern Louisiana and adjacent marine areas. Main impacts included storm surge inundation for coastal areas, as well as some wind damage across portions of Jackson and Harrison County, MS while Hurricane Sally was making landfall east across Gulf Shores, AL. Rainfall was of little impact across coastal MS and westward with only small areas of rainfall totaling around 3 inches reported in eastern Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At the time of highest recorded water levels, around 100 low lying roads in the county were covered by varying depths of water with around 10 becoming impassable. Areas impacted by flooding include Waveland, with water over Beach Blvd, as well as flooding over roadways in Shoreline Park in Bay St. Louis, MS. Other reports include flooding around homes in the Riverview area near Bay St. Louis and flooding over roadways and under elevated houses in Kiln, MS. Observations from NOS and USGS sites ranged from 3.66 MHHW at WYCM6 Waveland on the 15th at 12:06 CDT to 5.49 NAVD88 at EPCM6 Claiborne on the 15th at 13:30 CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Badger Fire began on September 12th at around 5 pm MDT and continued through the rest of September.   It grew to near 90,000 acres and was located 20 miles southwest of Oakley.   High winds and extremely dry fuels caused rapid spread including long range spotting and fire whirls.   There was an evacuation order for all residents on private land in Rock Creek Canyon and Dry Creek on the 18th but was lifted on 8 AM on Sunday, September 20th.  The Sawtooth National Forest issued the Badger Fire Road, Trail and Area closure on September 15th.   Drones were prohibited over the area.   Main fuels were timber (litter and understory), heavy logging slash, sub-alpine fir, lodgepole pine, juniper, mountain brush and grass.  The fire was around 85 percent contained by the end of September.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record breaking heatwave during the first week of September took a dramatic turn toward winter as a powerful storm system moved south through the Rocky Mountains on September 8, 2020. A powerful cold front shifted south and west through eastern New Mexico and plowed through gaps in the central mountain chain into the Rio Grande Valley on the morning of September 9, 2020. Canyon winds peaked during the late afternoon and evening hours when gusts of 70 to 80 mph were reported. These powerful winds affected the east side of the Albuquerque metro area for several hours before slowly tapering off through September 10, 2020. Dozens of trees, power lines, power poles, fences, and walls were blown down. Roof damage was also reported across the city. At least 15,000 customers were without power, and as many as a 1,000 customers had no power for three days after the event. Record breaking early snowfall also impacted the high terrain with this event. Many locations in the northern mountains reported two to six inches of snow while one to two inches fell at lower elevations of northern New Mexico. Fire and rescue personnel evacuated the Rio Chama RV Park as the combination of heavy snow and strong winds downed several large tree limbs onto at least two recreational vehicles. Several locations also set daily record low minimum and record low maximum temperatures on both September 9th and September 10th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local media reported that fire and rescue teams evacuated around 50 campers at the Rio Chama RV park around 100 am due to falling tree branches. The weight of heavy snow on fully leafed out trees along with strong winds toppled dozens of large branches. At least one recreational vehicle was destroyed and another one was damaged. Minor injuries were reported however the extent of the injuries was not known. Damage amounts are estimated for total loss of two small RVs.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought persisted across northern Aroostok county during August. The severe drought across northern Aroostook county had developed in early July. Above average temperatures were reported during August. Rainfall was mostly due to showers and thunderstorms...which resulted in variable rain totals. Most areas received 40 to 70 percent of normal rainfall for August...though some localized areas did receive greater rain totals with thunderstorms. Widespread rain did not occur during August. In Caribou...the 3 month period from June to August was the warmest and second driest on record. |Streamflows during August were generally at 15 to 35 percent of normal. At month's end many larger rivers were at near record low levels. Grain crops were significantly impacted during August. Potatoes and other crops required extensive irrigation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The severe drought conditions which had developed in early July persisted through the month of August.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Many areas across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw improvements in drought going into August. A couple of rain events help keep those areas from degradation during the month with some even improving by the end of the month. Northwest Cimarron County in Oklahoma was in extreme drought (D3) for the longest time until the end of the month after the August 29th event. An area in extreme drought in east central Texas Panhandle managed to leave the extreme drought category as well. However, the southwest Texas Panhandle kept missing out on rain with all storms passing to the north and northwest. Areas in severe drought and extreme drought are looking at a 6 to 12 inches deficit for rainfall year today. Many ranchers are either selling their cattle or buying feed as there are no rangeland grasses. Many dryland crops have failed thus far, even with the July and August rains that came just too late.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southern third of Roberts County began the month in severe (D2) to extreme (D3) drought with less dire conditions across the north. In August, near average rainfall of 2 to 4 inches led to an end of the severe to extreme drought across the county, however some moderate drought (D1) did persist.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After making landfall in southwest Louisiana on Wednesday, August 26, 2020, Hurricane Laura moved northward into Arkansas and weakened to a tropical storm on Thursday, August 27, then traveled eastward across Tennessee and Kentucky and weakened further to a tropical depression on Friday, August 28. The system brought numerous showers and thunderstorms to Middle Tennessee, some of which became severe and produced several reports of damaging winds along with two weak tornadoes. Rainfall totals across the area ranged from 1 to 3 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A damage survey by Warren County Emergency Management along with video by nearby residents indicate a brief and weak EF-0 tornado intermittently touched down in extreme southwest Warren County between Morrison and Viola. One barn sustained significant damage on Cecil Laxson Road and several trees were blown down along the roadway and in adjacent orchards. Another small barn was destroyed on Fred Hoover Road with a damage path noted through adjacent corn fields. This is the first known tornado to occur in Warren County in the month of August.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tropical wave emerged off of Africa during August 16 and then developed into a depression by the 20th. The system gradually became better organized as it passed across the Greater Antilles. It entered the Gulf of Mexico and became a hurricane on the 25th. Outer bands spread inland during the afternoon of the 26th and it made landfall at Cameron at 1AM local time on the 27th as the first category 4 hurricane to landfall in Southwest Louisiana and the strongest Louisiana hurricane since 1856. The highest storm surge to ever be recorded also occurred from Laura which was approximately 21 feet at Rutherford Beach and Creole. Damages totaled roughly $10.7 Billion and 27 fatalities occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a voluntary evacuation for the parish. Many trees and power lines were blown down across the parish. Homes and businesses were damaged by trees falling on them or the winds. Property south of the intracoastal waterway was flooded by the storm surge. Over 60 percent of the parish was without power immediately after the storm. Wind gusts ranged from 50 to 90 mph. Storm surge reached into the 8 to 12 feet range.

The primary impacts the storm brought to southwest Maine were gusty winds with widespread reports of wind gusts in the mid to upper 40s.  Numerous trees and branches were brought down with the winds resulting in peak power outages around 125,000 customers.  Additional boat damage was also reported on some area lakes due to the strong winds.  Overall storm impacts were brief with a period of gusty winds from the south to southeast on the evening of August 4th causing most of the damage. No coastal flooding was reported with the storm as the minor storm surge with this event of around 1 foot coincided at low tide.

An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico began to slowly slide back to the west on August 16th, as a weak cold front began to slide southeast across Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana. However, the combination of the upper ridge providing strong sinking motion, and compressional heating just ahead of the front over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulted in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during the 16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time as low level moisture pooled just ahead of the front, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly behind the weak mid-August cool front during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

There were 10 injuries reported in north central and northeast Illinois within the NWS Chicago/Romeoville County Warning Area (CWA).  Local officials estimated that nearly one million customers lost power across northern Illinois at the height of the derecho and some people were without power for several days. This resulted in a progressive, well-organized complex of storms for hundreds of miles and at times traveling nearly 70 mph.  After bringing extensive damage from extreme wind speeds in Iowa that morning, the damage transitioned across northern Illinois from widespread wind damage to narrow, brief and intense swaths associated with compact circulations within the thunderstorm line, some of which were associated with tornadoes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico continued to provide strong sinking motion and thus compressional heating over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulting in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during August 15th-16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly as a weak mid-August cold front moved through the region during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

A cold front moved across the ArkLaMiss region during the afternoon and evening of August 16th. Ahead of the front, temperatures in the mid to upper 90s helped to create a very unstable airmass. Storms that developed across the Golden Triangle quickly became better organized and plowed across central Mississippi, affecting locations generally along and east of the I-55 corridor during the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms brought damaging winds to the region, which resulted in downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on a car along 36th Avenue.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Laura made landfall along the Louisiana coast near Lake Charles in the early morning hours of August 27. It moved north into Central Louisiana during the morning and afternoon before turning to the northeast and tracking through Arkansas. Impacts from Laura were felt far from the center of the storm, which was mainly in the form of tropical storm force winds across portions of northeast Louisiana and southeast Arkansas. Farther east, into Mississippi, the tight pressure gradient that resulted from Laura was the cause for gusty winds across portions of western Mississippi. Winds were sustained 30 to 35 mph, gusting to 45 to 49 mph across portions of northeast Louisiana, southeast Arkansas and the northwest portion of Mississippi. This resulted in downed trees and power lines across the region. Since Laura moved inland fairly quickly, rainfall totals were not high. Rainfall amounts up to four inches occurred along and west of the Mississippi River and this resulted in some minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several streets had minor flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon/early evening of August 10th, 2020, scattered severe thunderstorms created damage across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms eventually congealed into a line as they exited the eastern Panhandles. Several reports of hail between the size of Pennies and Quarters were reported across the area and a few storms produced up to golf ball size hail. Thunderstorm wind damage was reported along with a network of weather equipment measuring wind gusts near 70 MPH. Some of the more significant damage included a couple trailers which were completed totaled near Perryton, TX as well as 2 miles of power poles downed near Spearman, TX. In eastern Oklahoma Panhandle there was also some rural flooding reported near Knowles, OK from heavy rains.

A few thunderstorms moved across the central Texas Panhandle on the evening of August 6th. Though instability and winds aloft were not great for widespread severe weather, a couple of these storms managed to produce wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. With weak winds aloft the updrafts of the storms collapsed on top of itself sending some rapidly descending air towards the surface. A mesonet (weather sensors) at both Stinnett and Borger managed to measure a gust of 72 and 59 MPH respectively.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Happy West wildfire began around 1135CST about nine miles southeast of Buffalo Lake Texas in Randall County. The wildfire consumed a measured four hundred and forty-three acres. There were no homes or other structures threatened, damaged or destroyed by the wildfire and there were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The Canyon Fire Department and the Randall County Fire Department responded to the wildfire which was contained and controlled around 1600CST.

An upper level disturbance high instability and moderate wind shear led to severe storm development across the Texas Panhandle. The strongest storm produced a swath of thunderstorm wind damage around 2 miles wide and 4 miles long occurred along the Fritch Highway near Webb Rd. Damage within the area included numerous broken or leaning power poles, downed power lines and damage to roofs, porches, and awnings at local residences, especially those facing west. In addition, many large tree limbs in the area were snapped and some out outbuildings and old barns in the area were destroyed. One single wide trailer was pushed off its blocks. Damage was consistent with straight line winds. All while this was going some places in north Amarillo saw large hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter and even some areas of accumulating hail up to 5 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Convectively enhanced vorticity max lead to initiation of storms overnight Sunday across southern South Dakota. These initial storms grew upscale given concurrent downstream destabilization through northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa. Widespread 80-100 mph winds developed through central/eastern Iowa as this derecho matured. Northern bookend and advection wing forcing led to some supercell structures across northern Illinois/southwest Wisconsin. Northern bookend turned northeast as it moved across Lake Michigan and tracked into western Michigan. As this occurred, attendant post convective wake low weakened as it crossed the lake. Thus the local area did not experience the 80 to 100 mph winds that N IL/E IA experienced. However the resultant slowing and breakup of the line as it moved across northwest Indiana/SW Michigan, yielded a LEWP and subsequent multiple small scale circulations developing along the line. These meso-vortices were associated with pockets of enhanced wind damage and brief tornado occurrences.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The initial gust front passed the Cook Buoy (45026) near Stevensville, MI around 5:55 pm when waves were reportedly one foot. By 6:20 pm, waves had climbed to four feet and a meteotsunami was reported by an off-duty NWS employee who was at Lion���s Park Beach. Water levels rose approximately one and one half foot above the mean levels by that time, and flooding was reported along Lion���s Park Drive through the evening. Wave heights at the Cook Buoy peaked at around five feet at 8:40 pm.  ||According to the Berrien County EMA, there was lakeshore flooding also reported in New Buffalo, MI, which lasted into the late evening hours. A seiche could be seen at various water level gauges across Lake Michigan into the next day (Tuesday August 11th, 2020), with the most extreme fluctuations extending from shortly after the storm passed until about 5 am EDT. Lesser fluctuations of up to one foot continued through around 10 am EDT. ||No specific damage amounts were noted as near record high water levels and periodic high wave action continue to cause extensive erosion.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa during the pre-dawn hours of August 10th.  As a moist and highly unstable airmass fed into the system, the storms quickly intensified and began racing eastward  as a derecho across Iowa into northern Illinois along a pre-existing boundary.  While the greatest damage and highest wind speeds remained along and north of the I-80 corridor, a trailing boundary sank southward into central Illinois creating wind gusts of 60-75 mph.  As a result, widespread wind damage was reported along and north of a Macomb...to Springfield...to Paris line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple tree limbs were blown down on the 5400 block of Galena Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and central New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of September 2020. As one of the worst monsoon seasons on record came to end, moderate to extreme drought worsened to nearly 100 percent of the state of which 40 percent was deemed as extreme to exceptional drought. An anomalous early season winter storm brought high terrain snow and rain to most of the area during the first week of September. Precipitation totals across central and western New Mexico generally ranged from half an inch to three quarters an inch while precipitation totals neared an inch across north central and northeast New Mexico. Portions of the higher terrain of south central New Mexico fared better with totals generally near an inch and a half. Despite this, the second half of the month was mostly dry with more record heat which contributed to the worsening drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe to extreme drought conditions from August 2020 continued in September. Portions of the southwest zone deteriorated to exceptional drought.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Sally initially formed as an area of disturbed weather over the Bahamas late on September 10th, 2020. Over the next few days, the system became better organized and became Tropical Depression Nineteen in the afternoon hours on September 11th. Later that night around midnight CDT on September 12th, TD Nineteen made landfall at Key Biscayne with peak winds of 35 mph and a central pressure of 1007mb (29.74 inHg). The system continued west emerging into the east-central Gulf of Mexico and quickly strengthened into a Tropical Storm later in the day on the 11th. This system continued to drift northwestward with time and strengthened into a hurricane in the morning hours on September 14th with maximum sustained winds of 85 mph and a central pressure of 985 mb (29.09 inHg) and continued to strengthen becoming a category 2 hurricane shortly after. Sally would then eventually weaken some, and slow down in forward speed before turning very slowly northwards making landfall near Gulf Shores, Alabama as a strong Category 2 hurricane with peak winds of 105 mph and a central pressure of 965mb (28.50 inHg) early in the morning hours on September 16th.||Impacts to southeastern Louisiana and southern Mississippi was mostly confined to coastal counties of southern Mississippi, southeastern Louisiana and adjacent marine areas. Main impacts included storm surge inundation for coastal areas, as well as some wind damage across portions of Jackson and Harrison County, MS while Hurricane Sally was making landfall east across Gulf Shores, AL. Rainfall was of little impact across coastal MS and westward with only small areas of rainfall totaling around 3 inches reported in eastern Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Impacts to portions of the parish were the result of storm surge and affected areas outside the HSDRRS Levees. Storm surge flooding overtopped ring levees in the Delacroix and Woodlake areas, resulting in one to two feet of inundation inside those leveed areas. The lower portion of the parish below the Verret Flood gates was cut off due to flooding. Observations across the area ranged in the 5.35 MHHW to 5.92 NAVD88 range in Bayou Dupree (BDML1) and Shell Beach (SHBL1) on the 15th between 12:12CDT and 13:00 CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record breaking heatwave during the first week of September took a dramatic turn toward winter as a powerful storm system moved south through the Rocky Mountains on September 8, 2020. A powerful cold front shifted south and west through eastern New Mexico and plowed through gaps in the central mountain chain into the Rio Grande Valley on the morning of September 9, 2020. Canyon winds peaked during the late afternoon and evening hours when gusts of 70 to 80 mph were reported. These powerful winds affected the east side of the Albuquerque metro area for several hours before slowly tapering off through September 10, 2020. Dozens of trees, power lines, power poles, fences, and walls were blown down. Roof damage was also reported across the city. At least 15,000 customers were without power, and as many as a 1,000 customers had no power for three days after the event. Record breaking early snowfall also impacted the high terrain with this event. Many locations in the northern mountains reported two to six inches of snow while one to two inches fell at lower elevations of northern New Mexico. Fire and rescue personnel evacuated the Rio Chama RV Park as the combination of heavy snow and strong winds downed several large tree limbs onto at least two recreational vehicles. Several locations also set daily record low minimum and record low maximum temperatures on both September 9th and September 10th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of heavy snow, high winds, and low visibility resulted in severe travel conditions along U.S. Highway 64 between mile markers 349 and 386 east of Raton. Snowfall amounts averaged one to three inches around Capulin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of Saturday, September 5th, elevated thunderstorms developed over west-central and southwest Minnesota along the nose of a strengthening low level jet. Steep lapse rates of 8-9 C/km and bulk shear values of 50-70 knots were ample enough to support rotating storms and strong updrafts. Thus, storms were capable of producing very large hail. The largest hail stone measured was 2 inches in diameter over southwest Minnesota near Sacred Heart. There were also numerous quarter to golf ball size hail stones that fell across southern Minnesota late Saturday evening, through early Sunday morning. Some of the storms transitioned to damaging winds over south central Minnesota where a few wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph occurred and caused damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe drought persisted across northern Aroostok county during August. The severe drought across northern Aroostook county had developed in early July. Above average temperatures were reported during August. Rainfall was mostly due to showers and thunderstorms...which resulted in variable rain totals. Most areas received 40 to 70 percent of normal rainfall for August...though some localized areas did receive greater rain totals with thunderstorms. Widespread rain did not occur during August. In Caribou...the 3 month period from June to August was the warmest and second driest on record. |Streamflows during August were generally at 15 to 35 percent of normal. At month's end many larger rivers were at near record low levels. Grain crops were significantly impacted during August. Potatoes and other crops required extensive irrigation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The severe drought conditions which had developed in early July persisted through the month of August.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Many areas across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw improvements in drought going into August. A couple of rain events help keep those areas from degradation during the month with some even improving by the end of the month. Northwest Cimarron County in Oklahoma was in extreme drought (D3) for the longest time until the end of the month after the August 29th event. An area in extreme drought in east central Texas Panhandle managed to leave the extreme drought category as well. However, the southwest Texas Panhandle kept missing out on rain with all storms passing to the north and northwest. Areas in severe drought and extreme drought are looking at a 6 to 12 inches deficit for rainfall year today. Many ranchers are either selling their cattle or buying feed as there are no rangeland grasses. Many dryland crops have failed thus far, even with the July and August rains that came just too late.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Randall County started the month out in widespread severe drought (D2) with a small area of extreme drought (D3) at the beginning of the month. Almost all of the rain events in August missed a good portion of the southern half of the county increasing the yearly deficit for precipitation. Canyon, TX and other areas of the county are around 6 to 12 inches below average year to date.  Top soil moisture is very poor with almost no grasses to be seen.  Hay prices in the TX PH were $10 to $20 higher per ton compared to the rest of the state. A lot of dry land crops were abandoned and non-irrigated crops did not grow. There was even a wildfire that burned just over 400 acres southeast of Buffalo Lake on August 11.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tropical wave emerged off of Africa during August 16 and then developed into a depression by the 20th. The system gradually became better organized as it passed across the Greater Antilles. It entered the Gulf of Mexico and became a hurricane on the 25th. Outer bands spread inland during the afternoon of the 26th and it made landfall at Cameron, Louisiana at 1AM local time on the 27th. The west side of the category 4 hurricane impacted Southeast Texas as the centered moved north across west Louisiana and caused damages totaling roughly $1.95 Billion.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a mandatory evacuation for Orange County, Texas. Storm surge backed up the Sabine and Neches waterways, as well as Adams and Cow Bayous. Numerous trees, power lines, and poles were blown down across the entire county. Homes and businesses were damaged from trees falling on them or directly from the winds. Over 90 percent of the county was without power immediately after the storm. One person died from carbon monoxide poisoning (indirect death). Wind gusts across the county ranged from 60 to 110 mph. Storm surge reached 2.08 feet MHHW at the Rainbow Bridge in Bridge City.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias was the first tropical storm to impact Maine since 2011.  The center of the storm tracked well west of the state, keeping all the heavy rain associated with the storm across New York.  The primary impacts the storm brought to southwest Maine were gusty winds with widespread reports of wind gusts in the mid to upper 40s.  Numerous trees and branches were brought down with the winds resulting in peak power outages around 125,000 customers.  Additional boat damage was also reported on some area lakes due to the strong winds.  Overall storm impacts were brief with a period of gusty winds from the south to southeast on the evening of August 4th causing most of the damage. No coastal flooding was reported with the storm as the minor storm surge with this event of around 1 foot coincided at low tide.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias brought limited impacts to Franklin County due wind gusts up to 45 mph. Scattered reports of snapped and uprooted trees along with broken branches caused downed power lines through the county. Franklin County reported 3,000 customers without power, with a restoration time for most outages within 24 hours. No flooding was reported.

An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico began to slowly slide back to the west on August 16th, as a weak cold front began to slide southeast across Southwest Arkansas, Northeast Texas, and Northern Louisiana. However, the combination of the upper ridge providing strong sinking motion, and compressional heating just ahead of the front over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulted in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during the 16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time as low level moisture pooled just ahead of the front, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly behind the weak mid-August cool front during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

During the late morning through the afternoon of Monday August 10th, a line of intense thunderstorms known as a derecho brought widespread severe wind damage across Iowa, northern Illinois and northern Indiana.||In north central and northeast Illinois alone, the severe winds of 60 to 100 mph downed or damaged tens of thousands of trees, as well as caused severe damage to homes, businesses, and infrastructure.  There were 10 injuries reported in north central and northeast Illinois within the NWS Chicago/Romeoville County Warning Area (CWA).  Local officials estimated that nearly one million customers lost power across northern Illinois at the height of the derecho and some people were without power for several days.  Damage was estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars in north central and northeast Illinois, with several billions of dollars in damages across the entire Corn Belt region including significant damage to crops and agriculture infrastructure.  While much of the damage was due to straight line winds, there were also 14 tornadoes documented in north central and northeast Illinois.||The combination of high moisture, explosive instability and very strong atmospheric wind flow for mid-summer had developed quickly over the Corn Belt region on the morning of August 10th.  This resulted in a progressive, well-organized complex of storms for hundreds of miles and at times traveling nearly 70 mph.  After bringing extensive damage from extreme wind speeds in Iowa that morning, the damage transitioned across northern Illinois from widespread wind damage to narrow, brief and intense swaths associated with compact circulations within the thunderstorm line, some of which were associated with tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several metal panels of a large shed were blown in on one side and blown out on another side.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico continued to provide strong sinking motion and thus compressional heating over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulting in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during August 15th-16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly as a weak mid-August cold front moved through the region during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

A cold front moved across the ArkLaMiss region during the afternoon and evening of August 16th. Ahead of the front, temperatures in the mid to upper 90s helped to create a very unstable airmass. Storms that developed across the Golden Triangle quickly became better organized and plowed across central Mississippi, affecting locations generally along and east of the I-55 corridor during the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms brought damaging winds to the region, which resulted in downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across a power line along East 7th Avenue in Morton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Laura made landfall along the Louisiana coast near Lake Charles in the early morning hours of August 27. It moved north into Central Louisiana during the morning and afternoon before turning to the northeast and tracking through Arkansas. Impacts from Laura were felt far from the center of the storm, which was mainly in the form of tropical storm force winds across portions of northeast Louisiana and southeast Arkansas. Farther east, into Mississippi, the tight pressure gradient that resulted from Laura was the cause for gusty winds across portions of western Mississippi. Winds were sustained 30 to 35 mph, gusting to 45 to 49 mph across portions of northeast Louisiana, southeast Arkansas and the northwest portion of Mississippi. This resulted in downed trees and power lines across the region. Since Laura moved inland fairly quickly, rainfall totals were not high. Rainfall amounts up to four inches occurred along and west of the Mississippi River and this resulted in some minor flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A roof was partially removed from a barn near Wilmot. Several trees and power lines were blown down across the county. A private weather station east of North Crossett recorded sustained winds of 41 mph with a peak gust of 56 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Riviera Park wildfire began around 0045CST about twelve to thirteen miles north of Amarillo in Potter County. The wildfire started around the Park Circle East location to the west of U.S. Highway 287 north of Amarillo Texas. The Texas A&M Forest Service responded to a request for assistance and was in unified command with local resources to manage the wildfire. The wildfire was actively burning in heavy fuels and ground resources worked to construct containment lines around the wildfire. The wildfire consumed a measured three thousand one hundred and forty-eight acres. There were no reports of any homes or other structures threatened, damaged or destroyed by the wildfire. There were also no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The wildfire was contained and brought under control by 1700CST on August 23.

On the evening of August 8th a main area of thunderstorms moved from New Mexico and Colorado into the northwest combined Panhandles. Some storms trained across the same area just to the northwest of Highway 54 between Dalhart and Stratford. These training storms dumped 2 to 3 inches in a matter of an hour over an area just north of Conlen, TX. This led to some rural flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report with a picture of rural flooding just north of Conlen was submitted to the NWS Amarillo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front associated with an upper level disturbance passed through deep South Texas on the evening of August 1st into the overnight hours. Strong thunderstorms formed along and ahead of this front in conjunction with preexisting convective boundaries in the area, bringing damaging winds and flooding rain to the lower Rio Grande Valley. The impacts were primarily felt in Hidalgo and Cameron County, which were still recovering from ample rainfall and remnant flooding from Hurricane Hanna at the end of July. Standing water from Hurricane Hanna was still reported across western Cameron, southeast Hidalgo, and southwest Willacy with road closures still in place at the beginning of August.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hidalgo County Emergency Manager reported flooding into homes in Monte Alto as well as in homes near the intersection of FM2812 and FM493 due to heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level disturbance high instability and moderate wind shear led to severe storm development across the Texas Panhandle. The strongest storm produced a swath of thunderstorm wind damage around 2 miles wide and 4 miles long occurred along the Fritch Highway near Webb Rd. Damage within the area included numerous broken or leaning power poles, downed power lines and damage to roofs, porches, and awnings at local residences, especially those facing west. In addition, many large tree limbs in the area were snapped and some out outbuildings and old barns in the area were destroyed. One single wide trailer was pushed off its blocks. Damage was consistent with straight line winds. All while this was going some places in north Amarillo saw large hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter and even some areas of accumulating hail up to 5 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Accumulating hail, and large tree blown into home in north Amarillo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cluster of thunderstorms developed ahead of an approaching cold front across eastern Nebraska and western Iowa during the pre-dawn hours of August 10th.  As a moist and highly unstable airmass fed into the system, the storms quickly intensified and began racing eastward  as a derecho across Iowa into northern Illinois along a pre-existing boundary.  While the greatest damage and highest wind speeds remained along and north of the I-80 corridor, a trailing boundary sank southward into central Illinois creating wind gusts of 60-75 mph.  As a result, widespread wind damage was reported along and north of a Macomb...to Springfield...to Paris line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown into power lines.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm complex moved across Washington County, including the City of St. George, during the evening hours, producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding, and an isolated severe wind gust.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and early nighttime hours, intense rainfall was observed in St. George. The St. George, UT Coop observer reported 2.00 inches of rainfall in two hours, corresponding to a recurrence interval of approximately 200 years. The Santa Clara River at St. George rose from 3 cfs to 1,586 cfs in 3 hours. Interstate 15 was closed in both directions, with five to six feet of water reported across roadways in the area producing additional road closures, including the Red Hills Parkway. Many cars were stalled and stranded, several sink holes were reported, and power outages occurred.  St. George Rehabilitation was partially evacuated. Flood damage was reported in apartment complexes and basements. Monetary damage to public infrastructure was $3,082,501, with an additional $2,302,000 in damage to private property.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures were experienced on August 23rd with high temperatures in the upper 90s in southwest Cochise County. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures 5 to 9 degrees above normal in the upper 90s occurred in southwest Cochise County causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on August 23rd. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male near the San Pedro River just north of the International Border.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures were experienced in the lower deserts of southeast Arizona from August 24th-27th. Many locations approached or exceeded 110 degrees and set new daily record high temperatures. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for four males in Pima County during the period.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures 9 to 12 degrees above normal occurred in the lower elevations of southeast Arizona, causing the High Heat Risk category to be reached August 24 through August 27. Record high temperatures were tied or set at most locations on multiple days during the period. The hottest record temperatures during this stretch were 115 degrees at Ajo on August 25; 113 at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument on August 25; 111 at Picacho on the 24th; 110 at Sells on the 24th; and 107 at Tucson International Airport on the 25th. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for four males on August 25th, one on Ironwood National Forest grounds west of Avra Valley, one just west of there near Queen's Well on the Tohono O'odham Nation, and two near Ajo.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Drought conditions across northern and central New Mexico continued to deteriorate during the month of September 2020. As one of the worst monsoon seasons on record came to end, moderate to extreme drought worsened to nearly 100 percent of the state of which 40 percent was deemed as extreme to exceptional drought. An anomalous early season winter storm brought high terrain snow and rain to most of the area during the first week of September. Precipitation totals across central and western New Mexico generally ranged from half an inch to three quarters an inch while precipitation totals neared an inch across north central and northeast New Mexico. Portions of the higher terrain of south central New Mexico fared better with totals generally near an inch and a half. Despite this, the second half of the month was mostly dry with more record heat which contributed to the worsening drought.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe drought conditions from August 2020 continued in September.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed over North-central Louisiana and Deep East Texas during the afternoon and evening hours on September 4th, along a weak surface boundary draped over these areas, as well as near a weak upper level trough extending from East Texas across North-central Louisiana. Strong heating atop a very moist and moderately unstable air mass contributed to clusters of strong thunderstorms, with an isolated severe thunderstorm developing over Central Shelby County Texas just east of Center, which downed numerous trees just east and south of town. This and the other storms quickly weakened shortly thereafter with the loss of daytime heating.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were downed on FM 414 just north of Highway 87. Other trees were downed nearby on County Road 2033 off of Highway 87.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Post-Tropical Cyclone Beta moved ashore across portions of extreme Southeast Texas during the morning hours of September 23rd, with deep tropical moisture associated with this system continuing to spread northeast across much of Louisiana from the 21st to the 23rd. Periods of showers and embedded thunderstorms developed and spread across North Louisiana from the 21st through the 22nd ahead of Beta, resulting in widespread rainfall amounts of 1.50 to in excess of 3 inches, with additional rainfall amounts of 1.50 to 3 inches falling over this area as the remnants of Beta tracked northeast across Central Louisiana and Western Mississippi. Given the saturated grounds due to rains over the prior few days, localized flooding was observed in Sterlington in Northern Ouachita Parish.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Street flooding was reported throughout the city of Sterlington.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed across portions of the greater Phoenix metropolitan area, mainly to the southeast of Phoenix, during the afternoon hours on September 8th. Small to moderate hailstones were also reported; at roughly 1700MST there was a report of hailstones about 0.88 inches in diameter near the intersection of Power and Germann Roads. At 1710MST a trained spotter located about 2 miles  southeast of Higley reported that outflow winds estimated to be as high as 60 mph downed multiple trees along Germann Road between Greenfield and Power Roads. There were no reports of injury due to the falling trees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Sally initially formed as an area of disturbed weather over the Bahamas late on September 10th, 2020. Over the next few days, the system became better organized and became Tropical Depression Nineteen in the afternoon hours on September 11th. Later that night around midnight CDT on September 12th, TD Nineteen made landfall at Key Biscayne with peak winds of 35 mph and a central pressure of 1007mb (29.74 inHg). The system continued west emerging into the east-central Gulf of Mexico and quickly strengthened into a Tropical Storm later in the day on the 11th. This system continued to drift northwestward with time and strengthened into a hurricane in the morning hours on September 14th with maximum sustained winds of 85 mph and a central pressure of 985 mb (29.09 inHg) and continued to strengthen becoming a category 2 hurricane shortly after. Sally would then eventually weaken some, and slow down in forward speed before turning very slowly northwards making landfall near Gulf Shores, Alabama as a strong Category 2 hurricane with peak winds of 105 mph and a central pressure of 965mb (28.50 inHg) early in the morning hours on September 16th.||Impacts to southeastern Louisiana and southern Mississippi was mostly confined to coastal counties of southern Mississippi, southeastern Louisiana and adjacent marine areas. Main impacts included storm surge inundation for coastal areas, as well as some wind damage across portions of Jackson and Harrison County, MS while Hurricane Sally was making landfall east across Gulf Shores, AL. Rainfall was of little impact across coastal MS and westward with only small areas of rainfall totaling around 3 inches reported in eastern Jackson county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: USACE observation PMPL1 Pass Manchac measured peak inundation caused by storm surge of 3.39ft NAVD88 on the 16th at 01:00 CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Teddy underwent extra-tropical transition to a strong 951 mb storm well off shore in the Gulf of Maine before moving north north towards Halifax, Nova Scotia. This powerful cyclone coincided with astronomically high tides bringing a second day of minor coastal flooding to the New Hampshire Seacoast. Although winds were offshore, large, long period swell entered the Gulf of Maine leading to splash-over and minor coastal flooding to coastal New Hampshire.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The astronomical tide in Hampton of 9.4 feet combined with minimal storm surge of 0.3 feet at high tide to reach a 9.5 foot storm tide (MLLW) which is short of flood stage inundation impacts. Flood stage in Hampton is 11.0 feet (MLLW).  Although winds were offshore, large, long period swell entered the Gulf of Maine leading to splash-over along the Seacoast of New Hampshire. Nearshore waves increased to 8 feet every 16 seconds at high tide. In Hampton, splash-over flooded portions of Asheworth and adjacent streets due to the large pounding surf and elevated coastal waters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record breaking heatwave during the first week of September took a dramatic turn toward winter as a powerful storm system moved south through the Rocky Mountains on September 8, 2020. A powerful cold front shifted south and west through eastern New Mexico and plowed through gaps in the central mountain chain into the Rio Grande Valley on the morning of September 9, 2020. Canyon winds peaked during the late afternoon and evening hours when gusts of 70 to 80 mph were reported. These powerful winds affected the east side of the Albuquerque metro area for several hours before slowly tapering off through September 10, 2020. Dozens of trees, power lines, power poles, fences, and walls were blown down. Roof damage was also reported across the city. At least 15,000 customers were without power, and as many as a 1,000 customers had no power for three days after the event. Record breaking early snowfall also impacted the high terrain with this event. Many locations in the northern mountains reported two to six inches of snow while one to two inches fell at lower elevations of northern New Mexico. Fire and rescue personnel evacuated the Rio Chama RV Park as the combination of heavy snow and strong winds downed several large tree limbs onto at least two recreational vehicles. Several locations also set daily record low minimum and record low maximum temperatures on both September 9th and September 10th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Albuquerque Sunport measured damaging wind gusts between 58 mph and 71 mph for several hours as gap winds plowed through Tijeras Canyon. Dozens of large trees were toppled across the city, including; one tree along Girard just south of Gibson, one tree along Sunport Loop near the Sheraton hotel, at least one tree on the University of New Mexico campus, and other large trees at Roosevelt Park and Hyder Park. A large pine tree at Jefferson Middle School fell over power lines along Girard Blvd. Another large pine tree fell over power lines into Girard near Campus Blvd. Roofing was damaged at the city courthouse in downtown Albuquerque and another roof was damaged at a hotel near the Sunport. Thousands of PNM customers were without power for one to two days and some others were without power for three to four days. Damage amounts are a rough estimate for damage to power infrastructure, roofs, and fences.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the evening of Saturday, September 5th, elevated thunderstorms developed over west-central and southwest Minnesota along the nose of a strengthening low level jet. Steep lapse rates of 8-9 C/km and bulk shear values of 50-70 knots were ample enough to support rotating storms and strong updrafts. Thus, storms were capable of producing very large hail. The largest hail stone measured was 2 inches in diameter over southwest Minnesota near Sacred Heart. There were also numerous quarter to golf ball size hail stones that fell across southern Minnesota late Saturday evening, through early Sunday morning. Some of the storms transitioned to damaging winds over south central Minnesota where a few wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph occurred and caused damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms developed across Long Island and portions of New York City during the early morning hours in association with a surface trough south of the area. With weak steering flow and high moisture content (precipitable water values 2+ on the Upton, NY sounding), this resulted in flash flooding across portions of Nassau and Suffolk Counties. While rainfall totals averaged 1-2 inches across New York City and Long Island, portions of southern Nassau County and southwestern Suffolk County received 3-5 inches of rain. Reports from automated weather observing stations include 3.34 in West Babylon, 3.39 in Freeport, 4.25 in West Gilgo Beach, and 4.46 in Merrick. CoCoRaHS observers reported 3.69 one mile NNE of Wantagh, 4.05 ENE of Copiague, and 5.41 one mile SSW of Massapequa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extensive street and highway flooding was reported in Merrick. Numerous intersections were reported flooded along Merrick Road, including Kenny Avenue, Fox Boulevard, and Henry Street, although no vehicles were stranded and no water rescues were needed. In addition, the parking lots of numerous stores and strip malls were inundated along Merrick Road between the Meadowbrook State Parkway and the Wantagh State Parkway and remained inaccessible through at least 11:00am. Additional flooding was reported at the intersections of Lindenmere Drive and Hedge Lane, Cheryl Road and Judith Drive, and Beach Drive and Florence Street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The U.S. Drought Monitor placed a large portion of West Central Texas in a Severe Drought for the month of August.  A period of very hot temperatures and below normal rainfall amounts led to a flash drought across a large part of West Central Texas.  These hot temperatures resulted in numerous grass fires.   According to the Texas Crop Report, dryland cotton across the northern Edwards Plateau and northwest Hill Country continued to show signs of stress where moisture had been inadequate.  Also, some ranchers, in this region, had to provide supplemental feed to their livestock because of the lack of grasses.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The U.S. Drought Monitor placed all of Coleman County into the severe drought category.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A small shower developed during the midday hour near the Tennessee River at Ditto Landing on the Madison-Marshall County line.  The shower produced a funnel cloud that descended at 1107 pm CST, and touched down as a tornado and/or waterspout from around 1113 pm CST and lifting around 1125 pm CST.  The tornado was observed by a local research meteorologist at Ditto Landing who called in the report to the National Weather Service.  The tornado from his viewpoint touched down at Hobbs Island, and possibly could have crossed onto the water as well.  However, no damage was reported.  Two other mesonet weather cameras also recorded the tornado from two different vantage points, one at the University of Alabama in Huntsville Severe Weather Institute - Radar and Lightning Laboratories (SWIRLL) and the Baron Critical Weather Institute camera in New Hope.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A local research meteorologist located at Ditto Landing witnessed a tornado and possibly a waterspout at times on and adjacent to Hobbs Island along the Tennessee River. Mesonet cameras including one from the University of Alabama in Hunstville at the Severe Weather Institute, Radar and Lightning Laboratories (SWIRLL) captured the event. No damages were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front, draped across the foothills and Piedmont and supported aloft by multiple waves of energy entering from the Tennessee Valley, provided the triggers for  scattered slow-moving thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon across the mountains and foothills.  Strong daytime heating provided the instability to allow some storms to intensify to severe levels, producing damaging winds and hail.  In addition, deep tropical moisture in place in the wake of Tropical Storm Isaias allowed some storms to produce heavy rain, with 2-4 inch per hour rainfall rates at times.  Light winds aloft made for slow storm movement, allowing storms to remain over the same locations for extended periods of time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe storm produced damaging winds, which knocked a tree onto a powerline along Mountain Valley Road, near the county line.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias was the first tropical storm to impact Maine since 2011.  The center of the storm tracked well west of the state, keeping all the heavy rain associated with the storm across New York.  The primary impacts the storm brought to southwest Maine were gusty winds with widespread reports of wind gusts in the mid to upper 40s.  Numerous trees and branches were brought down with the winds resulting in peak power outages around 125,000 customers.  Additional boat damage was also reported on some area lakes due to the strong winds.  Overall storm impacts were brief with a period of gusty winds from the south to southeast on the evening of August 4th causing most of the damage. No coastal flooding was reported with the storm as the minor storm surge with this event of around 1 foot coincided at low tide.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Isaias brought limited impacts to Franklin County due wind gusts up to 45 mph. Scattered reports of snapped and uprooted trees along with broken branches caused downed power lines through the county. Franklin County reported 3,000 customers without power, with a restoration time for most outages within 24 hours. No flooding was reported.

Local officials estimated that nearly one million customers lost power across northern Illinois at the height of the derecho and some people were without power for several days.  Damage was estimated to be in the hundreds of millions of dollars in north central and northeast Illinois, with several billions of dollars in damages across the entire Corn Belt region including significant damage to crops and agriculture infrastructure.  While much of the damage was due to straight line winds, there were also 14 tornadoes documented in north central and northeast Illinois.||The combination of high moisture, explosive instability and very strong atmospheric wind flow for mid-summer had developed quickly over the Corn Belt region on the morning of August 10th.  This resulted in a progressive, well-organized complex of storms for hundreds of miles and at times traveling nearly 70 mph.  After bringing extensive damage from extreme wind speeds in Iowa that morning, the damage transitioned across northern Illinois from widespread wind damage to narrow, brief and intense swaths associated with compact circulations within the thunderstorm line, some of which were associated with tornadoes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were estimated between 60 mph and 70 mph in Schaumburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level ridge centered over Central Texas and Eastern New Mexico continued to provide strong sinking motion and thus compressional heating over East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Western Louisiana, resulting in temperatures climbing into the upper 90s to in excess of 100 degrees across these areas during August 15th-16th. Little mixing of dewpoints occurred during this period of time, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-110 degrees. These temperatures cooled slightly as a weak mid-August cold front moved through the region during the early morning hours of the 17th, providing slightly cooler but drier air through the area.

A cold front moved across the ArkLaMiss region during the afternoon and evening of August 16th. Ahead of the front, temperatures in the mid to upper 90s helped to create a very unstable airmass. Storms that developed across the Golden Triangle quickly became better organized and plowed across central Mississippi, affecting locations generally along and east of the I-55 corridor during the late afternoon and evening hours. These storms brought damaging winds to the region, which resulted in downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of wind went through the eastern parts of Jefferson Davis County. Trees were blown down on Mt. Carmel Road, Granby Road and along Cavanaugh Road.
