EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread wind damage was reported in the northern part of Jefferson County.

A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed across the Mid-South region of Western Tennessee and Northern Mississippi and moved south-southwest into the Lower Mississippi Valley during the afternoon and evening hours of June 5th, along a weak upper level trough of low pressure that drifted southeast across these areas around a large upper level ridge of high pressure anchored over the Central and Southern Plains. Despite the weak wind shear in place, this thunderstorm complex tapped moderate to high amounts of instability in place as temperatures rose into the lower to mid 90s across much of Southern and Eastern Arkansas and North Louisiana, while shifting south southwest through Mississippi and into Southeast Arkansas and Northeast Louisiana during the early evening hours. While the majority of the severe weather remained just east of the Ark-La-Tex, isolated severe thunderstorms did develop over Central Union and Northern Hempstead Counties Arkansas, and produced golf ball size hail just east of El Dorado while also downing several trees near the McCaskill community. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed across the Mid-South region of Western Tennessee and Northern Mississippi and moved south-southwest into the Lower Mississippi Valley during the afternoon and evening hours of June 5th, along a weak upper level trough of low pressure that drifted southeast across these areas around a large upper level ridge of high pressure anchored over the Central and Southern Plains. Despite the weak wind shear in place, this thunderstorm complex tapped moderate to high amounts of instability in place as temperatures rose into the lower to mid 90s across much of Southern and Eastern Arkansas and North Louisiana, while shifting south southwest through Mississippi and into Southeast Arkansas and Northeast Louisiana during the early evening hours. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two separate rounds of mostly non-severe thunderstorms swept through South Central Nebraska from northwest-to-southeast on this Monday afternoon and evening. During the first round, one storm briefly pulsed up to severe levels over Polk County around 4:30 p.m. CDT, as estimated 60 MPH winds felled a large tree branch onto an attached garage in Osceola. Elsewhere in the area, a few near-severe-criteria storm reports included: 54 MPH gusts near Oxford (during the second round of storms), 52 MPH at York airport and penny to nickel size hail in Fillmore County. ||The first round of isolated to scattered convection affected mainly the northeastern one-third of the local area (primarily east of a Greeley-Aurora-Hebron line), first entering counties such as Greeley/Nance between 3-4 p.m. CDT and exiting Fillmore/Thayer counties between 6-7 p.m. CDT. Meanwhile, the second round of storms arrived a bit later and farther west (mainly affecting areas southwest of a Loup City-Hastings-Superior line), entering Dawson/Buffalo counties between 5:30-6:30 p.m. CDT and exiting southward into Kansas between 8-9 p.m. CDT. Long before reaching South Central Nebraska, both rounds of convection initiated well to the north-northwest (near the NE-SD border) early in the afternoon. This was a fairly classic northwest-flow-aloft event, as the Central Plains resided within the path of several small-scale disturbances tracking southeastward around the periphery of a larger-scale trough centered over south central Canada. Despite only modest low-level moisture in the wake of a secondary cold front, this convection made the most of steep low-level lapse rates and seasonably-cool mid level temps, with mid-late afternoon mesoscale parameters in South Central Nebraska featuring 1000-1500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 25-35 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

This was an active late Friday evening-early Saturday morning across this six-county North Central Kansas area, featuring limited severe weather in Rooks/Phillips counties and some relatively minor flooding mainly within the northeast one-third of Mitchell County. But for the majority of the area this was just a classic, stormy early-summer night (most places measured between 0.50-2.00 inches of rain). As for the handful of severe weather reports, the main issue was a brief burst of intense winds through Rooks County around 2 a.m. CDT, including measured unofficial gusts of 68 MPH north-northeast of Codell, 62 MPH in Stockton and 61 MPH at Plainville (no known damage reports). Hail-wise, the only report featured quarter size stones east of Phillipsburg shortly after 11 p.m. CDT. Regarding heavy rainfall/flooding, primarily northeast Mitchell County was drenched with multiple downpours between midnight-4 a.m. CDT, with several automated gauges and NWS/CoCoRaHS observers tallying 3-5, including 5.05 just northeast of Beloit (unofficial public report of 6 at Simpson). This prompted relatively minor/short-term flash flooding and areal flooding, and also drove the Solomon River out of its banks as the Beloit gauge crested around 22.4 feet on the afternoon of the 27th (flood stage 20 feet). ||Timing-wise, there were basically two main rounds of convection. The first round (mainly 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. CDT) featured generally isolated to scattered coverage, as storms developed directly overhead in response to the onset of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). Then, primarily 2-4 a.m. CDT the next round charged in from the west in the form of a fairly compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) that had gotten its act together well before midnight along the KS/CO border. By 4 a.m. CDT, storm intensity had waned considerably across local counties, although mainly stratiform lighter rain held on through around sunrise. This was a fairly typical setup for active nocturnal storms in the Central Plains. In the mid-upper levels, broad zonal flow reigned as a low amplitude wave rode eastward out of CO during the night. Meanwhile at the surface, a nearly stationary front resided directly through the area in east-northeast to west-southwest fashion, as evening dewpoints averaged mid-60s to around 70 F. Though fairly warm mid-level temps/weak capping held storms at bay until after sunset, the onset of the low level jet easily sparked convection given a healthy reservoir of 2000-3000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE, with the main limiting factor to a more robust severe threat being only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A variety of upper level short-wave troughs combined with a surface trough and frontal boundary to produce thunderstorms during the late afternoon, evening, and late night hours. A very unstable and highly sheared atmosphere allowed many of the storms to become severe, with large hail, damaging wind gusts, and two tornadoes. Some of the wind gusts were very strong with estimated speeds up to 90 mph, causing severe damage to buildings in McIntosh, Dickey, and Morton counties. Tornadoes occurred in McIntosh and Dickey counties. The tornadoes produced no damage to evaluate and so by National Weather Service policy they were both rated EF Unknown. The largest hail reported was the size of tennis balls, which occurred early in the episode over McIntosh County.

Individual cells formed over the central mountains during the afternoon hours, with some displaying supercellular nature. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A crossing shortwave trough, as well as a remnant mesoscale convective vortex from convection the previous night, acted as a trigger for another round of severe thunderstorms on the 4th of June. Surface-based CAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg and deep-layer shear of 30-40 knots set up the region for organized severe weather.  Storms initiated in central Ohio around midday and then congealed into a line which swept across the upper Ohio Valley through the middle to late afternoon hours. Severe weather reports were mainly limited to tree and power line damage, with only a few reports of damage to structures and vehicles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A healthy 20 foot tree and several branches were downed one half mile west of the I-80/I-70 interchange.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down across the intersection of Route 558 and Route 414.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A crossing shortwave trough led to the development of thunderstorms across the region during the midday and afternoon hours of the 22nd.  Much of the region was impacted by cloud cover early on and was not able to destabilize sufficiently for severe weather.  However, areas to the north and east of Pittsburgh, where more sun was seen and where the trough had yet to cross, saw thunderstorms take advantage of the synoptic support, instability and terrain influences. Indiana and Jefferson Counties took the brunt of the wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In Henderson Township, multiple trees were reported to be down and damage to several structures was noted.

A mesoscale convective system (MCS) developed across the Mid-South region of Western Tennessee and Northern Mississippi and moved south-southwest into the Lower Mississippi Valley during the afternoon and evening hours of June 5th, along a weak upper level trough of low pressure that drifted southeast across these areas around a large upper level ridge of high pressure anchored over the Central and Southern Plains. Despite the weak wind shear in place, this thunderstorm complex tapped moderate to high amounts of instability in place as temperatures rose into the lower to mid 90s across much of Southern and Eastern Arkansas and North Louisiana while shifting south southwest through Mississippi and into Southeast Arkansas and Northeast Louisiana during the early evening hours. While the majority of the severe weather remained just east of the Ark-La-Tex, isolated severe thunderstorms did develop over portions of Southwest and South-central Arkansas, producing isolated instances of large hail and damaging winds. These storms shifted southwest into portions of extreme Northeast Texas during the early morning hours of June 6th, and briefly became severe in Central Bowie County where strong winds damaged a roof and awning of a mobile home near New Boston. These storms eventually weakened with the loss of heating and reduction in instability throughout the overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The metal roof and awning to a mobile home just south of New Boston sustained damage from strong thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning and early afternoon of Saturday the 6th featured scattered, mainly weak thunderstorms within northern and especially western portions of South Central Nebraska (particularly areas west of the Highway 183 corridor). However, one storm briefly spiked up to severe levels over far northern Furnas and southern Gosper counties between 8:30-9:30 a.m. CDT, yielding reports of quarter size hail covering Highway 283 several miles north of Arapahoe along with nickel size hail south-southwest of Smithfield. ||This short-lived morning severe storm was a bit of a surprise, as earlier activity that drifted through counties north of I-80 before sunrise was fairly weak, as were other morning/early afternoon storms that developed across portions of mainly Furnas/Gosper/Dawson/Phelps counties. All convection departed/lifted north of the local area by 1-2 p.m. CDT. As best could be surmised, this flare up of early-day convection was tied to a burst of low-mid level warm air advection, within the exit region of a gradually-weakening low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). At the surface, a fairly well-defined warm front blasted north across Nebraska over the course of the day. In the mid-upper levels, flow was fairly anemic over the local area as ridging prevailed aloft, downstream from a potent shortwave trough ejecting north-northeast across the Intermountain West. Mesoscale severe weather parameters in the Gosper County area around the time of the brief severe storm were relatively modest, featuring around 1000-2000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE but only 25 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A smattering of strong to severe thunderstorms roamed South Central Nebraska from the early evening of Saturday the 20th into the very early morning of Sunday the 21st, prompting a few hail reports from widely-varying locations. The largest reported hail, ping pong to golf ball size, occurred in far southwestern Furnas County near Wilsonville. Later, quarter size stones fell from other storms at Wood River, Genoa and Silver Creek, although the late-night report from Silver Creek implied that much larger hail might have transpired (observer unable to confirm a maximum size). ||Isolated storms first drifted into western portions of the 24-county area between 6-8 p.m. CDT, after initiating a few hours prior in west-central Nebraska along a north-south oriented surface trough. These initial storms included the one that produced the large hail in Furnas County. Between 8-11 p.m. CDT the vast majority of limited storm activity was rather weak, with the main exception of the briefly-severe storm that produced the 1-inch hail in Hall County. Then, about the time it appeared that any severe threat had ended for the night, a small cluster of storms began intensifying over eastern Nance County around midnight CDT, likely in response to the onset of a fairly weak southwesterly low level jet. Over the next few hours, this convection briefly morphed into a supercell that drifted southeast across portions of Nance, Merrick and Polk counties (yielding the Genoa and Silver Creek hail reports) before departing the local area around 2 a.m. CDT. In the mid-upper levels, forcing was provided by a low-amplitude shortwave trough translating across Nebraska in west-northwest flow, well-south of a larger-scale trough anchored over south central Canada. Mesoscale parameters over South Central Nebraska during the evening were certainly supportive of severe storms, featuring around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and deep layer wind shear of 30-40 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Observer reported mainly pea to nickel size hail, with occasional larger stones. Size of largest hail is unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was an active late Friday evening-early Saturday morning across this six-county North Central Kansas area, featuring limited severe weather in Rooks/Phillips counties and some relatively minor flooding mainly within the northeast one-third of Mitchell County. But for the majority of the area this was just a classic, stormy early-summer night (most places measured between 0.50-2.00 inches of rain). As for the handful of severe weather reports, the main issue was a brief burst of intense winds through Rooks County around 2 a.m. CDT, including measured unofficial gusts of 68 MPH north-northeast of Codell, 62 MPH in Stockton and 61 MPH at Plainville (no known damage reports). Hail-wise, the only report featured quarter size stones east of Phillipsburg shortly after 11 p.m. CDT. Regarding heavy rainfall/flooding, primarily northeast Mitchell County was drenched with multiple downpours between midnight-4 a.m. CDT, with several automated gauges and NWS/CoCoRaHS observers tallying 3-5, including 5.05 just northeast of Beloit (unofficial public report of 6 at Simpson). This prompted relatively minor/short-term flash flooding and areal flooding, and also drove the Solomon River out of its banks as the Beloit gauge crested around 22.4 feet on the afternoon of the 27th (flood stage 20 feet). ||Timing-wise, there were basically two main rounds of convection. The first round (mainly 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. CDT) featured generally isolated to scattered coverage, as storms developed directly overhead in response to the onset of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). Then, primarily 2-4 a.m. CDT the next round charged in from the west in the form of a fairly compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) that had gotten its act together well before midnight along the KS/CO border. By 4 a.m. CDT, storm intensity had waned considerably across local counties, although mainly stratiform lighter rain held on through around sunrise. This was a fairly typical setup for active nocturnal storms in the Central Plains. In the mid-upper levels, broad zonal flow reigned as a low amplitude wave rode eastward out of CO during the night. Meanwhile at the surface, a nearly stationary front resided directly through the area in east-northeast to west-southwest fashion, as evening dewpoints averaged mid-60s to around 70 F. Though fairly warm mid-level temps/weak capping held storms at bay until after sunset, the onset of the low level jet easily sparked convection given a healthy reservoir of 2000-3000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE, with the main limiting factor to a more robust severe threat being only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24-hour rainfall amount of 5.05 inches was reported by a CoCoRaHs observer. In the south part of town, the NWS cooperative observer measured 4.20 inches.

The first round (mainly 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. CDT) featured generally isolated to scattered coverage, as storms developed directly overhead in response to the onset of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). Then, primarily 2-4 a.m. CDT the next round charged in from the west in the form of a fairly compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) that had gotten its act together well before midnight along the KS/CO border. By 4 a.m. CDT, storm intensity had waned considerably across local counties, although mainly stratiform lighter rain held on through around sunrise. This was a fairly typical setup for active nocturnal storms in the Central Plains. In the mid-upper levels, broad zonal flow reigned as a low amplitude wave rode eastward out of CO during the night. Meanwhile at the surface, a nearly stationary front resided directly through the area in east-northeast to west-southwest fashion, as evening dewpoints averaged mid-60s to around 70 F. Though fairly warm mid-level temps/weak capping held storms at bay until after sunset, the onset of the low level jet easily sparked convection given a healthy reservoir of 2000-3000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE, with the main limiting factor to a more robust severe threat being only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 24-hour rainfall amount of 4.56 inches was reported.

Most of this convection was non-severe, but there was a lone report of half dollar size hail in Franklin from a briefly-feisty storm that snuck north out of Kansas. Radar data also suggested that marginally-severe hail might have affected southern portions of Nuckolls/Thayer counties, but there were no substantiating reports. Rainfall-wise, most locations under the main swath of storms measured 0.50-1.50. ||These overnight storms represented the far northern fringes of convection that mainly concentrated just south of the area across northern Kansas. Activity blossomed after dark in response to the onset of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downburst winds blew across northern Barto, Eastern Soleer, and Mosse townships, snapping numerous trees in shelterbelts and farmsteads throughout the area. A steel clad pole shed was torn open and spread along a half mile path to the east, where a two stall shop was torn open.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A variety of upper level short-wave troughs combined with a surface trough and frontal boundary to produce thunderstorms during the late afternoon, evening, and late night hours. A very unstable and highly sheared atmosphere allowed many of the storms to become severe, with large hail, damaging wind gusts, and two tornadoes. Some of the wind gusts were very strong with estimated speeds up to 90 mph, causing severe damage to buildings in McIntosh, Dickey, and Morton counties. Tornadoes occurred in McIntosh and Dickey counties. The tornadoes produced no damage to evaluate and so by National Weather Service policy they were both rated EF Unknown. The largest hail reported was the size of tennis balls, which occurred early in the episode over McIntosh County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement estimated thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 mph.

Southeast Minnesota was hit with two rounds of severe storms during the afternoon and evening of June 2nd. The first round developed in the late afternoon and produced large hail that reached 2 inches in diameter in and around Winona and Pickwick (Winona County). The second round produced some sporadic wind damage. Three trees were blown down onto a house in Houston (Houston County), a semi was blown over north of Austin (Mower County) and an estimated 60 mph wind gust occurred southwest of Dover (Olmsted County). A fire at a Rochester (Olmsted County) apartment complex was started by a lightning strike.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe storms rolled across western Wisconsin during the late afternoon and evening of June 2nd. Some of these storms produced very large hail ranging in size from 1 inch up to 2.5 inches in diameter. One of the hardest hit areas by the hail was Holmen (La Crosse County) where it was estimated that between 4,000 and 5,000 homes would need new roofs. Up to golf ball sized hail also fell near Pray (Jackson County) and near Dodge (Buffalo County). The storms also produced damaging winds with trees blown down across parts of Jackson, Monroe, Vernon, Adams and Juneau Counties. In Tomah (Monroe County), the roof canopy was blown off a grandstand at the county fairgrounds. The metal siding was ripped off a grain mill southeast of Ontario (Vernon County). More than 6,600 customers in the La Crosse area (La Crosse County) were without power after the storms moved through.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An estimated 65 mph gust blew down trees and branches on the south side of Holmen. Wind blown hail also damaged siding, window screens, downspouts, and plants.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dew points in the 70s across the region. Heat indices in Northwest Ohio reached the upper 90s during the afternoon of the 10th. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over western Ohio around 3 PM on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms began as discrete or clustered cells over western Ohio before congealing into a squall line. This squall line propagated from west to east across northern Ohio but individual cell motion was from south-southwest to north-northeast as the line moved through northern Ohio on the evening of the 10th. The main threat from severe thunderstorms were damaging winds with the strongest winds occurring in Northwest Ohio. Storms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph in the Lake Erie Islands and adjacent mainland areas of Ottawa and Erie Counties in Ohio, with wind damage across Oak Harbor, Catawba Island, Port Clinton, Marblehead, South Bass Island, and Sandusky. Another powerful segment of the line moved across Marion County, including the city of Marion, prompting sporadic damage in the city with wind gusts up to 80 mph. There was one injury with this event in Marion as a facade of a building collapsed onto a nearby vehicle. The intensity of the squall line waned as it passed east of Interstate 71, though it remained severe with sporadic wind damage. As the squall line moved east of Interstate 77 after dark, the line intensified as the storms caught up to the outflow, and backed winds ahead of the line rejuvenated the thunderstorms. Some strong storms moved across Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, producing additional wind damage before moving into Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A local newspaper reported trees downed southeast of Hayesville. There was also a social media report of roof damage to a barn between Hayesville and Loudonville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A crossing shortwave trough, as well as a remnant mesoscale convective vortex from convection the previous night, acted as a trigger for another round of severe thunderstorms on the 4th of June. Surface-based CAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg and deep-layer shear of 30-40 knots set up the region for organized severe weather.  Storms initiated in central Ohio around midday and then congealed into a line which swept across the upper Ohio Valley through the middle to late afternoon hours. Severe weather reports were mainly limited to tree and power line damage, with only a few reports of damage to structures and vehicles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down onto a road in Unity, blocking the entire roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.

Much of the region was impacted by cloud cover early on and was not able to destabilize sufficiently for severe weather.  However, areas to the north and east of Pittsburgh, where more sun was seen and where the trough had yet to cross, saw thunderstorms take advantage of the synoptic support, instability and terrain influences. Indiana and Jefferson Counties took the brunt of the wind damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were down across Ringgold Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dissipating showers over parts of central and northeast South Dakota early in the morning produced heat bursts and high winds. Heat bursts produce sudden increases in surface temperatures and winds along with a decrease in surface humidity. High wind gusts ranged from around 65 to over 80 mph causing some tree and structural damage.  The highest wind gust with the heat bursts was 82 mph in Clark. Many other locations recorded strong wind gusts of 50 to 55 mph from heat bursts. Temperatures rose anywhere from 5 to 10 degrees from heat bursts.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP station at Keysville 2 S (KYSV2) measured 4.17 inches of rain in the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EDT which was the highest 1-day total  on record for any June day. EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP station at South Boston (SOBV2) had a 24-hour rain total of 5.55 inches ending at 700 AM on the 18th, the 2nd highest on record in the month of June, after the 6.98 inches on June 23rd, 1995. It was also the 4th highest for any calendar day. The station also had a 2-day rain total of 8.80 on and a 3-day total of 10.54 inches ending 700 AM on the 18th. This was the highest 2-day total for June. beating June 24, 1995 with 8.02 inches. It was also 2nd highest amount for any calendar 2-day period. The still-existing 2-day record is 8.83 inches September 6-7, 1996 during the passage of remains from Hurricane Fran. Data extends back to 1981 at this site. The 2-day, 8.80 inch amount is in the 90 percent confidence interval (7.90-9.57 inches) for a 100-year rain event (.01 annual chance of occurrence) per NOAA Atlas 14. The 3-day total was also a new record for the site, exceeding the 9.87 inches that also occurred during Fran in September, 1996. The 3-day, 10.54 inch amount is in the 90 percent confidence interval (9.29-11.4 inches) for a 200-year event (.005 annual chance of occurrence) per NOAA Atlas 14. Data extends back to 1981 at this station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A smattering of strong to severe thunderstorms roamed South Central Nebraska from the early evening of Saturday the 20th into the very early morning of Sunday the 21st, prompting a few hail reports from widely-varying locations. The largest reported hail, ping pong to golf ball size, occurred in far southwestern Furnas County near Wilsonville. Later, quarter size stones fell from other storms at Wood River, Genoa and Silver Creek, although the late-night report from Silver Creek implied that much larger hail might have transpired (observer unable to confirm a maximum size). ||Isolated storms first drifted into western portions of the 24-county area between 6-8 p.m. CDT, after initiating a few hours prior in west-central Nebraska along a north-south oriented surface trough. These initial storms included the one that produced the large hail in Furnas County. Between 8-11 p.m. CDT the vast majority of limited storm activity was rather weak, with the main exception of the briefly-severe storm that produced the 1-inch hail in Hall County. Then, about the time it appeared that any severe threat had ended for the night, a small cluster of storms began intensifying over eastern Nance County around midnight CDT, likely in response to the onset of a fairly weak southwesterly low level jet. Over the next few hours, this convection briefly morphed into a supercell that drifted southeast across portions of Nance, Merrick and Polk counties (yielding the Genoa and Silver Creek hail reports) before departing the local area around 2 a.m. CDT. In the mid-upper levels, forcing was provided by a low-amplitude shortwave trough translating across Nebraska in west-northwest flow, well-south of a larger-scale trough anchored over south central Canada. Mesoscale parameters over South Central Nebraska during the evening were certainly supportive of severe storms, featuring around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and deep layer wind shear of 30-40 knots.

While it appeared the big storms were over, there was one more round from west central into central sections of the state on the 29th. Clouds and downpours yielded  high temperatures of only 77 degrees at Conway (Faulkner County) and North Little Rock (Pulaski County), 78 degrees at Cabot (Lonoke County) and Little Rock (Pulaski County), and 79 degrees at Benton (Saline County) and Malvern (Hot Spring County). Multiple roads were flooded in Hot Springs (Garland County) after three to four inches of rain fell. There was about as much rain at Malvern (Hot Spring County) and Pine Ridge (Montgomery County), with tree damage at Magnet Cove and Social Hill (both in Hot Spring County). ||For the month, there was more than the usual rain at many locations. Surpluses of rain from one to more than three inches occurred at Little Rock (Pulaski County) and Pine Bluff (Jefferson County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding was noted downstream of Remmel Dam at Jones Mill on the Ouachita River, due to heavy rain and increased dam releases.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado snarled and snapped trees in multiple shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.

The largest hail reported was the size of tennis balls, which occurred early in the episode over McIntosh County.

Severe weather reports were mainly limited to tree and power line damage, with only a few reports of damage to structures and vehicles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree was blown down onto power lines in the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees and power lines were downed across the area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad closed upper low drifted across South Carolina and northwest back into southwest Virginia and West Virginia bringing persistent rainfall that eventually led to flooding. There were repeated rounds of heavy rainfall with widespread amounts of 2 to 5 inches, with isolated totals over 10 inches in a 3-day period in parts of Halifax County, VA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS Cooperative station at Copper Hill (COHV2) had its 2nd wettest June day on record, and 4th wettest of any calendar day, as 6.65 inches of rain fell in the 24-hours ending 700 AM EDT on the  18th. The existing June (and all-time) record is 8.21 inches on June 21, 1972 during the remnants of Hurricane Agnes. Per NOAA Atlas 14, for a 24-hour period, this rainfall total is in the 90 percent confidence interval (6.37 to 7.72 inches) for a 50-year recurrence (.02 annual exceedance probability). Complete data extends back to 1940 at this site.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A smattering of strong to severe thunderstorms roamed South Central Nebraska from the early evening of Saturday the 20th into the very early morning of Sunday the 21st, prompting a few hail reports from widely-varying locations. The largest reported hail, ping pong to golf ball size, occurred in far southwestern Furnas County near Wilsonville. Later, quarter size stones fell from other storms at Wood River, Genoa and Silver Creek, although the late-night report from Silver Creek implied that much larger hail might have transpired (observer unable to confirm a maximum size). ||Isolated storms first drifted into western portions of the 24-county area between 6-8 p.m. CDT, after initiating a few hours prior in west-central Nebraska along a north-south oriented surface trough. These initial storms included the one that produced the large hail in Furnas County. Between 8-11 p.m. CDT the vast majority of limited storm activity was rather weak, with the main exception of the briefly-severe storm that produced the 1-inch hail in Hall County. Then, about the time it appeared that any severe threat had ended for the night, a small cluster of storms began intensifying over eastern Nance County around midnight CDT, likely in response to the onset of a fairly weak southwesterly low level jet. Over the next few hours, this convection briefly morphed into a supercell that drifted southeast across portions of Nance, Merrick and Polk counties (yielding the Genoa and Silver Creek hail reports) before departing the local area around 2 a.m. CDT. In the mid-upper levels, forcing was provided by a low-amplitude shortwave trough translating across Nebraska in west-northwest flow, well-south of a larger-scale trough anchored over south central Canada. Mesoscale parameters over South Central Nebraska during the evening were certainly supportive of severe storms, featuring around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and deep layer wind shear of 30-40 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado was observed as it developed off the north end of a downburst corridor moving across Dieter and Ross townships. The tornado tracked through a farmstead, where it demolished a pole shed and spread debris for nearly a mile to the north. Numerous trees were also snapped. Peak winds were estimated at 105 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This Wednesday evening featured the first somewhat-widespread severe thunderstorm event of 2020 within South Central Nebraska, with several reports of damaging winds and large hail focused primarily near and northeast of a line from Loup City-Grand Island-Hebron. Overall, damaging winds were the bigger issue, highlighted by a measured gust of 79 MPH at the York airport shortly before 10 p.m. CDT. As these winds tore into town, they took down several large tree branches (a few entire trees), causing fairly widespread power outages and even partially-crushing an unoccupied car. About an hour before reaching York, measured winds of 70 MPH struck the Chapman area, flipping over irrigation pivots and taking down a light pole at a convenience store. Later in the evening, shortly before storms completely exited the local area, estimated 70 MPH winds took down a giant tree limb in Alexandria (3 ft. diameter/50 ft. long). Although the majority of wind damage focused within eastern counties, severe-criteria gusts were ongoing even as storms first entered the local area earlier in the evening, including 64 MPH at Ord airport. As for hail, the majority of limited reports were quarter size or smaller, although a few stones up to golf ball size were noted in North Loup.||Breaking down event timing and evolution, the scattered to numerous storms that eventually infiltrated South Central Nebraska first developed as separate storm clusters during the mid-late afternoon, one over northwest Nebraska and another in the NE/KS/CO border area. Between 7-9 p.m. CDT, both of these clusters entered northern and western portions of the local area. The southern one, which had been occasionally severe over southwest Nebraska, lost some steam as it moved east, yielding only slightly sub-severe wind gust reports in Furnas County. Meanwhile, the northern storm complex clearly established itself as dominant, charging southeastward as damaging winds peaked in intensity between 8:30-11:30 p.m. CDT. Shortly before midnight, the back edge of the now linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) exited southeast out of Thayer County, ending all storm activity for the night. Turning to the meteorological setup, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature in the mid-upper levels consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features across South Central Nebraska ahead of the storms were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and southerly-to-easterly breezes only around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, with damaging wind potential likely enhanced by fairly large surface dewpoint depressions heading into the evening (on the order of 25-30 degrees F). Evening mesoscale analysis over South Central Nebraska revealed 1000-2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and around 35-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Most hail stones were smaller than quarters, but a few were as large as golf ball size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface trough stretched across the islands, combined with abundant |moisture and instability converging over American Samoa, to generate a period of heavy rainfall and some flash flooding Thursday June 11th during the late morning and early afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The local weather office recorded 2.21 inches of rain from 10 AM to 2 PM prompting flash flooding in low lying areas and villages with poor drainage systems. Roads in Ottoville, the iliili golf course, and in the front of SAAB Pago were underwater for most of the day. Several reports from the public and the media included an SUV car stalled due to flooded roadways in the front of LDS State Center in Ottoville, and water filled homes in low-lying areas in the village of Malaeimi. After the event, huge crate-sized potholes were uncovered on the fagaima road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front drifting south from the Great Lakes reached the Ohio Valley on the afternoon of the 3rd, promoting showers and thunderstorms across southeast Ohio. Heavy downpours created by these showers and storms resulted in flooding issues in the region, particularly in Vinton and Athens Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: In the town of Pine Grove Heights, US-50 between Fisher Road and Union Lane was closed for a brief time due to flooding. Nearby in Athens, Richland Avenue became impassable due to high water flowing along the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A variety of upper level short-wave troughs combined with a surface trough and frontal boundary to produce thunderstorms during the late afternoon, evening, and late night hours. A very unstable and highly sheared atmosphere allowed many of the storms to become severe, with large hail, damaging wind gusts, and two tornadoes. Some of the wind gusts were very strong with estimated speeds up to 90 mph, causing severe damage to buildings in McIntosh, Dickey, and Morton counties. Tornadoes occurred in McIntosh and Dickey counties. The tornadoes produced no damage to evaluate and so by National Weather Service policy they were both rated EF Unknown. The largest hail reported was the size of tennis balls, which occurred early in the episode over McIntosh County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A power line blew down onto the road.

Individual cells formed over the central mountains during the afternoon hours, with some displaying supercellular nature. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A crossing shortwave trough, as well as a remnant mesoscale convective vortex from convection the previous night, acted as a trigger for another round of severe thunderstorms on the 4th of June. Surface-based CAPE of 1500-2000 J/kg and deep-layer shear of 30-40 knots set up the region for organized severe weather.  Storms initiated in central Ohio around midday and then congealed into a line which swept across the upper Ohio Valley through the middle to late afternoon hours. Severe weather reports were mainly limited to tree and power line damage, with only a few reports of damage to structures and vehicles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Carroll County Dispatch reported that multiple trees were blown down in the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although a few marginally-severe thunderstorms impacted the northwestern half of South Central Nebraska on this Sunday late afternoon/early evening, this event fell short of forecast expectations in terms of potential coverage/intensity of severe weather (more on this below). As for what actually happened, a handful of semi-discrete severe storms produced hail to half dollar size at Johnson Lake and nickel size near Sherman Reservoir, along with wind gusts around 60 MPH near Holdrege and Rockville. As for how the day played out, this seemed to be a case where factors such as the presence of early-day convection in/near the area, along with appreciable high level cloud cover much of the day, combined to hamper later-day airmass recovery and thus tempered the magnitude of the potential severe threat (SPC had upgraded most of South Central Nebraska to Enhanced Risk on morning Day 1 outlooks). ||The first sign of potential complications showed its hand early in the day as a few clusters of elevated, non-severe storms flared up between sunrise and late morning, affecting several counties along/east of Highway 281. Meanwhile, an unrelated batch of higher clouds rolled in from the west, prompting a multi-hour period of mostly cloudy skies over South Central Nebraska lasting well into the afternoon. Then, as skies started clearing and airmass recovery began, an extensive batch of strong/severe convection erupted to the south over Kansas, likely disrupting northward moisture advection and further inhibiting late afternoon destabilization. Nonetheless, despite these factors working against a local severe threat, a broken line of semi-discrete severe storms finally initiated around 6 p.m. CDT in northwestern counties, along a northeast-southwest oriented front. However, these storms did not maintain intensity long, weakening within 60-90 minutes. In their wake, one more rogue severe storm flared up around 8:30 p.m. CDT over Phelps/Harlan counties, but also faded fast. Finally, shortly after sunset a briefly-severe storm just west of the local area made a run toward Dawson County, but weakened as it moved in, effectively slamming the door on any further severe threat. Not surprisingly given the forecast expectations, the general synoptic setup appeared rather solid for severe storms. In the mid-upper levels, broad west-northwest flow prevailed over the Central Plains as a series of embedded disturbances rotated around the south side of a large-scale trough/closed low over south central Canada. At the surface, steady southerly breezes prevailed, to the east of a quasi-stationary front draped through western/north central NE. However, surface dewpoints remained fairly modest by late-June severe weather standards, averaging upper 50s-mid 60s F. Even so, afternoon mixed-layer CAPE reached 2000-3000 J/kg thanks to steep mid-level lapse rates, in the presence of  30-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

A strong surface low pressure area in central South Dakota along a stalled southwest to northeast surface boundary brought numerous severe thunderstorms to central and northeast South Dakota. The severe storms moved over the same areas multiple times into the early morning hours of June 8th. Large hail from quarter to golf ball size, wind gusts of 60 to 90 mph, along with four tornadoes occurred.  Numerous structures and trees were damaged or destroyed from these storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several buildings were damaged by estimated seventy mph winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad closed upper low drifted across South Carolina and northwest back into southwest Virginia and West Virginia bringing persistent rainfall that eventually led to flooding. There were repeated rounds of heavy rainfall with widespread amounts of 2 to 5 inches, with isolated totals over 10 inches in a 3-day period in parts of Halifax County, VA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flood waters were reported to have reached some mobile homes in the Wildwood Mobile Home Park. Some evacuations were conducted in the area.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The NWS Cooperative station at Covington, VA (CFPV2) set a date rainfall record for June 18th of 2.70 inches for the 24-hour period ending 700 AM EDT on the 18th. The previous date record was 1.49 inches set in 1973. It was also the 5th wettest June day on record, but well behind the record 4.20 inches on June 24, 2016. Nearly unbroken precipitation records exist at this station back to 1961 at this site.

An additional 0.5 to 1 of rainfall likely for the western portions of central Montana. Expect some flooding impacts to develop in the area highlighted by the Flood Watch along smaller creeks and streams and adjacent roadways as well as in lower lying areas where water collects. The Dearborn River is likely to see the sharpest increase, and will be closely monitored with latest forecasts projecting a rise to flood stage near Craig. The Sun, Teton and Marias Rivers will likely also rise, though not as sharply as the Dearborn.

The second round of thunderstorms occurred on June 3rd as a weak upper level disturbance moved across the area and interacted with a hot and humid air mass to produce thunderstorms across Scott and Muscatine Counties, before moving into parts of northwest Illinois during the late afternoon into the early evening hours. An isolated supercell thunderstorm produced nickel to golf ball sized hail and rain that caused  flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This Wednesday evening featured the first somewhat-widespread severe thunderstorm event of 2020 within South Central Nebraska, with several reports of damaging winds and large hail focused primarily near and northeast of a line from Loup City-Grand Island-Hebron. Overall, damaging winds were the bigger issue, highlighted by a measured gust of 79 MPH at the York airport shortly before 10 p.m. CDT. As these winds tore into town, they took down several large tree branches (a few entire trees), causing fairly widespread power outages and even partially-crushing an unoccupied car. About an hour before reaching York, measured winds of 70 MPH struck the Chapman area, flipping over irrigation pivots and taking down a light pole at a convenience store. Later in the evening, shortly before storms completely exited the local area, estimated 70 MPH winds took down a giant tree limb in Alexandria (3 ft. diameter/50 ft. long). Although the majority of wind damage focused within eastern counties, severe-criteria gusts were ongoing even as storms first entered the local area earlier in the evening, including 64 MPH at Ord airport. As for hail, the majority of limited reports were quarter size or smaller, although a few stones up to golf ball size were noted in North Loup.||Breaking down event timing and evolution, the scattered to numerous storms that eventually infiltrated South Central Nebraska first developed as separate storm clusters during the mid-late afternoon, one over northwest Nebraska and another in the NE/KS/CO border area. Between 7-9 p.m. CDT, both of these clusters entered northern and western portions of the local area. The southern one, which had been occasionally severe over southwest Nebraska, lost some steam as it moved east, yielding only slightly sub-severe wind gust reports in Furnas County. Meanwhile, the northern storm complex clearly established itself as dominant, charging southeastward as damaging winds peaked in intensity between 8:30-11:30 p.m. CDT. Shortly before midnight, the back edge of the now linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) exited southeast out of Thayer County, ending all storm activity for the night. Turning to the meteorological setup, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature in the mid-upper levels consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features across South Central Nebraska ahead of the storms were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and southerly-to-easterly breezes only around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, with damaging wind potential likely enhanced by fairly large surface dewpoint depressions heading into the evening (on the order of 25-30 degrees F). Evening mesoscale analysis over South Central Nebraska revealed 1000-2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and around 35-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were estimated to be near 70 MPH. Emergency management reported that a three foot diameter and 50 foot long tree limb and a 1.5 to 2 foot diameter tree limb were blown down and blocking Main Street in the community of Alexandria.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Albeit not as active as the previous evening, the evening of Thursday the 4th was the third consecutive with at least some severe storm activity in South Central Nebraska. This was truly a hit-and-miss, isolated to scattered event, as while storm coverage was fairly limited across the 24-county area as a whole, all four quadrants of it saw at least some convection. Overall, marginally-severe winds were the main issue, including measured gusts of 61 MPH at the Ord airport and 60 MPH at Waco, and estimated 60 MPH at Shelby, where the NWS cooperative observer reported downed tree branches up to 3 inches in diameter. Various other places clocked slightly sub-severe wind gusts of 50-55 MPH, including in or near Gothenburg, Johnson Lake, Arcadia, Gresham and Clay Center. Hail was less of an issue, with the only severe-criteria report consisting of quarter size stones in Sutton. ||Breaking down event evolution and timing, two small/separate storm clusters entered west-central and northern counties between 7-9 p.m. CDT, a continuation of activity that initiated hours earlier over the Nebraska Panhandle. These early evening storms produced strong-to-marginally severe winds mainly in Valley/Dawson/Gosper counties. Over the next few hours from 9-11:30 p.m. CDT, both of these storm clusters briefly weakened, only to re-intensify and even merge somewhat as they reached eastern portions of the area, prompting various hail/wind reports from counties such as Clay/Polk/York before exiting into eastern Nebraska. Meanwhile, back off to the southwest, a separate area of strong storms blossomed between 10 p.m. and midnight CDT in several counties along the Kansas border, but there were no ground-truth reports from this convection that departed into southeast Nebraska/northeast Kansas after midnight. Finally, one last weaker batch of storms roamed various northern/eastern counties between 1-4 a.m. CDT on Friday the 5th before all local storm activity ended for the night. Both at the surface and aloft, the same general environment that supported severe storms the prior evening remained in place for this round. In the mid-upper levels,  broad west-northwest flow containing various embedded, low-amplitude disturbances persisted over the region. At the surface, the same seasonably-hot and moderately unstable airmass persisted as well, as afternoon temperatures topped out in the low-mid 90s F with dewpoints ranging from upper 50s F in western counties to 65-70 F in the east. As strong to severe storms traversed the area in the evening, mesoscale parameters featured 1000-3000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts were estimated to be near 60 MPH in Shelby and the NWS cooperative observer 3 miles northeast of town reported downed tree branches up to 3 inches in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning and early afternoon of Saturday the 6th featured scattered, mainly weak thunderstorms within northern and especially western portions of South Central Nebraska (particularly areas west of the Highway 183 corridor). However, one storm briefly spiked up to severe levels over far northern Furnas and southern Gosper counties between 8:30-9:30 a.m. CDT, yielding reports of quarter size hail covering Highway 283 several miles north of Arapahoe along with nickel size hail south-southwest of Smithfield. ||This short-lived morning severe storm was a bit of a surprise, as earlier activity that drifted through counties north of I-80 before sunrise was fairly weak, as were other morning/early afternoon storms that developed across portions of mainly Furnas/Gosper/Dawson/Phelps counties. All convection departed/lifted north of the local area by 1-2 p.m. CDT. As best could be surmised, this flare up of early-day convection was tied to a burst of low-mid level warm air advection, within the exit region of a gradually-weakening low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). At the surface, a fairly well-defined warm front blasted north across Nebraska over the course of the day. In the mid-upper levels, flow was fairly anemic over the local area as ridging prevailed aloft, downstream from a potent shortwave trough ejecting north-northeast across the Intermountain West. Mesoscale severe weather parameters in the Gosper County area around the time of the brief severe storm were relatively modest, featuring around 1000-2000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE but only 25 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail was reported to be covering Highway 283 approximately 6 miles north of Arapahoe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although a few marginally-severe thunderstorms impacted the northwestern half of South Central Nebraska on this Sunday late afternoon/early evening, this event fell short of forecast expectations in terms of potential coverage/intensity of severe weather (more on this below). As for what actually happened, a handful of semi-discrete severe storms produced hail to half dollar size at Johnson Lake and nickel size near Sherman Reservoir, along with wind gusts around 60 MPH near Holdrege and Rockville. As for how the day played out, this seemed to be a case where factors such as the presence of early-day convection in/near the area, along with appreciable high level cloud cover much of the day, combined to hamper later-day airmass recovery and thus tempered the magnitude of the potential severe threat (SPC had upgraded most of South Central Nebraska to Enhanced Risk on morning Day 1 outlooks). ||The first sign of potential complications showed its hand early in the day as a few clusters of elevated, non-severe storms flared up between sunrise and late morning, affecting several counties along/east of Highway 281. Meanwhile, an unrelated batch of higher clouds rolled in from the west, prompting a multi-hour period of mostly cloudy skies over South Central Nebraska lasting well into the afternoon. Then, as skies started clearing and airmass recovery began, an extensive batch of strong/severe convection erupted to the south over Kansas, likely disrupting northward moisture advection and further inhibiting late afternoon destabilization. Nonetheless, despite these factors working against a local severe threat, a broken line of semi-discrete severe storms finally initiated around 6 p.m. CDT in northwestern counties, along a northeast-southwest oriented front. However, these storms did not maintain intensity long, weakening within 60-90 minutes. In their wake, one more rogue severe storm flared up around 8:30 p.m. CDT over Phelps/Harlan counties, but also faded fast. Finally, shortly after sunset a briefly-severe storm just west of the local area made a run toward Dawson County, but weakened as it moved in, effectively slamming the door on any further severe threat. Not surprisingly given the forecast expectations, the general synoptic setup appeared rather solid for severe storms. In the mid-upper levels, broad west-northwest flow prevailed over the Central Plains as a series of embedded disturbances rotated around the south side of a large-scale trough/closed low over south central Canada. At the surface, steady southerly breezes prevailed, to the east of a quasi-stationary front draped through western/north central NE. However, surface dewpoints remained fairly modest by late-June severe weather standards, averaging upper 50s-mid 60s F. Even so, afternoon mixed-layer CAPE reached 2000-3000 J/kg thanks to steep mid-level lapse rates, in the presence of  30-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
Very heavy rainfall of 3 to 5 inches brought widespread flooding to east central Hand County. Many roads were flooded with some roads washed out.  Many acres of cropland were also flooded for a time.

A few rounds of strong to marginally-severe thunderstorms affected this six-county North Central Kansas area between the pre-dawn and late afternoon hours on this Sunday. However, this event fell short of forecast expectations in terms of potential coverage/intensity of severe weather, yielding only a few reports of quarter size hail at Ionia (mid-morning) and near Natoma (mid-afternoon). As for how the day played out, this seemed to be a case where factors such as the presence of stubborn early-day convection, along with afternoon development initiating fairly early and in widespread fashion, combined to hinder appreciable airmass destabilization/recovery and thus tempered the magnitude of the potential severe threat (SPC assigned Enhanced Risk to North Central Kansas on Day 1 outlooks).||The first sign of potential complications showed its hand well-before sunrise, as a long-lived round of at least slightly-elevated storms initiated between 2-3 a.m. CDT over Phillips/Rooks/Osborne counties. Over the course of the next 11 hours or so (all the way into early afternoon) this activity evolved into a narrow/broken, north-south oriented band that slid eastward at a snail's pace as new cells continuously regenerated on its western flank. The majority of these storms were sub-severe, producing only small hail, but between 9 a.m. and noon CDT a few cores over Jewell/Mitchell counties pulsed up to severe levels per radar data and the lone ground-truth report of quarters at Ionia. At long last, this early-day convection finally (mostly) exited the local area around 1 p.m. CDT. However, because it had persisted so long into the day, it laid out an outflow boundary/effective warm front near the far southern edges of the local area. Thanks to afternoon heating and meager capping, it did not take long for several strong/severe storms to erupt within a few counties either side of the Interstate 70 corridor between 2-4 p.m. CDT. This resulted in considerable storm coverage across mainly Rooks/Osborne/Mitchell counties, but the only ground-truth severe report was quarter size hail near Natoma. Between 4-6 p.m. CDT, other strong storms moved up into Phillips County from the southwest. However, given that so much convection developed over the local area in a short time, along with the fact that a large severe complex had taken center stage in central/southwestern KS, storm intensity/coverage within North Central Kansas steadily dwindled and the area was all but storm-free by 7 p.m. CDT. Not surprisingly given the forecast expectations, the general synoptic setup appeared rather potent for severe storms. In the mid-upper levels, broad west-northwest flow prevailed over the Central Plains as a series of embedded disturbances rotated around the south side of a large-scale trough/closed low over south central Canada. At the surface, North Central Kansas resided southeast of a quasi-stationary front draped from northwest KS into northern NE. Prior to the eruption of mid-afternoon convection, mixed-layer CAPE reached 2000-4000 J/kg in the presence of 30-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A smattering of strong to severe thunderstorms roamed South Central Nebraska from the early evening of Saturday the 20th into the very early morning of Sunday the 21st, prompting a few hail reports from widely-varying locations. The largest reported hail, ping pong to golf ball size, occurred in far southwestern Furnas County near Wilsonville. Later, quarter size stones fell from other storms at Wood River, Genoa and Silver Creek, although the late-night report from Silver Creek implied that much larger hail might have transpired (observer unable to confirm a maximum size). ||Isolated storms first drifted into western portions of the 24-county area between 6-8 p.m. CDT, after initiating a few hours prior in west-central Nebraska along a north-south oriented surface trough. These initial storms included the one that produced the large hail in Furnas County. Between 8-11 p.m. CDT the vast majority of limited storm activity was rather weak, with the main exception of the briefly-severe storm that produced the 1-inch hail in Hall County. Then, about the time it appeared that any severe threat had ended for the night, a small cluster of storms began intensifying over eastern Nance County around midnight CDT, likely in response to the onset of a fairly weak southwesterly low level jet. Over the next few hours, this convection briefly morphed into a supercell that drifted southeast across portions of Nance, Merrick and Polk counties (yielding the Genoa and Silver Creek hail reports) before departing the local area around 2 a.m. CDT. In the mid-upper levels, forcing was provided by a low-amplitude shortwave trough translating across Nebraska in west-northwest flow, well-south of a larger-scale trough anchored over south central Canada. Mesoscale parameters over South Central Nebraska during the evening were certainly supportive of severe storms, featuring around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and deep layer wind shear of 30-40 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging in size from ping pong balls to golf balls was reported along this path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado was confirmed in northern Columbiana County |following a survey of damage in the Leetonia/Washingtonville area.|Damage began just north of the Leetonia High School and was most|concentrated along Leetonia Road, where numerous trees were|snapped or uprooted. Minor fascia damage also was noted in this|area.||The circulation then weakened as it progressed northeast, with|tree damage continuing to the county line, where debris evidence |seemed to end abruptly. NWS Pittsburgh observed no evidence of |wind damage continuing into Mahoning County, which is coincident|with a weakening trend in the radar-depicted circulation.||Damage earlier in the circulation's track across Salem Township was|sporadic and did not prove to be conclusively tornadic.||At its peak, tree damage was consistent with wind speeds of 70-75|mph near the beginning of the swath along Leetonia Road. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and muggy conditions prevailed over the area as the region had been on the backside of an Atlantic Ridge in the warm sector of an unstable air mass. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Although storm coverage within this portion of North Central Kansas was quite limited on this Saturday evening, the one legitimate severe storm in the coverage area produced notably large hail up to 3 inches in diameter over far southern Rooks County. This hailer entered the county from the southwest shortly before 8 p.m. CDT, after drifting northeast for a few hours as a left split from activity that initiated near the intersection of Gove/Trego/Ness counties. Between 8-8:20 p.m. CDT, reports of hail ranging from quarter to greater than baseball size occurred along a narrow swath from six miles south-southwest of Plainville up to the south side of Plainville proper. Shortly thereafter, the storm weakened rapidly, with only the faintest radar echoes remaining by 8:45 p.m. CDT. Elsewhere within the local area on this evening, a strong storm tracked southeastward from southwestern Phillips to central Rooks counties, but yielded no ground-truth reports. The initial convective development over west-central Kansas (that eventually spawned the Rooks County hail storm) developed near a somewhat-subtle, north-south oriented surface trough. Forcing aloft was also somewhat subtle, as northern Kansas only received a glancing blow from the southern fringes of a broad mid-level trough focused from central Nebraska northward into the Dakotas. Nonetheless, once storms got going, the environment was certainly supportive of severe activity as mesoscale analysis featured around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and deep layer wind shear around 40 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging in size from ping pong balls to 3 inches in diameter was reported along this path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between 7-10 p.m. CDT on this Monday evening, a broken line of thunderstorms swept across this six-county North Central Kansas area from northwest-to-southeast. The vast majority of this activity was sub-severe, producing only gusty winds as high as 40-50 MPH and brief rainfall. However, one small cell pulsed up just enough to produce a marginally-severe measured gust of 58 MPH near Speed in southwestern Phillips County, shortly before 8 p.m. CDT. Although this fairly low-key line of convection increased in coverage a bit by the time it reached North Central Kansas, its origins could actually be traced back roughly 300 miles to the northwest, to isolated-scattered storms initiating early in the afternoon over southwestern SD and northwestern NE. In the mid-upper levels, a fairly pronounced northwest flow regime ruled the Central Plains, as the region resided within the path of several small-scale disturbances tracking southeastward around the periphery of a larger-scale trough centered over south central Canada. Despite only modest low-level moisture in the wake of a secondary cold front, this convection made the most of steep low-level lapse rates and seasonably-cool mid level temps, with early-evening mesoscale parameters in North Central KS featuring around 1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 35-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

As a mesoscale convective system passed over portions of Pennsylvania during the morning hours of the 3rd, a boundary was laid out from northeast Ohio through central portions of Pennsylvania. This boundary served as a focus for storm initiation later in the day. Insolation, with continued warm and moist advection, was able to destabilize|the airmass with CAPE on the order of 3000 J/kg. A new shortwave and upper level jet streak were also able to increase deep-layer shear and feed the development of strong to severe thunderstorms.  Only a couple of instance of wind damage were noted in eastern Ohio, however.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large trees were reported to be blown down a half mile north of the intersection of South River Road and Route 555 along the Muskingum River.

A road or two was likely affected.

Hot and muggy conditions prevailed over the area as the region had been on the backside of an Atlantic Ridge in the warm sector of an unstable air mass.  A strengthening area of low pressure began to approach western Maine by midday along with a surface cold front.  A compact shortwave upper level trough dug into the region from Ontario increased the mid-level shear over Maine. Two distinct rounds of thunderstorms crossed the state with the first pre-frontal trough bringing damaging wind gusts around noon, with a second round of damaging thunderstorms by mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm wind gusts downed trees near Waterboro.
