EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two separate rounds of mostly non-severe thunderstorms swept through South Central Nebraska from northwest-to-southeast on this Monday afternoon and evening. During the first round, one storm briefly pulsed up to severe levels over Polk County around 4:30 p.m. CDT, as estimated 60 MPH winds felled a large tree branch onto an attached garage in Osceola. Elsewhere in the area, a few near-severe-criteria storm reports included: 54 MPH gusts near Oxford (during the second round of storms), 52 MPH at York airport and penny to nickel size hail in Fillmore County. ||The first round of isolated to scattered convection affected mainly the northeastern one-third of the local area (primarily east of a Greeley-Aurora-Hebron line), first entering counties such as Greeley/Nance between 3-4 p.m. CDT and exiting Fillmore/Thayer counties between 6-7 p.m. CDT. Meanwhile, the second round of storms arrived a bit later and farther west (mainly affecting areas southwest of a Loup City-Hastings-Superior line), entering Dawson/Buffalo counties between 5:30-6:30 p.m. CDT and exiting southward into Kansas between 8-9 p.m. CDT. Long before reaching South Central Nebraska, both rounds of convection initiated well to the north-northwest (near the NE-SD border) early in the afternoon. This was a fairly classic northwest-flow-aloft event, as the Central Plains resided within the path of several small-scale disturbances tracking southeastward around the periphery of a larger-scale trough centered over south central Canada. Despite only modest low-level moisture in the wake of a secondary cold front, this convection made the most of steep low-level lapse rates and seasonably-cool mid level temps, with mid-late afternoon mesoscale parameters in South Central Nebraska featuring 1000-1500 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 25-35 knots of deep-layer wind shear.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts estimated to be near 60 MPH resulted in small tree limbs being downed across Osceola, with a larger branch approximately 2 feet in diameter falling onto and damaging an attached garage on the far south side of town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was reported to be blown down on a car near Sharon Road, with heavy damage to the car.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The COOP observer at Bedford, VA (BDFV2) had its second highest date rainfall for the 24-hours ending 700 AM on June 17th with 2.49 inches, behind the 1934 record of 2.77 inches. The following 24-hour period ending at 700 AM on the 18th, again saw a second highest amount for the date with 2.39 inches, after the 1936 record of 2.80 inches. Precipitation data at this site date back to 1893 but with significant gaps in the record.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and muggy conditions prevailed over the area as the region had been on the backside of an Atlantic Ridge in the warm sector of an unstable air mass. Two distinct rounds of thunderstorms crossed the state with the first pre-frontal trough bringing damaging wind gusts around noon, with a second round of damaging thunderstorms by mid-afternoon.

Thunderstorms developed across portions of south central Nebraska during the evening of Tuesday, June 30th, along and just behind a cold front. Some of these thunderstorms became severe, bringing scattered instances of large hail, along with isolated severe wind. The first thunderstorm formed over Dawson County, just behind the cold front, around 8pm, and produced quarter size hail just north of Sumner. This storm continued to produce severe hail as it moved northeast into Custer County between 8pm and 9pm. A more extensive line of thunderstorms developed farther east around 8:30pm, from eastern Buffalo County northeast to Greeley County. This line moved east southeast. Southern portions of the line were the most intense and produced a swath of large hail reports ranging from quarter size up to half dollar size from Cairo into Grand Island. A severe wind gust of 62 mph was also measured at Central Nebraska Regional Airport (KGRI). The line of thunderstorms continued east southeast, affecting areas east of Highway 281 and north of Highway 6 between 9:45pm and midnight. However, no additional severe reports were received within these areas during this time.||The thunderstorms were supported by strong instability (mixed layer CAPE values of 4500-5500 J/kg) and modest effective shear (25-35kt). Steep mid level lapse rates near 8 C/km and a glancing influence from a progressive shortwave moving from Colorado into Nebraska Panhandle also aided in severe thunderstorm formation, though the position of this upper disturbance  kept the greatest deep layer shear displaced northwest from the cold front and strongest instability. The low level jet remained rather weak, thus the line of thunderstorms decreased in intensity after sunset with the onset of nocturnal cooling.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail ranging in size from quarters to ping pong balls was reported along the path.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was an active late Saturday evening-early Sunday morning of thunderstorms across much of South Central Nebraska, featuring several reports of large hail and especially damaging winds mainly between midnight-3 a.m. CDT as two storm complexes rolled through and eventually merged. Focusing first on severe winds, most estimated or measured gusts were in the 50-70 MPH range and associated with primarily tree damage. However a few isolated structural damage reports were more suggestive of at least 75-80 MPH, including: 1) 10 power poles blown down and three grain bins destroyed (along with some overturned irrigation pivots) west of Aurora...2) grain bin damage and overturned pivots north of Minden. Hail was more limited overall, but stones reached golf ball size at Pauline and ping pong ball size in Davenport, while Hastings saw nickel to quarter size hail. Rainfall amounts varied considerably (most of South Central Nebraska had less than one-half inch), but a fairly narrow swath of at least 1.50-2.50 targeted parts of primarily Thayer/Nuckolls/Clay counties, with one unofficial report as high as 3.17 near Belvidere. Flooding was fairly minimal, although one rural road along the Fillmore/Thayer County line still had water running across it around sunrise. ||As for storm mode/evolution, this was a somewhat complex event. The first local convection of the night entered the Furnas County area out of northwest Kansas after 11 p.m. CDT, in the form of a compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) on a weakening trend. But then, between midnight-1 a.m. CDT, a broken band of intense, semi-discrete storms erupted out ahead of this MCS along a west-east axis centered from Phelps-Adams-Thayer counties (likely in response to the onset of a healthy low level jet). However, these initially semi-discrete storms (which accounted for all large hail reports) quickly consolidated/grew upscale into a new linear MCS that charged north-northeast across the Highway 6/Interstate 80 corridors between 1-2 a.m. CDT, gradually merging with the initial MCS racing up from the southwest in the process. During the ensuing hour, the two complexes completed a full merger; the northern end weakening as it reached far northeastern counties (such as Nance/Polk), while the southern end remained severe through Fillmore/Thayer counties before departing the local area into southeast Nebraska. This ended any severe threat for the night, although weaker storms and broader showers persisted until around sunrise in some spots. This was a ripe setup for severe nocturnal storms, especially with the exit region of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars) aimed into the heart of South Central Nebraska after dark, and tapping into a large reservoir of most-unstable CAPE as high as 2000-3000 J/kg. In the mid-upper levels, flow over the region was not overly-strong, but contained various low-amplitude disturbances and was in the process of transitioning more southwesterly in response to a larger-scale trough setting up over the northwestern United States. There were no distinct surface features across the local area, but steady light southeast breezes prior to storm initiation maintained seasonably-high dewpoints in the mid-60s to low-70 F. Likely one of the main limiting factors against a more robust severe threat was only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gusts estimated to be near 75 MPH damaged a grain bin and a shed. Several trees were damaged and 2 pivots were overturned.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was an active late Friday evening-early Saturday morning across this six-county North Central Kansas area, featuring limited severe weather in Rooks/Phillips counties and some relatively minor flooding mainly within the northeast one-third of Mitchell County. But for the majority of the area this was just a classic, stormy early-summer night (most places measured between 0.50-2.00 inches of rain). As for the handful of severe weather reports, the main issue was a brief burst of intense winds through Rooks County around 2 a.m. CDT, including measured unofficial gusts of 68 MPH north-northeast of Codell, 62 MPH in Stockton and 61 MPH at Plainville (no known damage reports). Hail-wise, the only report featured quarter size stones east of Phillipsburg shortly after 11 p.m. CDT. Regarding heavy rainfall/flooding, primarily northeast Mitchell County was drenched with multiple downpours between midnight-4 a.m. CDT, with several automated gauges and NWS/CoCoRaHS observers tallying 3-5, including 5.05 just northeast of Beloit (unofficial public report of 6 at Simpson). This prompted relatively minor/short-term flash flooding and areal flooding, and also drove the Solomon River out of its banks as the Beloit gauge crested around 22.4 feet on the afternoon of the 27th (flood stage 20 feet). ||Timing-wise, there were basically two main rounds of convection. The first round (mainly 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. CDT) featured generally isolated to scattered coverage, as storms developed directly overhead in response to the onset of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars). Then, primarily 2-4 a.m. CDT the next round charged in from the west in the form of a fairly compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) that had gotten its act together well before midnight along the KS/CO border. By 4 a.m. CDT, storm intensity had waned considerably across local counties, although mainly stratiform lighter rain held on through around sunrise. This was a fairly typical setup for active nocturnal storms in the Central Plains. In the mid-upper levels, broad zonal flow reigned as a low amplitude wave rode eastward out of CO during the night. Meanwhile at the surface, a nearly stationary front resided directly through the area in east-northeast to west-southwest fashion, as evening dewpoints averaged mid-60s to around 70 F. Though fairly warm mid-level temps/weak capping held storms at bay until after sunset, the onset of the low level jet easily sparked convection given a healthy reservoir of 2000-3000 J/kg most-unstable CAPE, with the main limiting factor to a more robust severe threat being only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches were reported across the area, with the primary impact being numerous rural roads being covered in water and closed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed in the afternoon along a frontal boundary aligned north to south over the western and central parts of North Dakota. Initially, storms formed along the northern portions of the boundary, then developed south. A highly visible tornado developed over southern Morton County in the evening, then two tornadoes developed within minutes of each other in Bottineau County, with the second one damaging two properties. The largest hail was the size of a tennis ball, which occurred in Morton County. The strongest wind gust was 75 mph, and occurred in Bottineau County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported to be blown down across the city of Coshocton.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper disturbance moves eastward across the region, with a weak surface cold front moving eastward along and just ahead of the upper disturbance. Additionally, a northwest-southeast trough over north-central Montana serves as an additional focus of lift. Both surface boundaries result in low-level moisture convergence, but mainly focusing the best surface moisture across the north-central, central, and northeastern parts of the CWA. As a result, while showers possible just about anywhere in the CWA, the best chance for thunderstorms is mainly east of a line from Cut Bank to Fort Benton to Kings Hill Pass. With surface-based CAPE forecast over 1000 J/kg in most models, and mixed layer CAPE likely approaching if not exceeding 1000 J/kg, especially over Hill, Blaine, and NE'rn Chouteau, vigorous convection is possible. However, shear is minimal, with NW-W'ly winds of 10-25kts through the whole column, so storms are forecast to be very short-lived and/or 'pulse-y'. Some half-inch hail and gusty winds certainly possible. Severe hail or wind is not forecast. Showers and thunderstorms linger across north-central Montana through midnight, then die off overnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Half to one inch diameter hail reported. Minor street flooding and 53 mph wind gust also observed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms develop across western and southwest Montana, and continue to become more widespread. Daytime heating provides moderate instability for convective initiation. Inverted-v type soundings, characterized by a deep and dry boundary layer, support DCAPE values near 1000 J/kg. Thus, damaging wind gusts are the primary hazard associated with stronger thunderstorms. Shear profiles strengthen and may be enough to support a few supercell thunderstorms capable of producing locally heavy |rain, small hail, and with marginal support for an isolated larger hail event to the size of quarters. The severe storm potential peaks by early evening, although showers and thunderstorms continue to spread across the region overnight. This activity is associated with a passing upper level shortwave trough and its associated surface front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Corrected time. Reports strong winds brought rain into attic of house and knocked down trees. Also, reports a pile of peas sized hail. Wind speed and gust estimate not reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was an active late Saturday evening-early Sunday morning of thunderstorms across much of South Central Nebraska, featuring several reports of large hail and especially damaging winds mainly between midnight-3 a.m. CDT as two storm complexes rolled through and eventually merged. Focusing first on severe winds, most estimated or measured gusts were in the 50-70 MPH range and associated with primarily tree damage. However a few isolated structural damage reports were more suggestive of at least 75-80 MPH, including: 1) 10 power poles blown down and three grain bins destroyed (along with some overturned irrigation pivots) west of Aurora...2) grain bin damage and overturned pivots north of Minden. Hail was more limited overall, but stones reached golf ball size at Pauline and ping pong ball size in Davenport, while Hastings saw nickel to quarter size hail. Rainfall amounts varied considerably (most of South Central Nebraska had less than one-half inch), but a fairly narrow swath of at least 1.50-2.50 targeted parts of primarily Thayer/Nuckolls/Clay counties, with one unofficial report as high as 3.17 near Belvidere. Flooding was fairly minimal, although one rural road along the Fillmore/Thayer County line still had water running across it around sunrise. ||As for storm mode/evolution, this was a somewhat complex event. The first local convection of the night entered the Furnas County area out of northwest Kansas after 11 p.m. CDT, in the form of a compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) on a weakening trend. But then, between midnight-1 a.m. CDT, a broken band of intense, semi-discrete storms erupted out ahead of this MCS along a west-east axis centered from Phelps-Adams-Thayer counties (likely in response to the onset of a healthy low level jet). However, these initially semi-discrete storms (which accounted for all large hail reports) quickly consolidated/grew upscale into a new linear MCS that charged north-northeast across the Highway 6/Interstate 80 corridors between 1-2 a.m. CDT, gradually merging with the initial MCS racing up from the southwest in the process. During the ensuing hour, the two complexes completed a full merger; the northern end weakening as it reached far northeastern counties (such as Nance/Polk), while the southern end remained severe through Fillmore/Thayer counties before departing the local area into southeast Nebraska. This ended any severe threat for the night, although weaker storms and broader showers persisted until around sunrise in some spots. This was a ripe setup for severe nocturnal storms, especially with the exit region of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars) aimed into the heart of South Central Nebraska after dark, and tapping into a large reservoir of most-unstable CAPE as high as 2000-3000 J/kg. In the mid-upper levels, flow over the region was not overly-strong, but contained various low-amplitude disturbances and was in the process of transitioning more southwesterly in response to a larger-scale trough setting up over the northwestern United States. There were no distinct surface features across the local area, but steady light southeast breezes prior to storm initiation maintained seasonably-high dewpoints in the mid-60s to low-70 F. Likely one of the main limiting factors against a more robust severe threat was only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: It's quite rare that widespread/severe NON-thunderstorm winds take center stage over thunderstorms during June in South Central Nebraska, but that's exactly what happened on this Tuesday as an anomalously strong low pressure system (by June standards) churned through the Central Plains. For the vast majority of the local area, the number one story was several hours of intense north winds, commonly sustained 30-40 MPH and gusting 40-60+ MPH in the wake of a powerful late-spring cold front. Based on a variety of official/unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 67 MPH in Doniphan, 65 MPH near Gothenburg, Roseland and Oxford, and 64 MPH at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Other official peak airport gusts included 62 MPH at Hastings and 60 MPH in Kearney.  These winds undoubtedly caused numerous instances of at least minor damage within the area, but a few known ones included: a large tree in Holdrege fell on a car and blocked a street; a few large branches in west Hastings crashed onto power lines and at least one house; downed power lines in Arapahoe and Harvard; 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs downed in Deshler. Although the overall-strongest winds started/ended several hours earlier in far western local counties compared to far eastern counties, for the majority of the area the worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-10 p.m. CDT time frame.||Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening, the vast majority of the area was spared severe storms. This was mainly due to the strong surface cold front passing through prior to robust development being able to get going (in fact most of the area had seasonably-cool temperatures in the 50s-60s during the afternoon). That being said, a few severe storms did flare up in eastern counties during the afternoon, including one elevated hailer that dropped stones to around golf ball size in the Henderson and Hampton areas. Farther southeast along the actual front, radar indicated severe wind/hail potential with near-surface-based storms in/near Thayer County, but there were no verifying reports (although gustnado activity was noted in far southeastern Thayer County). Rainfall-wise, 24-hour totals fell short of forecast expectations across the majority of the area, as most places measured less than 1 inch. However, a few localized pockets closer to 2 inches occurred primarily in portions of southern Thayer and southwestern Buffalo counties, including a very isolated bullseye of 2.80 at Hubbell.||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east across northern KS over the course of the day, deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, far southeast counties dodged a potentially significant threat during the afternoon as the environment just north of the northern KS surface low became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes. In fact, mesoscale parameters in the Thayer County area briefly featured a potent combination of mixed-layer CAPE around 2000 J/kg, deep layer wind shear of 50-70 knots and 0-1 kilometer shear of 20-30 knots. As for the unusual nature of such intense northerly winds so late in the spring, it's worth noting that howling speeds of 50-70 knots a few thousand feet above the ground (at 850 millibars) registered 3-4 standard deviations above normal for the date...basically off the charts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 65 MPH was recorded at 6:09 PM CDT by a mesonet station located 5 miles north-northwest of Oxford. A gust of 62 MPH was recorded by mesonet stations located 1 mile north of Oxford and 2 miles north-northeast of Cambridge right at 5:54 PM  CDT. These two stations also recorded wind gusts of 60 MPH earlier in the day, between 1:30 and 2:30 PM CDT. Tree limbs up to 6 inches in diameter were downed in Cambridge, and power lines were knocked down in Arapahoe.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees were reported to be down near Route 313.

Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A roof was blown off of a house, and trees and wires were also reported to be down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front passing through the Pacific Northwest brought mostly dry and windy��conditions across the eastern half of Washington on June��24th. By early afternoon, isolated��showers and thunderstorms moved into the northern��mountains. With afternoon��convection, there were numerous��strong thunderstorm cells forming in Stevens and Pend Oreille counties. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This was an active late Saturday evening-early Sunday morning of thunderstorms across much of South Central Nebraska, featuring several reports of large hail and especially damaging winds mainly between midnight-3 a.m. CDT as two storm complexes rolled through and eventually merged. Focusing first on severe winds, most estimated or measured gusts were in the 50-70 MPH range and associated with primarily tree damage. However a few isolated structural damage reports were more suggestive of at least 75-80 MPH, including: 1) 10 power poles blown down and three grain bins destroyed (along with some overturned irrigation pivots) west of Aurora...2) grain bin damage and overturned pivots north of Minden. Hail was more limited overall, but stones reached golf ball size at Pauline and ping pong ball size in Davenport, while Hastings saw nickel to quarter size hail. Rainfall amounts varied considerably (most of South Central Nebraska had less than one-half inch), but a fairly narrow swath of at least 1.50-2.50 targeted parts of primarily Thayer/Nuckolls/Clay counties, with one unofficial report as high as 3.17 near Belvidere. Flooding was fairly minimal, although one rural road along the Fillmore/Thayer County line still had water running across it around sunrise. ||As for storm mode/evolution, this was a somewhat complex event. The first local convection of the night entered the Furnas County area out of northwest Kansas after 11 p.m. CDT, in the form of a compact linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) on a weakening trend. But then, between midnight-1 a.m. CDT, a broken band of intense, semi-discrete storms erupted out ahead of this MCS along a west-east axis centered from Phelps-Adams-Thayer counties (likely in response to the onset of a healthy low level jet). However, these initially semi-discrete storms (which accounted for all large hail reports) quickly consolidated/grew upscale into a new linear MCS that charged north-northeast across the Highway 6/Interstate 80 corridors between 1-2 a.m. CDT, gradually merging with the initial MCS racing up from the southwest in the process. During the ensuing hour, the two complexes completed a full merger; the northern end weakening as it reached far northeastern counties (such as Nance/Polk), while the southern end remained severe through Fillmore/Thayer counties before departing the local area into southeast Nebraska. This ended any severe threat for the night, although weaker storms and broader showers persisted until around sunrise in some spots. This was a ripe setup for severe nocturnal storms, especially with the exit region of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars) aimed into the heart of South Central Nebraska after dark, and tapping into a large reservoir of most-unstable CAPE as high as 2000-3000 J/kg. In the mid-upper levels, flow over the region was not overly-strong, but contained various low-amplitude disturbances and was in the process of transitioning more southwesterly in response to a larger-scale trough setting up over the northwestern United States. There were no distinct surface features across the local area, but steady light southeast breezes prior to storm initiation maintained seasonably-high dewpoints in the mid-60s to low-70 F. Likely one of the main limiting factors against a more robust severe threat was only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.

During the ensuing hour, the two complexes completed a full merger; the northern end weakening as it reached far northeastern counties (such as Nance/Polk), while the southern end remained severe through Fillmore/Thayer counties before departing the local area into southeast Nebraska. This ended any severe threat for the night, although weaker storms and broader showers persisted until around sunrise in some spots. This was a ripe setup for severe nocturnal storms, especially with the exit region of a 30-40 knot southerly low level jet (evident at 850 millibars) aimed into the heart of South Central Nebraska after dark, and tapping into a large reservoir of most-unstable CAPE as high as 2000-3000 J/kg. In the mid-upper levels, flow over the region was not overly-strong, but contained various low-amplitude disturbances and was in the process of transitioning more southwesterly in response to a larger-scale trough setting up over the northwestern United States. There were no distinct surface features across the local area, but steady light southeast breezes prior to storm initiation maintained seasonably-high dewpoints in the mid-60s to low-70 F. Likely one of the main limiting factors against a more robust severe threat was only modest deep-layer wind shear around 30 knots.

On the evening of Tuesday the 2nd into the very early morning of Wednesday the 3rd, a cluster of strong to briefly-severe thunderstorms rumbled through the southwestern quadrant of South Central Nebraska (primarily affecting counties south of Interstate 80 and west of Highway 281). While most of this activity was sub-severe, a briefly-more-intense storm prompted a lone report of quarter size hail near Stamford around 10:45 p.m. CDT (penny size hail occurred in Beaver City shortly before this). ||Initially, South Central Nebraska remained mostly storm-free during the peak heating of late afternoon/early evening, but not by very far, as counties slightly to the west within southwest Nebraska and northwest Kansas saw a few strong to severe storms develop near a slow-moving cold front. Eventually, between 8-10 p.m. CDT, a loosely-organized cluster of multicell convection that evolved from this early activity propagated east into far southwestern local counties. Then, between 10 p.m. and midnight CDT a few embedded cells intensified enough to prompt severe thunderstorm warnings for parts of Furnas/Harlan/Phelps counties (although the quarter size hail near Stamford was the only ground-truth verification). After midnight, the dominant cell within the cluster gradually weakened as it traversed parts of Franklin/Kearney counties, dissipating by 2 a.m. CDT over western Adams County. While the evening mesoscale environment in South Central Nebraska was obviously sufficient for a marginally-severe storm, it was not supportive of widespread severe activity given that respectable mixed-layer CAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg was offset by weak deep-layer wind shear of no more than 25 knots. In the mid-upper levels, the local area resided under fairly anemic quasi-zonal flow, as the primary upper jet (and resultant stronger shear) resided farther north over the Dakotas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: It's quite rare that widespread/severe NON-thunderstorm winds take center stage over thunderstorms during June in South Central Nebraska, but that's exactly what happened on this Tuesday as an anomalously strong low pressure system (by June standards) churned through the Central Plains. For the vast majority of the local area, the number one story was several hours of intense north winds, commonly sustained 30-40 MPH and gusting 40-60+ MPH in the wake of a powerful late-spring cold front. Based on a variety of official/unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 67 MPH in Doniphan, 65 MPH near Gothenburg, Roseland and Oxford, and 64 MPH at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Other official peak airport gusts included 62 MPH at Hastings and 60 MPH in Kearney.  These winds undoubtedly caused numerous instances of at least minor damage within the area, but a few known ones included: a large tree in Holdrege fell on a car and blocked a street; a few large branches in west Hastings crashed onto power lines and at least one house; downed power lines in Arapahoe and Harvard; 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs downed in Deshler. Although the overall-strongest winds started/ended several hours earlier in far western local counties compared to far eastern counties, for the majority of the area the worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-10 p.m. CDT time frame.||Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening, the vast majority of the area was spared severe storms. This was mainly due to the strong surface cold front passing through prior to robust development being able to get going (in fact most of the area had seasonably-cool temperatures in the 50s-60s during the afternoon). That being said, a few severe storms did flare up in eastern counties during the afternoon, including one elevated hailer that dropped stones to around golf ball size in the Henderson and Hampton areas. Farther southeast along the actual front, radar indicated severe wind/hail potential with near-surface-based storms in/near Thayer County, but there were no verifying reports (although gustnado activity was noted in far southeastern Thayer County). Rainfall-wise, 24-hour totals fell short of forecast expectations across the majority of the area, as most places measured less than 1 inch. However, a few localized pockets closer to 2 inches occurred primarily in portions of southern Thayer and southwestern Buffalo counties, including a very isolated bullseye of 2.80 at Hubbell.||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east across northern KS over the course of the day, deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, far southeast counties dodged a potentially significant threat during the afternoon as the environment just north of the northern KS surface low became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes. In fact, mesoscale parameters in the Thayer County area briefly featured a potent combination of mixed-layer CAPE around 2000 J/kg, deep layer wind shear of 50-70 knots and 0-1 kilometer shear of 20-30 knots. As for the unusual nature of such intense northerly winds so late in the spring, it's worth noting that howling speeds of 50-70 knots a few thousand feet above the ground (at 850 millibars) registered 3-4 standard deviations above normal for the date...basically off the charts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak wind gusts were estimated to be near 60 MPH based on surrounding area observations. Emergency management reported that 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs were downed in Deshler.

The largest hail was the size of a tennis ball, which occurred in Morton County. The strongest wind gust was 75 mph, and occurred in Bottineau County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Shingles were blown off of a roof on Jefferson Avenue, with tree limbs also blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Complex upper level pattern across the western half of the CONUS, with broad troughing up and down the Pacific Coast and ridging extending north from the Central Plains into Northern Alberta/Saskatchewan. Within the base of the trough axis a robust |shortwave quickly lifts north northeastward from the eastern Great Basin/Central Rockies. This shortwave continues to quickly lift northeastward to over Eastern Montana. All the while an area of low pressure develops over southeast Montana and retrogrades northwest towards the Montana/Alberta/Saskatchewan borders by Sunday morning. This allows for numerous showers and thunderstorms to develop and lift northeast across the CWA through the remainder of the afternoon and into the morning hours on Sunday. Anomalously high precipitable water, characterized by values of 0.75 to 1.25,  continue to stream northward within southerly mid- to upper level flow through the night, allowing showers/storms to be efficient rain producers. Daytime heating and surface dewpoints in the mid 40s to mid 50s allow the atmosphere to become marginally unstable, which combined with 0-6km bulk shear of 40- 50kts continues to support the potential for at least some isolated severe thunderstorms through the evening hours despite widespread cloud cover. The biggest threat from any elevated storm over this time frame is large hail approaching half dollar size; however, can't rule out some damaging wind gusts of 60-70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large tree blown down on Madison/Gilbert Street in Helena. Wind speed and gust estimate not reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of Tuesday the 2nd into the very early morning of Wednesday the 3rd, a cluster of strong to briefly-severe thunderstorms rumbled through the southwestern quadrant of South Central Nebraska (primarily affecting counties south of Interstate 80 and west of Highway 281). While most of this activity was sub-severe, a briefly-more-intense storm prompted a lone report of quarter size hail near Stamford around 10:45 p.m. CDT (penny size hail occurred in Beaver City shortly before this). ||Initially, South Central Nebraska remained mostly storm-free during the peak heating of late afternoon/early evening, but not by very far, as counties slightly to the west within southwest Nebraska and northwest Kansas saw a few strong to severe storms develop near a slow-moving cold front. Eventually, between 8-10 p.m. CDT, a loosely-organized cluster of multicell convection that evolved from this early activity propagated east into far southwestern local counties. Then, between 10 p.m. and midnight CDT a few embedded cells intensified enough to prompt severe thunderstorm warnings for parts of Furnas/Harlan/Phelps counties (although the quarter size hail near Stamford was the only ground-truth verification). After midnight, the dominant cell within the cluster gradually weakened as it traversed parts of Franklin/Kearney counties, dissipating by 2 a.m. CDT over western Adams County. While the evening mesoscale environment in South Central Nebraska was obviously sufficient for a marginally-severe storm, it was not supportive of widespread severe activity given that respectable mixed-layer CAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg was offset by weak deep-layer wind shear of no more than 25 knots. In the mid-upper levels, the local area resided under fairly anemic quasi-zonal flow, as the primary upper jet (and resultant stronger shear) resided farther north over the Dakotas.

This Wednesday evening featured the first somewhat-widespread severe thunderstorm event of 2020 within South Central Nebraska, with several reports of damaging winds and large hail focused primarily near and northeast of a line from Loup City-Grand Island-Hebron. Overall, damaging winds were the bigger issue, highlighted by a measured gust of 79 MPH at the York airport shortly before 10 p.m. CDT. As these winds tore into town, they took down several large tree branches (a few entire trees), causing fairly widespread power outages and even partially-crushing an unoccupied car. About an hour before reaching York, measured winds of 70 MPH struck the Chapman area, flipping over irrigation pivots and taking down a light pole at a convenience store. Later in the evening, shortly before storms completely exited the local area, estimated 70 MPH winds took down a giant tree limb in Alexandria (3 ft. diameter/50 ft. long). Although the majority of wind damage focused within eastern counties, severe-criteria gusts were ongoing even as storms first entered the local area earlier in the evening, including 64 MPH at Ord airport. As for hail, the majority of limited reports were quarter size or smaller, although a few stones up to golf ball size were noted in North Loup.||Breaking down event timing and evolution, the scattered to numerous storms that eventually infiltrated South Central Nebraska first developed as separate storm clusters during the mid-late afternoon, one over northwest Nebraska and another in the NE/KS/CO border area. Between 7-9 p.m. CDT, both of these clusters entered northern and western portions of the local area. The southern one, which had been occasionally severe over southwest Nebraska, lost some steam as it moved east, yielding only slightly sub-severe wind gust reports in Furnas County. Meanwhile, the northern storm complex clearly established itself as dominant, charging southeastward as damaging winds peaked in intensity between 8:30-11:30 p.m. CDT. Shortly before midnight, the back edge of the now linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) exited southeast out of Thayer County, ending all storm activity for the night. Turning to the meteorological setup, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature in the mid-upper levels consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features across South Central Nebraska ahead of the storms were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and southerly-to-easterly breezes only around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, with damaging wind potential likely enhanced by fairly large surface dewpoint depressions heading into the evening (on the order of 25-30 degrees F). Evening mesoscale analysis over South Central Nebraska revealed 1000-2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and around 35-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot and muggy conditions prevailed over the area as the region had been on the backside of an Atlantic Ridge in the warm sector of an unstable air mass.  A strengthening area of low pressure began to cross the region by midday along with a surface cold front.  A compact shortwave upper level trough dug into the region from Ontario increased the mid-level shear over New Hampshire. Two distinct rounds of thunderstorms crossed the state with the first pre-frontal trough bringing damaging wind gusts around noon, with a second round of damaging thunderstorms by mid-afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorm wind gusts downed multiple healthy trees between Cove Road and Leisure  Lane.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of June 28th, a warm front was draped across central New Hampshire. A very moist air mass was in place as thunderstorms begin to develop along this frontal boundary. Storms continued to train across the same area along this boundary with very high rainfall rates, which led to localized flash flooding across Carroll County. In addition, a few thunderstorms resulted in hail.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms dumped 3 to 5 inches of rain in 3 hours causing flooding on Walsh Road and Lovell Lake Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed in the afternoon along a frontal boundary aligned north to south over the western and central parts of North Dakota. Initially, storms formed along the northern portions of the boundary, then developed south. A highly visible tornado developed over southern Morton County in the evening, then two tornadoes developed within minutes of each other in Bottineau County, with the second one damaging two properties. The largest hail was the size of a tennis ball, which occurred in Morton County. The strongest wind gust was 75 mph, and occurred in Bottineau County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado touched down west-southwest of Breien. The tornado produced no damage to evaluate and so by National Weather Service policy was rated EF Unknown.

Tornado winds were estimated, based on the damage done, at around 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of long period swell, gusty northeast to east winds, and astronomical influences from the lunar perigee supported a moderate risk of rip currents for the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tybee Island lifeguards reported numerous moderate to strong rip currents along the entire length of Tybee Island Beach, some of which were the largest they have experienced in years. At least 7 people had been rescued during the day.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms impacted central Pennsylvania on June 4, 2020. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Across Coal Mine Road, a tree was blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Complex upper level pattern across the western half of the CONUS, with broad troughing up and down the Pacific Coast and ridging extending north from the Central Plains into Northern Alberta/Saskatchewan. Within the base of the trough axis a robust |shortwave quickly lifts north northeastward from the eastern Great Basin/Central Rockies. This shortwave continues to quickly lift northeastward to over Eastern Montana. All the while an area of low pressure develops over southeast Montana and retrogrades northwest towards the Montana/Alberta/Saskatchewan borders by Sunday morning. This allows for numerous showers and thunderstorms to develop and lift northeast across the CWA through the remainder of the afternoon and into the morning hours on Sunday. Anomalously high precipitable water, characterized by values of 0.75 to 1.25,  continue to stream northward within southerly mid- to upper level flow through the night, allowing showers/storms to be efficient rain producers. Daytime heating and surface dewpoints in the mid 40s to mid 50s allow the atmosphere to become marginally unstable, which combined with 0-6km bulk shear of 40- 50kts continues to support the potential for at least some isolated severe thunderstorms through the evening hours despite widespread cloud cover. The biggest threat from any elevated storm over this time frame is large hail approaching half dollar size; however, can't rule out some damaging wind gusts of 60-70 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Metal fence panels blown over at Catamount Street and Blackbird Drive. Branches broken in the city of Bozeman. Wind speed and gust estimate not reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An offshore trough swung inland into the Inland Northwest on June 12th. With it, a shortwave took on a strong negative tilt and moved in a moist, very unstable air mass.  This brought strong to locally severe thunderstorms through far eastern Washington and southern Idaho Panhandle. A few large cells moved through the Idaho Panhandle counties of Latah and Nez Perce in the afternoon and early evening hours. These storms produced small hail, winds with gusts to 25 mph, and isolated lightning. Rain was light in Lewiston, but there was a funnel cloud reported outside the Lewiston area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A storm chaser reported a brief funnel cloud with an area of convection approaching the Lewiston area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front passing through the Pacific Northwest brought mostly dry and windy��conditions across the Idaho Panhandle on June��24th. By mid-day, isolated��showers and thunderstorms moved into the northern��Idaho Panhandle. With afternoon��convection, there were numerous��strong thunderstorm cells forming in Bonner and Boundary counties. These thunderstorms brought gusty winds, brief heavy downpours, and produced isolated hail. There were reports of hail sizing from 0.25 to 1.5 inches in diameter. With the hail, some locations received an additional rainfall up to 1 inch that afternoon. The winds, with gusts up to 55 mph, resulted in trees down, power outages, and rough lake conditions, especially at Lake Pend Oreille and Priest Lake. Other locations within the Idaho Panhandle, only received a trace to 0.03 inch of rain. There were widespread winds with gusts reaching 25-40 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported downed trees on power lines across Elmira Road due to thunderstorm winds. Time of report was estimated based on radar.

A broad closed off upper low drifted across South Carolina and northwest back into southwest Virginia and West Virginia bringing persistent rainfall that eventually led to flooding. There were repeated rounds of heavy rainfall with widespread amounts of 2 to 5 inches. The  most notable rainfall was a fairly localized thunderstorm near Alderson, WV that caused severe flash flood damage on the afternoon of June 17th.

Dark Hollow Road was flooded out and the bridge possibly damaged. At least one person was reported trapped in their home and requiring rescue. Follow-up reports mentioned several mudslide and some very significant road and culvert damage in parts of the area.

Radar-estimated rainfall of 2 to 4 inches in less than 3 hours occurred near and south of Tannersville in Tazewell County and in far northern Smyth County near Broadford.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This Wednesday evening featured the first somewhat-widespread severe thunderstorm event of 2020 within South Central Nebraska, with several reports of damaging winds and large hail focused primarily near and northeast of a line from Loup City-Grand Island-Hebron. Overall, damaging winds were the bigger issue, highlighted by a measured gust of 79 MPH at the York airport shortly before 10 p.m. CDT. As these winds tore into town, they took down several large tree branches (a few entire trees), causing fairly widespread power outages and even partially-crushing an unoccupied car. About an hour before reaching York, measured winds of 70 MPH struck the Chapman area, flipping over irrigation pivots and taking down a light pole at a convenience store. Later in the evening, shortly before storms completely exited the local area, estimated 70 MPH winds took down a giant tree limb in Alexandria (3 ft. diameter/50 ft. long). Although the majority of wind damage focused within eastern counties, severe-criteria gusts were ongoing even as storms first entered the local area earlier in the evening, including 64 MPH at Ord airport. As for hail, the majority of limited reports were quarter size or smaller, although a few stones up to golf ball size were noted in North Loup.||Breaking down event timing and evolution, the scattered to numerous storms that eventually infiltrated South Central Nebraska first developed as separate storm clusters during the mid-late afternoon, one over northwest Nebraska and another in the NE/KS/CO border area. Between 7-9 p.m. CDT, both of these clusters entered northern and western portions of the local area. The southern one, which had been occasionally severe over southwest Nebraska, lost some steam as it moved east, yielding only slightly sub-severe wind gust reports in Furnas County. Meanwhile, the northern storm complex clearly established itself as dominant, charging southeastward as damaging winds peaked in intensity between 8:30-11:30 p.m. CDT. Shortly before midnight, the back edge of the now linear mesoscale convective system (MCS) exited southeast out of Thayer County, ending all storm activity for the night. Turning to the meteorological setup, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature in the mid-upper levels consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features across South Central Nebraska ahead of the storms were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and southerly-to-easterly breezes only around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, with damaging wind potential likely enhanced by fairly large surface dewpoint depressions heading into the evening (on the order of 25-30 degrees F). Evening mesoscale analysis over South Central Nebraska revealed 1000-2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and around 35-40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

This was truly a hit-and-miss, isolated to scattered event, as while storm coverage was fairly limited across the 24-county area as a whole, all four quadrants of it saw at least some convection. Overall, marginally-severe winds were the main issue, including measured gusts of 61 MPH at the Ord airport and 60 MPH at Waco, and estimated 60 MPH at Shelby, where the NWS cooperative observer reported downed tree branches up to 3 inches in diameter. Finally, one last weaker batch of storms roamed various northern/eastern counties between 1-4 a.m. CDT on Friday the 5th before all local storm activity ended for the night. Both at the surface and aloft, the same general environment that supported severe storms the prior evening remained in place for this round. In the mid-upper levels,  broad west-northwest flow containing various embedded, low-amplitude disturbances persisted over the region. At the surface, the same seasonably-hot and moderately unstable airmass persisted as well, as afternoon temperatures topped out in the low-mid 90s F with dewpoints ranging from upper 50s F in western counties to 65-70 F in the east. As strong to severe storms traversed the area in the evening, mesoscale parameters featured 1000-3000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 40 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

It's quite rare that widespread/severe NON-thunderstorm winds take center stage over thunderstorms during June in South Central Nebraska, but that's exactly what happened on this Tuesday as an anomalously strong low pressure system (by June standards) churned through the Central Plains. For the vast majority of the local area, the number one story was several hours of intense north winds, commonly sustained 30-40 MPH and gusting 40-60+ MPH in the wake of a powerful late-spring cold front. Based on a variety of official/unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 67 MPH in Doniphan, 65 MPH near Gothenburg, Roseland and Oxford, and 64 MPH at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Other official peak airport gusts included 62 MPH at Hastings and 60 MPH in Kearney.  These winds undoubtedly caused numerous instances of at least minor damage within the area, but a few known ones included: a large tree in Holdrege fell on a car and blocked a street; a few large branches in west Hastings crashed onto power lines and at least one house; downed power lines in Arapahoe and Harvard; 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs downed in Deshler. Although the overall-strongest winds started/ended several hours earlier in far western local counties compared to far eastern counties, for the majority of the area the worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-10 p.m. CDT time frame.||Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening, the vast majority of the area was spared severe storms. This was mainly due to the strong surface cold front passing through prior to robust development being able to get going (in fact most of the area had seasonably-cool temperatures in the 50s-60s during the afternoon). That being said, a few severe storms did flare up in eastern counties during the afternoon, including one elevated hailer that dropped stones to around golf ball size in the Henderson and Hampton areas. Farther southeast along the actual front, radar indicated severe wind/hail potential with near-surface-based storms in/near Thayer County, but there were no verifying reports (although gustnado activity was noted in far southeastern Thayer County). Rainfall-wise, 24-hour totals fell short of forecast expectations across the majority of the area, as most places measured less than 1 inch. However, a few localized pockets closer to 2 inches occurred primarily in portions of southern Thayer and southwestern Buffalo counties, including a very isolated bullseye of 2.80 at Hubbell.||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east across northern KS over the course of the day, deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, far southeast counties dodged a potentially significant threat during the afternoon as the environment just north of the northern KS surface low became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes. In fact, mesoscale parameters in the Thayer County area briefly featured a potent combination of mixed-layer CAPE around 2000 J/kg, deep layer wind shear of 50-70 knots and 0-1 kilometer shear of 20-30 knots. As for the unusual nature of such intense northerly winds so late in the spring, it's worth noting that howling speeds of 50-70 knots a few thousand feet above the ground (at 850 millibars) registered 3-4 standard deviations above normal for the date...basically off the charts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report received via mPING.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mesoscale convective complex moved from southeast Missouri and southwest KY into northwest Tennessee during the evening hours of June 30, 2020. The airmass across West Tennessee was very unstable and a storm became severe with damaging winds in Benton County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down in Benton County near Sulphur Creek Road and Hicks Road south of Big Sandy.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Depression Cristobal tracked across much of the mid and upper Mississippi River Valley on the morning and afternoon of June 9, 2020. Very high levels of moisture were present, bringing very heavy rainfall to much of the region, especially eastern Iowa. Rainfall amounts of 2-4 inches fell roughly west of a line from Keosauqua IA, to Burlington IA, to Guttenberg IA. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few trees were downed by wind across Briar Hill Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: It's quite rare that widespread/severe NON-thunderstorm winds take center stage over thunderstorms during June in South Central Nebraska, but that's exactly what happened on this Tuesday as an anomalously strong low pressure system (by June standards) churned through the Central Plains. For the vast majority of the local area, the number one story was several hours of intense north winds, commonly sustained 30-40 MPH and gusting 40-60+ MPH in the wake of a powerful late-spring cold front. Based on a variety of official/unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 67 MPH in Doniphan, 65 MPH near Gothenburg, Roseland and Oxford, and 64 MPH at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Other official peak airport gusts included 62 MPH at Hastings and 60 MPH in Kearney.  These winds undoubtedly caused numerous instances of at least minor damage within the area, but a few known ones included: a large tree in Holdrege fell on a car and blocked a street; a few large branches in west Hastings crashed onto power lines and at least one house; downed power lines in Arapahoe and Harvard; 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs downed in Deshler. Although the overall-strongest winds started/ended several hours earlier in far western local counties compared to far eastern counties, for the majority of the area the worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-10 p.m. CDT time frame.||Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening, the vast majority of the area was spared severe storms. This was mainly due to the strong surface cold front passing through prior to robust development being able to get going (in fact most of the area had seasonably-cool temperatures in the 50s-60s during the afternoon). That being said, a few severe storms did flare up in eastern counties during the afternoon, including one elevated hailer that dropped stones to around golf ball size in the Henderson and Hampton areas. Farther southeast along the actual front, radar indicated severe wind/hail potential with near-surface-based storms in/near Thayer County, but there were no verifying reports (although gustnado activity was noted in far southeastern Thayer County). Rainfall-wise, 24-hour totals fell short of forecast expectations across the majority of the area, as most places measured less than 1 inch. However, a few localized pockets closer to 2 inches occurred primarily in portions of southern Thayer and southwestern Buffalo counties, including a very isolated bullseye of 2.80 at Hubbell.||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east across northern KS over the course of the day, deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, far southeast counties dodged a potentially significant threat during the afternoon as the environment just north of the northern KS surface low became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes. In fact, mesoscale parameters in the Thayer County area briefly featured a potent combination of mixed-layer CAPE around 2000 J/kg, deep layer wind shear of 50-70 knots and 0-1 kilometer shear of 20-30 knots. As for the unusual nature of such intense northerly winds so late in the spring, it's worth noting that howling speeds of 50-70 knots a few thousand feet above the ground (at 850 millibars) registered 3-4 standard deviations above normal for the date...basically off the charts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Peak wind gusts were estimated to be near 60 MPH based on surrounding area observations.

Based on a variety of official/unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 67 MPH in Doniphan, 65 MPH near Gothenburg, Roseland and Oxford, and 64 MPH at Central Nebraska Regional Airport in Grand Island. Other official peak airport gusts included 62 MPH at Hastings and 60 MPH in Kearney.  These winds undoubtedly caused numerous instances of at least minor damage within the area, but a few known ones included: a large tree in Holdrege fell on a car and blocked a street; a few large branches in west Hastings crashed onto power lines and at least one house; downed power lines in Arapahoe and Harvard; 6-8 inch diameter tree limbs downed in Deshler. Although the overall-strongest winds started/ended several hours earlier in far western local counties compared to far eastern counties, for the majority of the area the worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-10 p.m. CDT time frame.||Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of South Central Nebraska during the afternoon and evening, the vast majority of the area was spared severe storms. This was mainly due to the strong surface cold front passing through prior to robust development being able to get going (in fact most of the area had seasonably-cool temperatures in the 50s-60s during the afternoon). That being said, a few severe storms did flare up in eastern counties during the afternoon, including one elevated hailer that dropped stones to around golf ball size in the Henderson and Hampton areas. Farther southeast along the actual front, radar indicated severe wind/hail potential with near-surface-based storms in/near Thayer County, but there were no verifying reports (although gustnado activity was noted in far southeastern Thayer County). Rainfall-wise, 24-hour totals fell short of forecast expectations across the majority of the area, as most places measured less than 1 inch. However, a few localized pockets closer to 2 inches occurred primarily in portions of southern Thayer and southwestern Buffalo counties, including a very isolated bullseye of 2.80 at Hubbell.||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east across northern KS over the course of the day, deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, far southeast counties dodged a potentially significant threat during the afternoon as the environment just north of the northern KS surface low became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes. In fact, mesoscale parameters in the Thayer County area briefly featured a potent combination of mixed-layer CAPE around 2000 J/kg, deep layer wind shear of 50-70 knots and 0-1 kilometer shear of 20-30 knots. As for the unusual nature of such intense northerly winds so late in the spring, it's worth noting that howling speeds of 50-70 knots a few thousand feet above the ground (at 850 millibars) registered 3-4 standard deviations above normal for the date...basically off the charts.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 63 MPH was recorded at 6:19 PM CDT by a mesonet station located 5 miles north of Inavale.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: It's quite rare that widespread/severe NON-thunderstorm winds take center stage over thunderstorms during June in North Central Kansas, but that's exactly what happened on this Tuesday as an anomalously strong low pressure system (by June standards) advanced through the Central Plains. For sure, the number one weather story across these six counties was several hours of intense north winds, commonly sustained 30-40 MPH and gusting 40-60+ MPH in the wake of a powerful late-spring cold front. Based on a variety of unofficial sensors, some of the highest afternoon-evening gusts featured: 66 MPH near Logan, 62 MPH in rural eastern Rooks County, 59 MPH near Kirwin and 58 MPH at Phillipsburg airport and also near Webber. These winds undoubtedly caused several instances of mainly minor damage within the area, but ground-truth reports were quite limited. For the majority of this area, the overall-worst winds concentrated during portions of the noon-midnight CDT time frame. Turning to thunderstorms, while non-severe activity was common across much of North Central Kansas during the late afternoon and especially evening, this area narrowly dodged a severe storm threat due mainly to a strong surface cold front and dryline passing through prior to robust development taking place along these boundaries. However, a few strong to severe storms materialized just barely off to the east-northeast within counties such as Republic KS and Thayer NE. ||Both in the mid-upper levels and at the surface, the intensity of this weather system was quite abnormal for June...more reminiscent of those that sometimes occur earlier in the spring. Aloft, a deep closed low slowly tracked from eastern CO around daybreak on the 9th to northeast KS by sunset, eventually departing the Central Plains into northern MO by sunrise on the 10th. The associated surface low center lumbered east through northern KS over the course of the day (nearly directly across the local area), deepening to around 993 millibars in the process. While the position and track of the surface low/cold front spared most of the area from severe storms, especially Jewell/Mitchell counties dodged a potentially significant threat as the environment briefly became conditionally supportive of supercells and possible tornadoes during the afternoon. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Atlantic Tropical Cyclone Cristobal lifted across Lake Superior and into northern Ontario. Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms developed on the 10th. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This tornado tracked intermittently to the north-northeast for over 7 miles, roughly 2 miles of the track in Steele County, then the remainder of the 5 miles in Grand Forks County (where it ended around 442 pm CDT). The tornado blew out the back wall of a pole shed and tore off some of its steel sheathing. It also snapped or uprooted several cottonwood and pine trees in shelterbelts along its path. Peak winds were estimated at 95 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dew points in the 70s across the region. Heat indices in Northwest Ohio reached the upper 90s during the afternoon of the 10th. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over western Ohio around 3 PM on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms began as discrete or clustered cells over western Ohio before congealing into a squall line. This squall line propagated from west to east across northern Ohio but individual cell motion was from south-southwest to north-northeast as the line moved through northern Ohio on the evening of the 10th. The main threat from severe thunderstorms were damaging winds with the strongest winds occurring in Northwest Ohio. Storms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph in the Lake Erie Islands and adjacent mainland areas of Ottawa and Erie Counties in Ohio, with wind damage across Oak Harbor, Catawba Island, Port Clinton, Marblehead, South Bass Island, and Sandusky. Another powerful segment of the line moved across Marion County, including the city of Marion, prompting sporadic damage in the city with wind gusts up to 80 mph. There was one injury with this event in Marion as a facade of a building collapsed onto a nearby vehicle. The intensity of the squall line waned as it passed east of Interstate 71, though it remained severe with sporadic wind damage. As the squall line moved east of Interstate 77 after dark, the line intensified as the storms caught up to the outflow, and backed winds ahead of the line rejuvenated the thunderstorms. Some strong storms moved across Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, producing additional wind damage before moving into Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wyandot County Sheriff Dispatch reported a tree down on County Road 330 near County Road 81.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm, moist advection during the morning and early afternoon hours of the 10th led to humid and very warm conditions.  Mean-layer CAPE of around 2000 J/kg, highest over eastern Ohio, illustrated the very unstable conditions.  A few discrete thunderstorm cells were able to form over southwest PA initially, with a few hail and wind damage reports.  However, the bulk of the severe weather was the result of the passage of a negatively-tilted upper trough and a strong cold front, which crossed during the late afternoon and evening hours. Bulk shear of 40 to 50 knots and the cold front allowed for the development of a quasi-linear convective system, resulting in widespread reports of wind damage.  Gusts of 70-80 MPH were estimated in some cases, leading to numerous reports of damage to trees and power lines, as well as mostly minor structural damage to roofing and shingles. Mesovortices in the QLCS also led to the development and confirmation of three tornadoes in the NWS Pittsburgh forecast area. The strongest was in Beaver County PA, with EF-2 damage observed.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous instances of wind damage were noted in Dellroy.
