EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two main areas of thunderstorms developing during the early afternoon hours: 1) Hi-Line due to convergence zone location (southwest and northeast surface winds), and 2) southwest/central Montana mountains due to orographic lift/terrain heating. As the |afternoon progresses and instability continues to build, thunderstorms continue to increase in areal coverage and intensity, especially across portions of southwest and central Montana where wave/left exit region of an upper level jet moves across and promotes additional lift. The threat for severe weather is maximized during the afternoon and early evening across Southwest and Central Montana where 0-6km bulk shear of 45-65kts and MLCAPE approaching 1500J/kg is found. The SPC continues to maintain a slight risk for severe thunderstorms south of a line from Helena, to Raynesford, to Winifred and generally north of the I-90 corridor; with a marginal |risk for the remainder of the CWA southeast of a Choteau to Havre line. Thunderstorms that become severe could produce large hail to the size of half dollars and wind gusts to 60 mph. In addition, these thunderstorms are  capable of producing torrential rainfall given PWATs approaching the 90% moving average.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported 55 KT winds gust.

Residents described a wispy funnel that first touched down in a field damaged a carport and uprooted several trees as it moved into a wooded area. Some minor damage occurred to an old barn as well as minor structural damage to a couple of houses.

For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.

These storms tracked through the Devils Lake region toward Hillsboro by mid to late afternoon, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 7th, 500mb ridging had set up over eastern Minnesota into Wisconsin, with southwest flow over the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. At the surface, by mid afternoon, a cold front had moved into central North Dakota, with a stationary boundary just to the east of the Red River Valley. It was hot and windy over eastern North Dakota into the Valley, with temperatures peaking in the upper 80s to upper 90s (Fargo set a record high of 99 degrees), and dew points in the 60s to low 70s. South winds were strong all day, gusting into the 45 mph range consistently. East of the Red River Valley, in northwest Minnesota, temperatures were cooler with lower wind speeds. By mid afternoon, thunderstorms flared up over northwest Minnesota. Through the rest of the late afternoon and evening, numerous severe storms occurred over eastern North Dakota into the Red River Valley, producing large hail, damaging winds, and even a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured at the Fargo airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours of June 3, 2020, then moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting the central New Jersey coast during the early afternoon hours, approximately 130 PM. Damaging winds in excess of 60 MPH were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread. Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. ||Because this derecho moved off the coast by 200 PM, the warm afternoon sun was able to sufficiently destabilize the atmosphere for the formation of another round of severe thunderstorms over some of the same areas that experience them earlier in the day. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport. The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed power poles and wires on State Highway 29 north of Pleasant Valley Road near Titusville. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured by a RWIS mesonet sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and strong Pacific storm approached the Great Basin on Friday, June 5th. Hot, dry and windy conditions preceded this moisture which led to critical fire weather conditions across a large portion of the region Friday afternoon. Grand Junction, Colorado also reached a record high of 100 degrees that day. Thunderstorms formed on the nose of the arriving moisture late in the afternoon on the 5th across the Four Corners region. A strong, northward moving outflow boundary was produced from these initial storms and survived to the Wyoming border by late in the evening. The fast movement of the boundary enhanced the wind threat from thunderstorms forming along it which led to numerous reports of strong outflow winds and localized damage. In addition, lightning and strong winds exacerbated the growth of existing fires and contributed to numerous fire starts across western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 60 mph was measured by an automated weather station west-southwest of Hiawatha.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low-level convergence along an eastward-moving surface trough axis contributed to the development of scattered thunderstorms over northern Ohio during the afternoon and early evening of the 21st. Vertical wind shear was weak. However, moderate instability and DCAPE amidst steep low-level lapse rates near 7.5C/km to 9.5C/km allowed multiple thunderstorms to generate damaging straight-line winds. There were also several instances of penny to quarter-size hail. In addition to the severe winds and hail, heavy rain over Holmes and Wayne Counties produced flooding as observed rainfall totals reached as much as 4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees down two miles NE of Andover.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dew points in the 70s across the region. Heat indices in Northwest Ohio reached the upper 90s during the afternoon of the 10th. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over western Ohio around 3 PM on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms began as discrete or clustered cells over western Ohio before congealing into a squall line. This squall line propagated from west to east across northern Ohio but individual cell motion was from south-southwest to north-northeast as the line moved through northern Ohio on the evening of the 10th. The main threat from severe thunderstorms were damaging winds with the strongest winds occurring in Northwest Ohio. Storms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph in the Lake Erie Islands and adjacent mainland areas of Ottawa and Erie Counties in Ohio, with wind damage across Oak Harbor, Catawba Island, Port Clinton, Marblehead, South Bass Island, and Sandusky. Another powerful segment of the line moved across Marion County, including the city of Marion, prompting sporadic damage in the city with wind gusts up to 80 mph. There was one injury with this event in Marion as a facade of a building collapsed onto a nearby vehicle. The intensity of the squall line waned as it passed east of Interstate 71, though it remained severe with sporadic wind damage. As the squall line moved east of Interstate 77 after dark, the line intensified as the storms caught up to the outflow, and backed winds ahead of the line rejuvenated the thunderstorms. Some strong storms moved across Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, producing additional wind damage before moving into Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Erie County Emergency Management, Sheriff Dispatch, members of the media, and trained spotters reported several areas of wind damage in the Sandusky area. Wind damage generally spanned south to north across the city. Trees, power lines, and power poles were downed across the area. A fire station on US Route 250 lost portions of its roof. The most notable damage was to the Sandusky State Theater in Downtown Sandusky. Winds in excess of 70 mph allowed for a wall of the theater to collapse and the roof to sustain major damage.

A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dew points in the 70s across the region. Heat indices in Northwest Ohio reached the upper 90s during the afternoon of the 10th. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over western Ohio around 3 PM on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms began as discrete or clustered cells over western Ohio before congealing into a squall line. This squall line propagated from west to east across northern Ohio but individual cell motion was from south-southwest to north-northeast as the line moved through northern Ohio on the evening of the 10th. The main threat from severe thunderstorms were damaging winds with the strongest winds occurring in Northwest Ohio. Storms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph in the Lake Erie Islands and adjacent mainland areas of Ottawa and Erie Counties in Ohio, with wind damage across Oak Harbor, Catawba Island, Port Clinton, Marblehead, South Bass Island, and Sandusky. Another powerful segment of the line moved across Marion County, including the city of Marion, prompting sporadic damage in the city with wind gusts up to 80 mph. There was one injury with this event in Marion as a facade of a building collapsed onto a nearby vehicle. The intensity of the squall line waned as it passed east of Interstate 71, though it remained severe with sporadic wind damage. As the squall line moved east of Interstate 77 after dark, the line intensified as the storms caught up to the outflow, and backed winds ahead of the line rejuvenated the thunderstorms. Some strong storms moved across Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, producing additional wind damage before moving into Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters and amateur radio operators reported trees and power lines downed in the Fredericksburg area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter estimated winds of 60 to 70 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 7th, 500mb ridging had set up over eastern Minnesota into Wisconsin, with southwest flow over the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. At the surface, by mid afternoon, a cold front had moved into central North Dakota, with a stationary boundary just to the east of the Red River Valley. South winds were strong all day, gusting into the 45 mph range consistently. East of the Red River Valley, in northwest Minnesota, temperatures were cooler with lower wind speeds. By mid afternoon, thunderstorms flared up over northwest Minnesota. Through the rest of the late afternoon and evening, numerous severe storms occurred over eastern North Dakota into the Red River Valley, producing large hail, damaging winds, and even a tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours of June 3, 2020, then moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting the central New Jersey coast during the early afternoon hours, approximately 130 PM. Damaging winds in excess of 60 MPH were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread. Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The wind gust was measured by a NDAWN mesonet sensor.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and strong Pacific storm approached the Great Basin on Friday, June 5th. Hot, dry and windy conditions preceded this moisture which led to critical fire weather conditions across a large portion of the region Friday afternoon. Grand Junction, Colorado also reached a record high of 100 degrees that day. Thunderstorms formed on the nose of the arriving moisture late in the afternoon on the 5th across the Four Corners region. A strong, northward moving outflow boundary was produced from these initial storms and survived to the Wyoming border by late in the evening. The fast movement of the boundary enhanced the wind threat from thunderstorms forming along it which led to numerous reports of strong outflow winds and localized damage. In addition, lightning and strong winds exacerbated the growth of existing fires and contributed to numerous fire starts across western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A peak wind gust of 70 mph was measured by the automated weather station at the Meeker Coulter Field Airport.

Some of the storms were huge, and exhibited structure found in springtime tornadic supercells (storms with rotating updrafts). In this case, rotation was found well aloft (10,000 to 15,000 feet), and did not make it to the ground. No Tornado Warnings were issued. Trees were uprooted at Arkadelphia (Clark County), Delight (Pike County), and just north of Star City (Lincoln County). At Donaldson (Hot Spring County), downed trees fell on a house and a vehicle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low-level convergence along an eastward-moving surface trough axis contributed to the development of scattered thunderstorms over northern Ohio during the afternoon and early evening of the 21st. Vertical wind shear was weak. However, moderate instability and DCAPE amidst steep low-level lapse rates near 7.5C/km to 9.5C/km allowed multiple thunderstorms to generate damaging straight-line winds. There were also several instances of penny to quarter-size hail. In addition to the severe winds and hail, heavy rain over Holmes and Wayne Counties produced flooding as observed rainfall totals reached as much as 4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter-size hail at Northside Christian Church, located about three miles north of Wadsworth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and lower 90s and dew points in the 70s across the region. Heat indices in Northwest Ohio reached the upper 90s during the afternoon of the 10th. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over western Ohio around 3 PM on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms began as discrete or clustered cells over western Ohio before congealing into a squall line. This squall line propagated from west to east across northern Ohio but individual cell motion was from south-southwest to north-northeast as the line moved through northern Ohio on the evening of the 10th. The main threat from severe thunderstorms were damaging winds with the strongest winds occurring in Northwest Ohio. Storms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph in the Lake Erie Islands and adjacent mainland areas of Ottawa and Erie Counties in Ohio, with wind damage across Oak Harbor, Catawba Island, Port Clinton, Marblehead, South Bass Island, and Sandusky. Another powerful segment of the line moved across Marion County, including the city of Marion, prompting sporadic damage in the city with wind gusts up to 80 mph. There was one injury with this event in Marion as a facade of a building collapsed onto a nearby vehicle. The intensity of the squall line waned as it passed east of Interstate 71, though it remained severe with sporadic wind damage. As the squall line moved east of Interstate 77 after dark, the line intensified as the storms caught up to the outflow, and backed winds ahead of the line rejuvenated the thunderstorms. Some strong storms moved across Trumbull and Mahoning Counties, producing additional wind damage before moving into Pennsylvania.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotters and amateur radio operators reported trees and power lines downed in the Smithville area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and an isolated damaging microburst occurred.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter reported 6 inches of rain in 3 hours.

A tight pressure gradient between a subtropical high in the Atlantic and Tropical Depression Cristobal over the Yucatan Peninsula helped to loft deep tropical moisture into South Florida. An outflow boundary racing northward from Cuba and strengthening southwesterly flow in the upper levels in association with an upper-level trough over the northern Gulf of Mexico provided sufficient lift and enough synoptic ascent for thunderstorms to develop in the afternoon and evening hours. With the abundant moisture in place, flash flooding occurred across Palm Beach. A Flood Watch was in Effect through 8PM EDT June 6.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tequesta Police Department reported numerous streets flooded in the town from significant flooding. Streets included: Old Dixie Highway, Country Club Drive, Fairway West, Riverside Drive, and Yacht Club Place. Water was between waist and knee high in these areas. Several vehicles had to be towed/pushed from deep water. Over 4 inches of rain was measured by nearby gauges, with hourly rates of over 3 inches per hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm developed in the warm sector region south of an approaching, weakening cold front. As high pressure slid east off into the Atlantic Ocean, southeast flow increased, enhancing moisture throughout the column. Daytime heated steepened lapse rates which destabilized the atmosphere. A thunderstorm was able to capitalize on available instability to producing damaging winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts downed power lines and trees across the Montz area. A mobile home canopy was damaged by thunderstorm wind gusts on Hollywood Park Drive.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: NWS employee reported winds of 60 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: By the morning of June 9 remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal pushed north into Iowa, drenching central and eastern Iowa for most of the day before lifting into the Great Lakes region by evening. The quick exit of Cristobal was due in part to a strong shortwave moving across the northern plains that helped to kick Cristobal from the area. This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public recorded 3.00 inches of rainfall over the last 24 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public works director for La Porte City, IA reported over 75 homes impacted from the flooding with some homes reporting flooding impacts that extended to include both basements and part of the main level of the home. Flooding continued to block roads in town in areas that hadn't seen flood impacts since widespread flooding from the floods of 2008.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overnight convection across the central plains moved into Iowa during the early morning hours of June 28th. While storms had diminished in strength, a damaging wind gust did occur. The precipitation associated with this mesoscale convective vortex continued to weaken through the morning, however, the environment in its wake exhibited high low-level vorticity that supported funnel cloud development later in the day.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two funnel clouds spotted with storms northwest of Lake City, Iowa.

For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hail ranged in size from 2 to 3 inches in diameter.

On June 7th, 500mb ridging had set up over eastern Minnesota into Wisconsin, with southwest flow over the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. At the surface, by mid afternoon, a cold front had moved into central North Dakota, with a stationary boundary just to the east of the Red River Valley. It was hot and windy over eastern North Dakota into the Valley, with temperatures peaking in the upper 80s to upper 90s (Fargo set a record high of 99 degrees), and dew points in the 60s to low 70s. South winds were strong all day, gusting into the 45 mph range consistently. East of the Red River Valley, in northwest Minnesota, temperatures were cooler with lower wind speeds. By mid afternoon, thunderstorms flared up over northwest Minnesota. Through the rest of the late afternoon and evening, numerous severe storms occurred over eastern North Dakota into the Red River Valley, producing large hail, damaging winds, and even a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hail fell along Interstate 29, near the sugar beet plant.

A derecho developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours of June 3, 2020, then moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting the central New Jersey coast during the early afternoon hours, approximately 130 PM. Damaging winds in excess of 60 MPH were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread. Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. ||Because this derecho moved off the coast by 200 PM, the warm afternoon sun was able to sufficiently destabilize the atmosphere for the formation of another round of severe thunderstorms over some of the same areas that experience them earlier in the day. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport. The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree on U.S. Highway 130 southbound south of Browning Road in Pennsauken. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of thunderstorms, some of them severe, moved from northwest to southeast across southeastern Pennsylvania during the mid-morning hours on Wednesday, June 3rd.  Then a derecho, which developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours, moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting off the New Jersey coast by early afternoon (130 PM). Damaging winds associated with this derecho were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread.  Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey.  Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows:  83 MPH at Reading Regional Airport (Berks County), 76 MPH in Pottstown (Montgomery County), 75 MPH in Malvern (Chester County), and 71 MPH in the Holmesburg section of Philadelphia.  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning, heavy rain, and a few instances of hail were also reported throughout the area.  ||Tragically, four deaths were reported in eastern Pennsylvania as a result of these severe wind gusts.  Three fatalities in Montgomery County were due directly to falling trees.  The fourth fatality in Delaware County was due to a house fire caused by an electrical malfunction from a fallen tree.  This is the highest number of fatalities from a derecho event in Pennsylvania since 1950.  ||Over 208,000 power outages were reported in southeastern Pennsylvania as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. Numerous road closures were also reported due to fallen trees.|A seven story 150 unit apartment building took severe roof damage in Lansdale Borough, Montgomery County. The Montgomery County Community Based COVID-19 Testing Site shut down at noon due to the storms. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport.  The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours. Initially, many of these storms contained strong enough outflow winds to produce damage to trees as well as a couple of structures. As these storms moved farther east of U.S. Highway 23 into the mid evening hours closer to sunset, they weakened below severe limits. Additionally, stronger upper level forcing across northern to central Kentucky versus southern Kentucky helped to spare southeast Kentucky from any damaging winds.||As the cold front moved through during the late evening hours to just after midnight, strong winds accompanied the frontal passage across isolated portions of Floyd and Pike Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Kentucky Transportation Cabinet reported a tree downed along Kentucky Highway 89 near Foxtown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed over Southeast Texas during the mid and late afternoon hours, along the tail end of an upper trough axis that extended from Western Arkansas across Western Louisiana and extreme Eastern Texas. Afternoon temperatures in the lower 90s within the moist air mass contributed to moderate instability developing as these storms shifted north-northeast, with an isolated severe thunderstorm developing as it moved along the Cherokee/Angelina County Texas line. This storm produced damaging winds which downed power lines just southeast of Wells before quickly weakening as it moved into Southwest Nacogdoches County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Power lines were downed on County Road 2 just southeast of Wells.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed this afternoon and evening in the vicinity of a slow-moving upper level low pressure system. Several storms briefly became strong, with one producing large hail across portions of Jackson County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Citizens observed hail up to the size of quarters from McKee to Tyner.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thick morning clouds and rain held temperatures down east of the Red River Valley on June 20th. Breaks in the clouds along and west of the Valley allowed for afternoon heating and highs in the low to mid 70s. Although most severe ingredients were marginal, there was a cold pool aloft that helped sustain several pulse (briefly severe) storms. Most of these storms produced hail, although there were also a few funnel cloud reports.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hail was mostly nickel sized, but a few were up to 1.25 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The severe weather outbreak on Wednesday, June 17th, had a similar set up to the ones from June 7th and 8th. By the mid afternoon of June 17th, a stationary boundary was located over the central Dakotas, with eastern North Dakota and the adjacent area of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. Temperatures in the warm sector peaked in the upper 80s to middle 90s, with dew points in the 60s to around 70 degrees. The 500mb pattern featured ridging over the Great Lakes, with southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. A lone thunderstorm initially formed over western Marshall County (Minnesota), and tracked northeast, passing west of Roseau. By that time, additional storms had formed between Jamestown and Grand Forks. This line of storms then tracked to the northeast, passing through the central and northern Red River Valley and Lake of the Woods region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Considerable tree damage was reported in town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very moist and strong Pacific storm approached the Great Basin on Friday, June 5th. Hot, dry and windy conditions preceded this moisture which led to critical fire weather conditions across a large portion of the region Friday afternoon. Grand Junction, Colorado also reached a record high of 100 degrees that day. Thunderstorms formed on the nose of the arriving moisture late in the afternoon on the 5th across the Four Corners region. A strong, northward moving outflow boundary was produced from these initial storms and survived to the Wyoming border by late in the evening. The fast movement of the boundary enhanced the wind threat from thunderstorms forming along it which led to numerous reports of strong outflow winds and localized damage. In addition, lightning and strong winds exacerbated the growth of existing fires and contributed to numerous fire starts across western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service employee estimated a peak wind gust of 60 mph. A large portion of the employee's fence was blown down as a result of the winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper ridge was west of Arkansas and not directly over the state allowing thunderstorms to develop around its eastern periphery. Trees were knocked down at Lead Hill (Boone County).||During the afternoon of the 5th, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked through eastern sections of the state from north to south producing severe weather. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low-level convergence along an eastward-moving surface trough axis contributed to the development of scattered thunderstorms over northern Ohio during the afternoon and early evening of the 21st. However, moderate instability and DCAPE amidst steep low-level lapse rates near 7.5C/km to 9.5C/km allowed multiple thunderstorms to generate damaging straight-line winds. In addition to the severe winds and hail, heavy rain over Holmes and Wayne Counties produced flooding as observed rainfall totals reached as much as 4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and dew points in the 70s across Northwest Pennsylvania. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over Ohio during the afternoon hours on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms over Ohio morphed into a squall line and reached Northwest Pennsylvania after dark on the 10th. This squall line produced damaging wind gusts in Erie and Crawford Counties with estimated wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Crawford County was hit hardest during the event with widespread tree damage noted in the western half of the county, including several falling onto cars.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Erie County Sheriff Dispatch reported trees down across Lunger Road in Harborcreek Township.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and an isolated damaging microburst occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six utility poles were broken on the west side of Paducah.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge across much of the midwest brought the first round of summer-like temperatures to the area in early June. By late in the day a shortwave moving across the northern plains flattened the nose of the ridge a pulled a cool front across northern Iowa. Convection developed along this boundary in the evening in the form of gusty winds across northern Iowa. Convection then diminished overnight as the front continued to sink south across the state. By early morning the front had made it to central Iowa where storms restrengthened, dropping large hail and producing gusty winds. By mid-morning the front had pushed south of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of golf ball sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station reported a 24 hour rain total of of 2.20 inches.

A stationary front was draped from the Carolina's through the northeastern Bahamas, with a zone of deeper moistures situated across South Florida. Prevailing east-southeasterly flow allowed for both the Gulf Atlantic sea breeze to progress inland through peak heating hours. Several pockets of cooler, drier air aloft worked in concert with steepening low-level lapses to produce sufficient accent for showers and thunderstorms to develop within the saturated airmass. Collisions between the sea breeze boundaries and additional outflow boundaries resulted in a few stronger storms that produced a funnel cloud and flooding across Palm Beach.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: CoCoRaHS reported a 24 hour rain total of 2.04 inches.

Between 9 p.m. and midnight CDT on this Wednesday evening, a smattering of mostly-weak thunderstorms rumbled from west-to-east across portions of this six-county North Central Kansas area, as the vast majority of severe storms in the region focused at least slightly off to the north and east. However, between 10:30-11:15 p.m. CDT, one small storm cluster flared up to severe levels over Jewell County, yielding a lone ground-truth report of measured 68 MPH winds in the far northeast corner of the county near Webber. Radar also indicated that this storm might have produced severe-criteria hail over mainly central sections of the county, but there were no verifying reports. In the mid-upper levels, this was not a strongly-forced event, with the main feature consisting of a low-amplitude shortwave trough tracking east-southeast across Nebraska out of western SD over the course of the afternoon-evening. Surface features in North Central Kansas during the evening were fairly nondescript, dominated by weak high pressure and generally southerly breezes around 10 MPH or less. However, fairly steep low-mid level lapse rates were in place, as evening mesoscale analysis revealed around 2000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 35 knots of deep-layer wind shear.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 7th, 500mb ridging had set up over eastern Minnesota into Wisconsin, with southwest flow over the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. At the surface, by mid afternoon, a cold front had moved into central North Dakota, with a stationary boundary just to the east of the Red River Valley. It was hot and windy over eastern North Dakota into the Valley, with temperatures peaking in the upper 80s to upper 90s (Fargo set a record high of 99 degrees), and dew points in the 60s to low 70s. South winds were strong all day, gusting into the 45 mph range consistently. East of the Red River Valley, in northwest Minnesota, temperatures were cooler with lower wind speeds. By mid afternoon, thunderstorms flared up over northwest Minnesota. Through the rest of the late afternoon and evening, numerous severe storms occurred over eastern North Dakota into the Red River Valley, producing large hail, damaging winds, and even a tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dime to nickel sized hail fell.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours of June 3, 2020, then moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting the central New Jersey coast during the early afternoon hours, approximately 130 PM. Damaging winds in excess of 60 MPH were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread. Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. ||Because this derecho moved off the coast by 200 PM, the warm afternoon sun was able to sufficiently destabilize the atmosphere for the formation of another round of severe thunderstorms over some of the same areas that experience them earlier in the day. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport. The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Downed tree on State Highway 47 near Broadway Avenue in Cherry Hill. Time estimated from radar.

Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. ||Because this derecho moved off the coast by 200 PM, the warm afternoon sun was able to sufficiently destabilize the atmosphere for the formation of another round of severe thunderstorms over some of the same areas that experience them earlier in the day. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport. The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees onto power lines on Borton Landing Road between Creek Road and Hartford Road in Moorestown. Some power poles leaning over the road. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of thunderstorms, some of them severe, moved from northwest to southeast across southeastern Pennsylvania during the mid-morning hours on Wednesday, June 3rd.  Then a derecho, which developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours, moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting off the New Jersey coast by early afternoon (130 PM). Damaging winds associated with this derecho were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread.  Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey.  Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows:  83 MPH at Reading Regional Airport (Berks County), 76 MPH in Pottstown (Montgomery County), 75 MPH in Malvern (Chester County), and 71 MPH in the Holmesburg section of Philadelphia.  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning, heavy rain, and a few instances of hail were also reported throughout the area.  ||Tragically, four deaths were reported in eastern Pennsylvania as a result of these severe wind gusts.  Three fatalities in Montgomery County were due directly to falling trees.  The fourth fatality in Delaware County was due to a house fire caused by an electrical malfunction from a fallen tree.  This is the highest number of fatalities from a derecho event in Pennsylvania since 1950.  ||Over 208,000 power outages were reported in southeastern Pennsylvania as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. Numerous road closures were also reported due to fallen trees.|A seven story 150 unit apartment building took severe roof damage in Lansdale Borough, Montgomery County. The Montgomery County Community Based COVID-19 Testing Site shut down at noon due to the storms. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees and power lines were blown down in the Wahpeton-Breckenridge area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Well above normal levels of tropical moisture over Martin County allowed an area of heavy showers and thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon and move slowly across an area saturated from excessive rain which fell over previous days. Flooding quickly redeveloped, with water entering into several homes, mainly in the town of Hobe Sound.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two to four inches of rain fell within two hours, across an area which received 7 to 13 inches of rain over the previous three days. With saturated soils and standing water remaining in many areas, flooding quickly developed. Flood waters entered several homes, mainly within Hobe Heights. Some homes may have experienced water intrusion two days earlier from the first period of flooding. Numerous roadways within Hobe Sound became inpassable due to high levels of standing water.

Additional damage occurred on Bristol Circle and Ashley Court where several fences were blow over, small trees toppled, medium tree branches downed, and loose backyard items tossed into adjacent properties.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted trough moved through western Colorado on the morning and afternoon of Saturday, June 6th, causing a widespread severe weather event that would become the first derecho to impact the Western Slope in well over a decade. Severe storms produced wind gusts upwards of 60 to 80 mph on average with some gusts topping 80 to 100 mph in some areas due to strong downburst winds. There were multiple reports of uprooted trees, downed power lines, at least one roof was torn off with others damaged, and several houses/cabins and vehicles were damaged by falling trees and/or large hail. Very heavy rain also fell which led to flash flooding in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Debris left over from the 2019 avalanches became dislodged by heavy rain in the Marshall Creek Basin. A large amount of trees, wood, and other debris from old mining structures travelled down the drainage until it reached the culvert near CR K-69, near the Idarado mine. The water and debris overwhelmed the drainage and began flowing across the roadway. The downstream portion of the roadway began to scour with water and eroded the embankment along the southern shoulder. The road was closed for a few hours.

A very moist and strong Pacific storm approached the Great Basin on Friday, June 5th. Hot, dry and windy conditions preceded this moisture which led to critical fire weather conditions across a large portion of the region Friday afternoon. Grand Junction, Colorado also reached a record high of 100 degrees that day. Thunderstorms formed on the nose of the arriving moisture late in the afternoon on the 5th across the Four Corners region. A strong, northward moving outflow boundary was produced from these initial storms and survived to the Wyoming border by late in the evening. The fast movement of the boundary enhanced the wind threat from thunderstorms forming along it which led to numerous reports of strong outflow winds and localized damage. In addition, lightning and strong winds exacerbated the growth of existing fires and contributed to numerous fire starts across western Colorado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service employee reported a downed power line across the road in Orchard Mesa, caused by wind gusts estimated to be around 64 mph. Additionally, a trained spotter nearby had a moderate to large tree uprooted and blown down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Three separate severe weather events affected central Pennsylvania on June 3, 2020. The first event occurred during the pre-dawn hours, as strong thunderstorms pushed southward out of the Buffalo, NY area into the northwest mountains and produced wind damage before dissipating. The second event comprised of an MCS that dropped quickly southeastward across the area during the late morning hours and produced occasional wind damage along it's path. The third event saw scattered thunderstorms, including one long-lived supercell, develop during the afternoon hours and drift southeastward through the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down trees onto wires southwest of Narvon.

On the 3rd, scattered storms popped up during the heat of the afternoon, with spotty severe weather in the north. There was quarter size hail at Mount Judea, and a tree was toppled onto a home in Parthenon (both in Newton County). Enough rain fell to flood Highway 327 southeast of Jasper (Newton County). There was also a landslide in the same area. ||Early the next morning, strong to severe storms swept from Missouri into northern Arkansas. While the storms generally weakened with time, there was a 60 mph gust measured at the airport just northwest of Harrison (Boone County). Trees were knocked down at Lead Hill (Boone County).||During the afternoon of the 5th, a cluster of thunderstorms tracked through eastern sections of the state from north to south producing severe weather. In addition, there was a whole lot more wind damage in northern and central Mississippi. Cool outflow from the storms took off to the west.||As the outflow oozed westward through central and southern Arkansas, thunderstorms erupted. Some of the storms were huge, and exhibited structure found in springtime tornadic supercells (storms with rotating updrafts). In this case, rotation was found well aloft (10,000 to 15,000 feet), and did not make it to the ground. No Tornado Warnings were issued. Trees were uprooted at Arkadelphia (Clark County), Delight (Pike County), and just north of Star City (Lincoln County). At Donaldson (Hot Spring County), downed trees fell on a house and a vehicle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Golfball sized hail was reported at UAMS in downtown Little Rock.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low-level convergence along an eastward-moving surface trough axis contributed to the development of scattered thunderstorms over northern Ohio during the afternoon and early evening of the 21st. Vertical wind shear was weak. However, moderate instability and DCAPE amidst steep low-level lapse rates near 7.5C/km to 9.5C/km allowed multiple thunderstorms to generate damaging straight-line winds. There were also several instances of penny to quarter-size hail. In addition to the severe winds and hail, heavy rain over Holmes and Wayne Counties produced flooding as observed rainfall totals reached as much as 4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two trees down in Centerburg.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal entered the western Great Lakes region on June 9th, extending a warm front across the Ohio Valley during the evening hours. A hot, moist, and tropical air mass entered the region behind the front for June 10th, resulting in high temperatures in the upper 80s and dew points in the 70s across Northwest Pennsylvania. A shortwave trough and associated surface cold front entered from the west, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop over Ohio during the afternoon hours on the 10th in the warm, unstable air mass. Storms over Ohio morphed into a squall line and reached Northwest Pennsylvania after dark on the 10th. This squall line produced damaging wind gusts in Erie and Crawford Counties with estimated wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Crawford County was hit hardest during the event with widespread tree damage noted in the western half of the county, including several falling onto cars.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Crawford County Sheriff Dispatch reported several trees down in the Conneautville area, including several trees down on vehicles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of very weak flow aloft and an anomalously unstable and moist environment along a residual outflow boundary promoted the development of thunderstorms across the mid Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys through the late afternoon into mid evening. A weak shortwave slowly advanced eastward along the bootheel of Missouri, while a weak impulse moved southeast from the northern border of Missouri. An outflow boundary was the primary focus for renewed development of thunderstorms in the afternoon. The environment was characterized by anomalously high precipitable water values, on the order of 1.8 to 2.1 inches, which is roughly 2 standard deviations above the climatological mean. A strong instability gradient existed as well, upwards of 5000 J/kg surface based cape across southern MO to northwest TN. A southwesterly inflow of 20-30 kts at 850 mb impinged on the boundary, sustaining the high precipitable water values and maximizing the convergence. Rain rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common, and pockets of damaging wind were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Six-inch tree branches were broken off.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A training thunderstorm complex during the night of June 27th into the 28th produced significant flash flooding, as well as minor river flooding on the Green River. The maximum axis of rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches occurred over portions of northwest Kentucky, just south of the cities of Owensboro and Henderson. A weak mid-level disturbance advanced east early in the morning across eastern IL. This energy helped foster thunderstorm activity across portions of southern IL, southern IN, and Kentucky. The air mass around the southern flank of the disturbance was still at least modestly unstable with mixed layer capes around 1000 j/kg early in the morning. A west-southwest low-level wind flow between 30 and 40 knots focused strong moisture transport into the storms. The storms trained over the same area for three to five hours. Precipitable water values across the region were on the order of 1.7 to 1.9 inches, fueling rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding of roads became rather widespread. Some roads were impassable. Water rescues were conducted from vehicles that were stranded in floodwaters. Rainfall amounts were heaviest in southeast parts of the county, where close to 8 inches fell in a 48-hour period. Much of that rain fell early on the 28th. A trained spotter just east of Corydon measured 7.85 inches during the daytime hours on the 28th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge across much of the midwest brought the first round of summer-like temperatures to the area in early June. By late in the day a shortwave moving across the northern plains flattened the nose of the ridge a pulled a cool front across northern Iowa. Convection developed along this boundary in the evening in the form of gusty winds across northern Iowa. Convection then diminished overnight as the front continued to sink south across the state. By early morning the front had made it to central Iowa where storms restrengthened, dropping large hail and producing gusty winds. By mid-morning the front had pushed south of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter report of nickle sized hail.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A surface low to the northwest of Iowa allowed for convection to develop in the warm sector and along the surface boundary as it pushed across northern Iowa through the afternoon and evening of the 21st. These storms caused damaging winds and large hail across northern and central Iowa. Localized areas received heavy rain that resulted in flooding overnight. Another shortwave embedded within the parent longwave trough allowed for additional rain across the state on the 22nd that lasted through the afternoon. This second round of rain exacerbated the ongoing flooded areas, resulting in flooding that lingered into the morning of the 24th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of 2.55 inches of rain in the last 24 hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A northward moving frontal boundary brought deep tropical moisture across South Florida. The abundant moisture translated into heavy rainfall across the east coast metro, where flooding materialized across areas in Palm Beach and Broward that received repeated rounds of showers and thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snap map video of street flooding occurring near the intersection of US highway 1 and 13th avenue North in Lake Worth. Water had pooled to a depth of a few inches on street.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: South-southwesterly flow allowed for deep tropical moisture to stay in place across South Florida. This prevailing flow also allowed the Gulf sea breeze to progress further inland, pinning the Atlantic sea breeze to the coast, becoming the focus for afternoon showers and thunderstorm. As a mid-upper level shortwave rotated across the region aloft through the day, coverage of thunderstorms increased along the east coast and brought gusty winds and heavy rainfall that lead to flash flooding in Broward and Palm Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public reported Flash Flooding from heavy rainfall that fell in about an hour on St. Andrews boulevard near Town Center Mall in Boca Raton that left several vehicles stranded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wet end to the 3rd week of June and continued moderate to heavy rainfalls into the middle of the 4th week of June caused rivers across the eastern portions of the Des Moines CWA to swell and reach flood stage from as little as a few hours near Tama to a few days around Cedar Falls, Waterloo, and Hudson.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Cedar River at Cedar Falls crested at 0030 UTC on June 25th at 91.78 feet. Flood stage is 89.0 feet.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved across the midwest, pulling a surface boundary across the state. In the afternoon weak convection developed along this boundary, but most storms tended to be short-lived in nature with relatively weak shear profiles. These storms resulted in mainly wind damage reports across east-central Iowa. Convection continued to bubble through the evening with continued wind damage reports. Shortly after midnight convection out of the Dakotas made it to northern Iowa. This broken line of storms pushed across the state all night, with essentially no breaks in reports of large hail and damaging winds through sunrise. Additionally, some locations received heavy rain. Storms cleared the Des Moines metro area shortly after five in the morning and diminished in strength shortly after that.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station reported a 24-hour rainfall total of 2.10 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: By the morning of June 9 remnants of Tropical Storm Cristobal pushed north into Iowa, drenching central and eastern Iowa for most of the day before lifting into the Great Lakes region by evening. The quick exit of Cristobal was due in part to a strong shortwave moving across the northern plains that helped to kick Cristobal from the area. This secondary system moved into Iowa the evening of June 9th, and while for the most part remained sub-severe, damaging winds were reported in west-central Iowa with a stronger cell.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public weather station measured 2.1 inches of rain. Beginning time estimated by radar. Rain ongoing at observation time.

Thunderstorms developed during the morning hours in an area of low level warm air advection and elevated shear. Two storms became severe with damaging wind gusts. The first storm, near Bismarck, produced a measured 87 mph wind gust which damaged a camper, trailer, and play set. The next storm, near Turtle Lake, produced estimated 80 mph wind gusts which blew down multiple barns. Additional thunderstorms developed over central North Dakota later in the day which are addressed in a separate episode for this date.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple barns were blown down by the thunderstorm wind gusts, with debris scattered a good distance away from the original location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple thunderstorms developed over central North Dakota as an upper level trough approached the area. Very strong instability was present, but thunderstorms were having trouble becoming surface based due to convection during the morning hours, which is addressed in a separate episode on this same date, keeping cloud cover over the area. One storm over Wells County became very slow moving, producing torrential rain in the Harvey area. This was preceded by rain during the morning, and followed by another round of rain in the early evening. Total rainfall amounts between six and seven inches led to flash flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A negatively tilted trough moved through eastern Utah on the morning and afternoon of Saturday, June 6th, causing a widespread severe weather event that would become the first derecho to impact the Great Basin in well over a decade. Severe storms produced large hail up to golf ball size in southeast Utah. Wind gusts upwards of 60 to 80 mph were reported on average with some gusts topping 80 to 100 mph in some areas due to strong downburst winds. There were multiple reports of uprooted trees, downed power lines, and several houses/cabins and vehicles were damaged by falling trees and/or large hail. Very heavy rain also fell which led to flash flooding in some areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A severe thunderstorm produced large hail measured to be the size of quarters at the Valley of the Gods north of Mexican Hat.

For this event, the 500mb pattern featured ridging over eastern Minnesota and Wisconsin, with south-southwest flow over eastern North Dakota and the northwest quarter of Minnesota. At the surface, by the early afternoon of June 8th, a cold front had set up along a line from Cavalier to Oakes, North Dakota, with the Red River Valley into adjacent areas of the northwest quarter of Minnesota in the warm sector. In this warm sector, temperatures ranged in the 80s with dew points around 70. By the mid afternoon, thunderstorms initially formed along the boundary over northeast North Dakota and tracked into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. By late afternoon, additional storms formed around Cooperstown, North Dakota, and also tracked northeast into the far northwest corner of Minnesota. Kittson County, Minnesota, received several rounds of heavy rainfall. By mid evening, most storms tracked between Thief River Falls and Lake of the Woods. Finally, more storms formed and tracked across portions of west central Minnesota during the early morning hours of June 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous cottonwood and ash trees were snapped or uprooted around town.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On June 7th, 500mb ridging had set up over eastern Minnesota into Wisconsin, with southwest flow over the Dakotas into northwest Minnesota. At the surface, by mid afternoon, a cold front had moved into central North Dakota, with a stationary boundary just to the east of the Red River Valley. It was hot and windy over eastern North Dakota into the Valley, with temperatures peaking in the upper 80s to upper 90s (Fargo set a record high of 99 degrees), and dew points in the 60s to low 70s. South winds were strong all day, gusting into the 45 mph range consistently. East of the Red River Valley, in northwest Minnesota, temperatures were cooler with lower wind speeds. By mid afternoon, thunderstorms flared up over northwest Minnesota. Through the rest of the late afternoon and evening, numerous severe storms occurred over eastern North Dakota into the Red River Valley, producing large hail, damaging winds, and even a tornado.

A derecho developed just southeast of Lake Erie during the early morning hours of June 3, 2020, then moved rapidly southeast across Pennsylvania before exiting the central New Jersey coast during the early afternoon hours, approximately 130 PM. Damaging winds in excess of 60 MPH were sporadic over western and central Pennsylvania, but as the thunderstorm complex moved into increasingly unstable air in the eastern part of the state just before noon, wind damage reports became more numerous and widespread. Most of these reports were confined within a 50-mile wide swath extending from Berks County eastward to the Philadelphia metro area, then further east to the Ocean County shoreline in New Jersey. Wind gust reports between 60 and 70 MPH were common within this swath, with some of the highest gusts as follows: 89 MPH in Beach Haven, 87 MPH in Brick (both in Ocean County), 76 MPH in Brielle (Monmouth County), and 67 MPH in Jacksonville (Burlington County).  In addition to these destructive wind gusts, frequent to continuous cloud to ground lightning and heavy downpours were also reported throughout the area.||Over 112,000 power outages were reported in southern New Jersey as a result |of fallen trees on power lines.  Some localities were without power for several days. ||Because this derecho moved off the coast by 200 PM, the warm afternoon sun was able to sufficiently destabilize the atmosphere for the formation of another round of severe thunderstorms over some of the same areas that experience them earlier in the day. Reported wind gusts associated with these thunderstorms generally ranged between 45 and 65 MPH, with a 65 MPH wind gust measured at the Philadelphia International Airport. The remaining thunderstorms then moved offshore by 1000 PM, which brought an end to the day's severe weather.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple large trees down and at least one power pole snapped in Cinniminson. Report via social media with photos. Time estimated from radar.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous showers and thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front by mid-late afternoon across central Kentucky, moving into eastern Kentucky during the late afternoon and evening hours.
